Free State and Northern Cape at 3 Barnes Street, Arboretum, Bloemfontein

Limpopo at Gateway Park, Polokwane

Mpumalanga at 29@Marloth, Nelspruit

And one final note, around R257 million in lottery prizes currently sits unclaimed across South Africa from the previous operator. Therefore, checking old ticket numbers against those drawn (up to one year ago) costs you nothing and might just turn up forgotten money. You can do so by clicking past results HERE.

World.title: Expats share real reasons behind return to South Africa
World.content:
An expat family are documenting their return to South Africa. Images via Instagram

Two South African expats living in the UK are documenting their decision to return home after living abroad for many years.

According to data, around one million Saffas live abroad, with substantial numbers residing in the United Kingdom, Australia, and the United States

SOUTH AFRICAN EXPAT: ‘WE’RE COMING HOME’

On his Instagram account, South African expat Jenz Robinson has been documenting the process of his family of five returning home



The gym owner and motivational speaker emigrated to the UK almost 20 years ago.

While he has set up a successful business and has made connections and friends in his adoptive country, Robinson felt compelled to return home

Robinson – who has three children with his wife, Jolsy – called the decision the “wildest ride of our lives”



He shared: “This isn’t a ‘screw the UK’ kind of post. I love it here. But Africa is calling me home.

His decision was heavily motivated by the life he wanted to provide for his children.

He continued: “We want our children to know where they come from. To grow up around family. To experience the mountains, the wildlife, and the beaches, as home”.



‘I DON’T LIKE IT HERE’

Another former South African expat, Shashika Dhupelia, has also been documenting her decision to return home on her social media platforms

For the content creator and mom-of-two, the decision to leave a “first-world country” was more about feeling disconnected from the UK.



She shared in a TikTok: “It didnt feel like the right fit. When I landed in Manchester, I got out of the airport and said, ‘I don’t like it here’. No valid reason to back up my feelings. I then spent the next year trying to make it work

Dhupelia shared how she felt detached from a community and struggled to build connections with other like-minded people

She also shared that the cost of living was unaffordable for much of the working class.



“For me, it wasn’t a first world lifestyle”, she added.

World.title: Derick Hougaard GoFundMe: How much cash has been donated?
World.content:
A GoFundMe campaign created to raise funds for embattled former Springbok Derick Hougaard continues to rake in donations from around the world.

The retired rugby player has appealed to the public for assistance, after cryptically claiming that he was in “big trouble”.

The 43-year-old – once known as the Liefling van Loftus – retired from the sport in 2015 after a series of serious head injuries. He has since faced multiple health setbacks.



DERICK HOUGAARD GOFUNDME- HOW MUCH HAS IT RAISED?

At the time of publishing, the GoFundMe campaign set up in Derick Hougaard’s name has raised close to AUD $2 200, or around R25 000.

Its target has been set at AUD 28 000, roughly R320 000.

The campaign was set by Springbok fan Lizelle Gers, who lives in Australia.

One of the biggest donors was Ockert Kruger, a former Bulls player, who played alongside Derick during their stint at the Pretoria club. He donated AUD $511 (almost R6 000) towards his pal.

WHAT WILL THE DONATIONS BE USED FOR?

Derick Hougaard’s GoFundMe campaign is listed under the “rent, food and monthly bills” category.

Campaign founder Lizelle Gers shared: “He [Derick] has recently reached out for help, and I believe this is our opportunity to stand behind someone who once gave so much to South African rugby.



“If each of us contributes just a little, together we can make a meaningful difference. No donation is too small.

“Whether you’re in South Africa or anywhere else in the world, let’s show Derick that he is not alone and that the rugby community and South Africans never forget those who have proudly represented us”.

Since his health setback in 2023, when he spent weeks in a coma after contracting respiratory pneumonia, Derick has spent extensive time in rehabilitation.

He is also believed to have spent time in a psychiatric hospital over his addiction to prescription pills.

He has likely needed financial assistance for medical and rehabilitation expenses, and possibly the inability to work because of his health.

World.title: R370 a month, 20km to the SASSA office – Northern Cape man’s reality
World.content:
A Northern Cape man knows what it means to make R370 disappear before the month is out, and unemployment isn’t making it any easier.

The man in his late forties supports between three and five dependants on the Social Relief of Distress grant. The R370 payment goes straight to food, and it’s never enough. By month end, he says there’s nothing left in his account. For the past one to three years, this grant has been his household’s main source of income, even though it was designed as short-term relief.

Distance adds to the burden

Getting help isn’t simple either. He must travel more than 20 kilometres to reach his nearest SASSA office, a trip that eats into an already stretched budget. In a province as vast as the Northern Cape, that distance also limits job opportunities, keeping residents locked into a cycle they can’t easily break.



Despite having completed matric and skills in construction and general labour, he remains unemployed and actively job hunting in a region where positions are scarce to begin with.

What SASSA could do differently?

He rates his overall SASSA experience as adequate. His payments are deposited directly into his bank account, and he’s had no issues with the application process itself. But he says he wasn’t aware of any other support programmes that might help ease the strain, a gap that could be quietly limiting his household’s options.

Asked what single change would make the biggest difference, his answer was simple: increase the grant amount. At R370 a month, the SRD grant hasn’t kept up with rising food prices, let alone transport costs or the price of searching for work. For him and millions like him nationally, the grant remains a lifeline, just one that’s stretched dangerously thin.
