World.title: Rented, stripped, relisted
World.content:
Homeowners, prospective buyers, and renters are being urged to use real estate agents to minimise their risks.

AS short-term rental scams become more sophisticated, real estate expert Roger Allen is warning that fraudsters are misusing booking platforms like Airbnb in many ways, including renting homes then illegally listing them online without the property owners’ consent, and using fake listings to swindle unsuspecting customers.

The second vice-president of the Realtors Association of Jamaica (RAJ) said the extent of booking platforms-related fraud became apparent during a meeting with the Jamaica Constabulary Force (JCF) last year, during which he and other members of the RAJ were briefed on numerous scams involving short-term rental properties.

“There are persons thinking that they have more or less rented a property or leased an Airbnb and, in terms of the payments, some of them are being urged to go outside of the platform to make payment and that sort of thing,” Allen told the Jamaica Observer.

He added that he is also aware of instances in which people rented a property listed on Airbnb, removed its furniture, then listed it for rent, bilking individuals out of thousands of dollars.

In a recent post on X, formerly Twitter, one user recounted how a woman she knew was allegedly defrauded of $190,000 through a similar scheme. According to the post, the woman signed a rental agreement and was given keys to the property, only to later discover that the house was an Airbnb rental and the individual who collected her deposit had no authority to rent it.

Allen said another emerging scam involves fraudsters renting properties legitimately before listing them on booking platforms as short-term vacation rentals without the owners’ knowledge or consent.

“In our space, in terms of the realtors in our groups…I could tell you that for last year 2025, even up to Christmas, I have seen and received information from members of over 20 instances. A number of them, I recall, have been reported…One of the things that we have found out, and the JCF has also said, is that from embarrassment and otherwise, given the circumstances of some of these situations, some of the property owners are just choosing to deal with the matter through their own ways, which again is not recommended because, as much as possible, persons need to be brought under the full book of the law,” he told the

Sunday Observer.

He noted that as these scams become increasingly sophisticated, real estate professionals are adapting their practices and strengthening verification measures to reduce the risk of fraud for both property owners and prospective tenants.

“One of the things we say to clients is that, ‘You may want to insist in the contract, in the lease agreement, that there’s no subletting of the property,’ because some of the persons even want to legitimately operate the property in short-term rentals and some of them will try to get in the property and not even disclose that if they’re going to sublet it,” said Allen.

He urged homeowners, prospective buyers, and renters to use real estate agents to minimise their risks.

“We are what you call licensed operators. We are licensed annually. It’s not that we get the licence when we do the certification and we have the licence for life. Every year we have to renew that licence, and importantly, we have continued professional development courses and other regulatory stuff in keeping with proceeds of crime, anti-money laundering, all these things, and not to mention strict guidelines in terms of the Real Estate [Dealers and] Developers Act in terms of how we operate,” insisted Allen.

He urged the public to keep an eye out for warning signs, noting that every realtor has a dealer number and a licence number that can be checked and verified. If these numbers are not displayed or an individual wants to confirm a realtors status, he said individuals can make checks to confirm the legitimacy of realtors at the Realtors Association of Jamaica website.

“Remember, scammers are looking for any and every opportunity to please persons. If you want to go and see a property, whether you want to lease it or whether you want to buy it, there is no deposit that is required. We do some vetting on all of that, but nothing like that in terms of collecting fees, so we want to alert the public in that regard,” he added.

World.title: ‘We are nowhere’
World.content:
Jamaicans must demand meaningful constitutional reform from the political directorate.

WITH Jamaica on the cusp of its 64th Independence celebrations, constitutional reform advocate Robert Stephens is urging the political directorate to end the politicisation of the country’s constitutional reform and establish an independent committee, headed by civil society, to chart the course towards Jamaica becoming a republic.

His call comes as the Government continues to blame the parliamentary Opposition for stalling the constitutional reform process, while Opposition Leader Mark Golding maintains that Jamaica’s transition to a republic should not proceed unless the Caribbean Court of Justice (CCJ) replaces the United Kingdom-based Privy Council as the country’s final appellate court.

Stephens, a member of the Advocates Network, said the failure of the previous constitutional reform process indicates that a new committee needs to be established.

“It [the Constitutional Reform Committee] shouldn’t be led by a politician. It should be led by somebody from civil society, preferably a judge, and it should have members from the two major political parties, but also from civil society. Let us seriously move now towards establishing consensus on a new approach to a new constitution, which has to include the fact that we become far more independent from the king and the queen and the monarchy. The time has come for us to get serious because that last attempt…was totally unsuccessful,” said Stephens.

He stressed that when two political parties have differences of opinion, those differences cannot be easily resolved by having someone who is a member of one party head the committee.

“What you need is some independence, and there needs to be serious dialogue about how we’re going to move towards being a republic, and that requires public education and discussion, and involving the people of every parish of the island. The approach that was taken before was definitely not the right way to do it, where a politician was, as a minister, in charge of the whole committee, and then you had selected members, which were packed with people who were mainly government appointees. I think what you need is a far more independent group that is going to seriously address all of the shortcomings of our current constitution,” he told the Jamaica Observer.

He also questioned the value taxpayers have received from the constitutional reform exercise, pointing to the millions of dollars already allocated to the process despite little tangible progress.

“That’s unacceptable. The other thing is the headquarters for the previous ministry is sitting there locked up. Now, are we paying rent for that still? Taxpayers’ money is not something to be spent idly. Really and truly, we need far more responsive and responsible governance in terms of the way that our money is being handled,” said Stephens.

Weighing in on the topic, Justice and Constitutional Affairs Minister Delroy Chuck argued that the Opposition is responsible for delaying the process after refusing to support the Constitution (Amendment) (Republic) Bill, 2024, unless it also includes provisions to replace the Privy Council with the CCJ. He called on the leader of the Opposition to resume the process.

Chuck said the Government had already conducted extensive public consultations through islandwide town hall meetings and believed there had been agreement on removing the British monarch before the Opposition altered its position.

“At the very last moment, the Opposition decided that they would not proceed unless the CCJ was decided on; that is what is holding up the process. There is no need to go back into any further discussion islandwide. As far as we are concerned, it’s a decision that has been held up by the Opposition.

“There might be a bit of tweaking as to how that president should be nominated and selected and approved. A Bill was put in Parliament, and all that is necessary is for it to be debated, and we move forward. Moving towards a republic has been decided on, but it has been inordinately delayed by the position of the Opposition,” Chuck told the Sunday Observer.

Providing an update on the progress made, Chuck said, “We are nowhere” as it relates to making Jamaica a republic.

“We have not moved for over a year now, so nothing really has been done. Everything is at a standstill because the Opposition is not prepared to move forward until the Government commits to joining the CCJ, which in my mind is most unfortunate on their part,” said the minister.

“There is no doubt that once we move forward with the republic, then we can again put a constitutional commission together to look at other areas of the constitution; that is not a problem. But, remember, we have just come out of a broad-based constitutional commission. Yes, you might not support everything they did, but at least there was consensus on moving forward with the republic, so let’s do that and not allow the work of the last constitutional commission to be totally wasted.

“If you don’t allow something to come out of it, then we may have another constitutional commission and nothing comes out of it,” Chuck stressed.

The Opposition leader has argued in several public statements and interviews that replacing the king as head of State without simultaneously adopting the CCJ would amount to only partial decolonisation.

“The Opposition’s position has been consistent. We are not in favour of a piecemeal approach to decolonisation at this stage of our nation’s journey of national development. We support full decolonisation now,” Golding told the Sunday Observer.

He recalled that last year September he wrote to Prime Minister Andrew Holness requesting to meet with him to see how the process could move forward, but that request was not granted.

“That is a counterproductive approach, given that these reforms will require bipartisan support in order to proceed…It is the Government, not the Opposition, that is delaying the process,” insisted the Opposition leader.

He stressed that it would be an anomaly for Jamaica to move away from the British monarch as our head of State but retain the British monarch’s court as our final court, and that anomaly would also perpetuate the existing system which has, for centuries, denied the vast majority of Jamaicans access to their final court.

“Because of the legislative history of this matter over the past two decades, we would only support the two things being done separately if the adoption of the CCJ as our final court is the first step of an agreed pathway to full decolonisation and Jamaica becoming a republic. However, our preference would be to pass the legislation for both things simultaneously, followed by the required referendum on the UK monarch being replaced as head of State by a Jamaican president,” said Golding.

He added that the Opposition also has concerns about the proposed manner of appointing the president, and the proposed changes to the composition and voting of the Senate. Additionally, he said there needs to be a consensus on term limits; fixed election dates; a procedure for the recall of delinquent MPs; a procedure for the impeachment of parliamentarians who bring their office into disrepute; a different arrangement for the appointment of the Speaker of the House to ensure greater independence and fairness; and the resumption of the convention whereby parliamentary committees are chaired by the Opposition.

“It will be important for there to be both public education and public consultations on these matters, and on any other constitutional reforms for which there is significant public support,” said Golding.

He further urged Jamaicans to put pressure on the Government to commence authentic dialogue with the Opposition as to a pathway for achieving full decolonisation.

Constitutional reform has been talked about for decades in Jamaica, across different political administrations.

Different committees have been established by both parties, with the most recent being the Constitutional Reform Committee established by the Andrew Holness-led Government in 2023.

World.title: JA celebrates!
World.content:
Fireworks display at Grand Gala celebrations inside the National Stadium..

For the annual week-long celebrations commemorating Jamaica’s ‘Emancipendence’, party-lovers and cultural enthusiasts have planned a calendar of activities unlike any other. From cultural showcases and gospel concerts to all-night parties and special holiday menus, Emancipendence 2026 has something for everyone.

Whether you’re looking to wave the black, green, and gold at a community event, dance until sunrise at a nightclub, or indulge in specially curated festive cuisine at your favourite restaurant, the island’s social calendar is packed with activities guaranteed to keep the celebratory spirit alive.

The festivities truly began with the naming of the winner of the 2026 Festival Song competition, and it continued in earnest on Saturday last with the grand coronation show for the 2026 Festival Queen, one of the season’s most cherished traditions. The event, which celebrates the intelligence, talent and cultural awareness of Jamaican women, has long been a staple of the Emancipendence calendar.

For those seeking spiritual inspiration, earlier on Saturday was the annual Come Alive Gospel Concert on the East Lawns at King’s House — an evening of worship, uplifting performances, and messages of hope.

Kingston’s nightlife scene is equally poised to come alive. Popular entertainment hot spot MECA has lined up several events throughout the holiday period, ensuring that revellers have no shortage of options to celebrate Jamaica’s rich culture and infectious energy.

According to MECA boss Michael Dawson, “Emancipendence is the time of year when the best of our culture and history is celebrated.” He shared that at MECA, the team feels “duty-bound to provide the nightlife to support that”. On their calendar is the weekly Dolly Sundays, An Evening With Tanya Stephens on Tuesday, and Nigy Boy in concert on Thursday.

Food lovers won’t be left out either, as Usain Bolt’s Tracks and Records (UBT&R) has rolled out a special Emancipendence menu, giving patrons the opportunity to savour local flavours and culinary favourites while embracing the festive spirit.

According to the Jizell Cowan, marketing manager at UBT&R, the menu is about “celebrating Jamaican culture, cuisine, and creativity”.

“Jamaicans love to ‘tun dem hand mek fashion’ in the kitchen, and this menu proves it,” she said. “We took our motto ‘Out of Many, One People’ and put it on a plate with fusion dishes like our Oxtail Boa Bus with an Asian twist, the Yaad Burrito with Hispanic flavour, and Curry Goat Pizza with an Italian touch.”

“It’s a delicious way for lovers of Jamaican cuisine to indulge and celebrate all month long this August. Plus it’s Rum Month and we are featuring Jamaican crafted rum like Appleton Estate Spanish Sherry,” she added.

Meanwhile, in Montego Bay, Dream Weekend party lovers are expected to continue celebrations. With activities having started on Thursday night, hundreds of party lovers have already descended on the second city eager to soak up the vibrant atmosphere that has become synonymous with the summer season.

But Emancipendence is about more than parties and late-night entertainment. It’s a season rooted in history — a celebration of the abolition of slavery in 1838 and Jamaica’s attainment of Independence in 1962. Every concert, every flag raised and every gathering serves as a reminder of the resilience, creativity, and pride that define the Jamaican people.

The celebrations will culminate on August 6 with the annual Grand Gala, the country’s premier Independence event. Slated for the National Stadium, the event will be filled with cultural performances, musical tributes, and dazzling fireworks. The spectacle is expected to bring thousands together in a fitting conclusion to a season dedicated to freedom and nationhood.

So whether you’re planning to sing, dance, pray, or simply bask in the festive atmosphere, one thing is certain: Jamaica is ready to celebrate.

World.title: Former PM Golding urges US to rebuild true friendship with Jamaica
World.content:
GOLDING...new rules are being handed down, not after discussions and negotiations, but unilaterally by social media postings at 2:30 in the morning when most of us are asleep

FORMER Prime Minister Bruce Golding on Saturday night expressed hope that the United States would soften the tone of its relationship with Jamaica and rekindle the strong, decades-old bond of ties between both nations as current demands made by Washington are at odds with the very essence of true friendship.

Golding delivered the message in an address to the Jamaica 64th Independence Gala staged by Team Jamaica Bickle in Philadelphia, during which he juxtaposed impressive economic and social gains in the island over the past few years with what he described as “an even more pressing and unnecessary challenge at this time” created by a global order that has “become topsy-turvy”.

“How we live, how we govern ourselves, how we progress is determined, to a great extent, by the environment in which we live and how we are able to operate within that environment. That environment has always been challenging, testing our mettle and fortitude. We went through 45 years of the Cold War when we became the bully beef in the sandwich that the two superpowers were fighting over, but I have never witnessed anything like what we are facing now,” said Golding, who served as Jamaica’s eighth prime minister from September 2007 to October 2011.

He argued that established rules are being discarded and “new rules are being handed down, not after discussions and negotiations, but unilaterally by social media postings at 2:30 in the morning when most of us are asleep”.

“The long discredited Monroe doctrine has been reincarnated. New tariffs were imposed last year on our exports to America, although America enjoys a huge trade surplus with us. What we export to the United States is less than a quarter of what we import from them,” Golding stated.

He pointed to the discontinuation of the Cuban medical mission programme, America’s fierce opposition to China’s investments in Jamaica, and the highly controversial third-country nationals arrangement between the US and a number of Caribbean countries as examples of action that run counter to harmonious relations.

“True friends don’t abuse your friendship; they don’t make unreasonable demands of you; they should be there to help you. Holding a gun to our head and insisting that we must be reasonable and do things your way is not friendship. The United States has put us under severe stress — that’s not what friends are for,” Golding told his audience.

“There are many at home and abroad who are outraged at what is taking place, who are incensed at the bullying being meted out to us, who are angry that we have not pushed back, that we haven’t stood up like President [Luiz Inacio] Lula [da Silva] who declared that ‘Brazil’s destiny is for Brazilians alone to determine — without foreign interference or subservience,’ ” Golding said.

“But we must pause for a moment to understand who we are and the pickle we are in. Brazil is a large country and provides a US$57-billion market for American exports. We are not in that league. We struggle to find markets for our goods. The US market accounts for a half of our total exports. If our exports to the US were slapped with a 50 per cent tariff, our manufacturing sector would fall apart and thousands of persons would lose their jobs,” Golding pointed out.

“An airline ticket from Philadelphia to Montego Bay attracts federal taxes of around US$65. Bear in mind that the US accounts for 70 per cent of the tourists who come to Jamaica. If that ticket were slapped with an additional tax of US$200, do you understand what that would do to our tourism industry that is so vital to our economy?” Golding posited.

Pointing out that remittances from the US to Jamaica amounted to more than US$2.6 billion last year, he said that since January this year a one per cent federal tax was imposed on such remittances.

“What if the tax on remittances to Jamaica were increased to 25 per cent or disallowed altogether as a form of punishment? We don’t have to pause to wonder what that would mean to thousands of families that cannot survive without it,” the former head of Government argued.

“Our correspondent bank arrangements are tied to the US financial system. That’s what facilitates transactions between Jamaica and the rest of the world. What if those arrangements were cut off? Our economy would be literally paralysed,” he added.

“What if companies that want to do business with us were told that they would be penalised if they did so? What would that do to our investment flows?

“Scores of people gather at the US Embassy every day hoping to obtain a visa so they can visit their family members in the US or seek better opportunities here. What if the US were to restrict the granting of visas to Jamaicans, as has been done to countries like Sierra Leone and Haiti?” he asked.

Jamaica, he argued, is not alone, as all Caribbean countries are at risk and are extremely vulnerable.

“If our governments say or do anything that the White House finds displeasing, punishment will be meted out to us as sure as night follows day. Tariffs have become the weapon of choice and retribution a foreign policy tool. Canada was recently threatened with a 50 per cent tariff because smoke from wildfires there had drifted into America,” Golding pointed out.

“So when Caribbean governments adopt a measured, cautious approach in dealing with America’s bullying tactics, it is because they understand the pickle we are in. Make a wrong move, defiantly defend the Cuban assistance programmes and our partnership with China and they pay the price. They understand how careful they have to be when their hand is in the mouth of an angry lion,” he argued.

“Some of us, in the national interest, have to be restrained in what they say; others of us, in the national interest, have to say what needs to be said, and I will continue to voice my concerns as to how America’s dictates affect Jamaica and impair the hopes and aspirations of our people. Putting America first should not mean putting Jamaica in jeopardy,” Golding insisted.

“I cautiously cling to the hope that this will pass, that the hemisphere will once again be a neighbourhood of peace, mutual understanding, and respect, where true friendship prevails, where all of its people can pursue their own destiny with dignity and purpose, and where we can look upon America as a friend indeed,” the former prime minister said before ending his address with hope for divine favour for Jamaica and the US: “God bless all of you as you continue to make us proud and keep the black, green and gold flying. God bless the United States of America, which, if it is so minded, can hold hands with us in a spirit of true friendship. God bless the land we love — Jamaica — and guide us with His mighty hand through these troubling times.”

See full text of former Prime Minister Golding’s address online at jamaicaobserver.com

World.title: Sunshine joy!
World.content:
The Sunshine Girls celebrate after reaching the finals of the Commonwealth Games (Photo: Commonwealth Games Glasgow)

Jamaica will continue their hunt for an elusive Commonwealth Games netball gold medal when they face New Zealand in today’s final at the Hydro Arena in Glasgow, Scotland.

The Sunshine Girls booked back-to-back appearances in the final after edging defending champions Australia 46-45 in a thrilling semi-final on Saturday, ending the Australians’ streak of reaching every Commonwealth Games final.

Today’s title match will be a rematch of the Pool B meeting, which New Zealand won 53-48. The Kiwis will be seeking a third Commonwealth Games title after winning back-to-back gold medals in 2006 and 2010.

Australia and England will meet in the bronze medal match after New Zealand beat England 61-54 in the other semi-final.

The Sunshine Girls produced one of their best performances in recent years, avenging the heartbreak of losing to Australia in the Birmingham final four years ago. Jamaica’s defence stifled the usually prolific Australians in the closing minutes, with Sophie Dwyer missing two shots in the final two minutes, including one at the buzzer that would have forced extra time.

Led by the shooting of Romelda Aiken-George and Shanice Beckford, Jamaica opened a 46-42 lead with just over three-and-a-half minutes remaining before Australia scored three unanswered goals to close the gap.

Dwyer also missed an opportunity to cut Australia’s deficit to three goals with 2:16 left before her final miss sparked wild celebrations among the Jamaican players and supporters.

Jamaica led 13-10 after the first quarter and 23-21 at half-time before Australia levelled the scores at 35-35 heading into the final quarter. Australia then took a 38-37 lead early in the fourth before Jamaica regained control.

Aiken-George led Jamaica with 29 goals from 32 attempts, while Beckford scored 17 from 18.

Kiera Austin scored 22 goals from 23 attempts for Australia, Cora Koenen added 18 from 20, Sophie Garbin scored four, and Dwyer finished with one goal.

World.title: The Nature of Luxury
World.content:
Floyd’s Pelican Bar, Treasure Beach. An unlikely place to begin a conversation about luxury. (Photo: Dwayne Watkins Photography, Indulge Magazine)

Luxury has become predictable. Gold, marble, 1,000-thread count sheets. We have been taught to look for it in particular places. But some of the most luxurious experiences never look the part.

This bar shouldn’t exist.

A mile off the coast of Treasure Beach in Jamaica, a small driftwood bar stands on stilts in the middle of the Caribbean Sea.

The first time I went there, years ago for a photo shoot, the boat slowed before we arrived, and this structure seemed to rise out of the horizon. Driftwood. Weathered surfaces. Nothing polished or extravagant. No fancy amenities, and beyond it, only the vastness of sea and sky.

It is, by almost every conventional measure, the antithesis of luxury.

And yet, sitting on its balcony, my feet treading in the clearest water, feeling smaller by the moment, I felt something I have spent years of my working life trying to create for others.

The structure is humble. It doesn’t compete with the ocean. It surrenders to it. The sea remains the spectacle. The breeze, the salty air, and the light glistening on the waves guide the moment as if the bar, like me, understood its place within something larger.

That feeling has a name.

Psychologists call it awe — the emotion we experience when we encounter something so vast or unexpected that our minds don’t have a ready reference for it. This is what separates grandness from ordinary beauty. It moves beyond simply pleasing us. It changes us.

A study by Paul Piff has shown that awe drawn from nature moves us more than awe from anything man-made, which ultimately makes us more open to each other.

This does not surprise me. It is a feeling I’ve experienced time and again. I felt it that day on a rustic, wooden deck in the middle of the sea off the coast of Jamaica.

Still, we often regard beauty as optional — pleasant but unnecessary. Yet, when life becomes burdensome, where do we go? To the sea, to the shade of old, towering trees. For walks to inhale the crisp morning air and to climb hills to watch the sun rise. We send flowers to our loved ones in times of sickness and grief. We gather in beautiful places to celebrate the happiest moments of our lives. And, in the ordinary moments, we take off our shoes to simply feel the earth beneath our feet.

Instinctively, we already know what science is beginning to explain: Beauty restores us.

Perhaps, that has always been the real point of luxury.

World.title: Former PM Golding questions US-Jamaica friendship
World.content:
Former Prime Minister Bruce Golding

Below is the full text of former Prime Minister Bruce Golding’s address to the Jamaica 64th Independence Gala hosted by Team Jamaica Bickle in Philadelphia on August 1, 2026.

Thank you so much for your warm and gracious welcome. I haven’t been to Philly in a long, long time and it is so delightful to be here today and to be here among family. The outstanding contributions you make here and your unbreakable ties back home make us extremely proud.

When Irwine invited me, one of the first questions I asked him was “How are the Jamaicans there doing?” and he said “They’re doing well despite the challenges and the odds”. I’m going to speak to some of that this evening because we back home are facing some of those same challenges and odds but, as Irwine said, we are resilient – we’re little but we tallawah; we are nice but we are tough.

Team Jamaica Bickle

Let me thank Team Jamaica Bickle for the privilege of sharing some thoughts with you as we celebrate our 64th anniversary of independence. We celebrate, as well, more than 30 years of outstanding work by Team Jamaica Bickle. No commendation is too great for the efforts of Irwine Clare and Blane Stoddart in recognizing that there was a need, in conceptualizing a response, in persevering even when it appeared too ambitious and in growing the organization to what it is today.

Its initial focus was on taking care of our young athletes when they arrived to compete in the Penn Relays. Many of them were travelling abroad for the first time, found themselves in an environment where they knew no one other than their teammates and coaches but had to prepare themselves physically and mentally for the competitive challenges that faced them. Few people would have recognized that something important was missing, that they needed to be acclimatized, that their dietary needs had to be carefully managed if they were to be at their best and that they needed to be made to feel at home as much as possible. But Irwine and Blade recognized it and Team Jamaica Bickle is a legacy of which they can be proud and for which they must be saluted.

It has contributed immensely to the development of our athletes, some of whom like Usain Bolt, Shelly-Ann Fraser-Pryce, Elaine Thompson-Herah, Shericka Jackson, Asafa Powell, Merlene Ottey, Veronica Campbell-Brown (and I could name so many others) have gone on to be world champions.

But Team Jamaica Bickle didn’t stop at providing hospitality. It has provided grants to schools to assist them in developing their sports infrastructure and programmes, recognizing that our schools are the nursery for future champions. A major accomplishment has been its donation of well over a hundred defibrillators to equip the schools to deal with medical emergencies that athletes sometimes encounter.

And Team Jamaica Bickle didn’t out of patriotism confine its endeavors to Jamaican student athletes but extended its generosity to young athletes from other Caribbean countries. That it has served over 3,500 athletes since it came into being is a truly remarkable achievement and I ask you all to stand and give a rousing applause of commendation and gratitude to Team Jamaica Bickle.

It couldn’t have done it alone and we must celebrate, as well, all the sponsors, donors and volunteers without whose contributions much of this would not have been possible.

Jamaica’s progress

On Thursday of next week Jamaica will mark 64 years of independence. America recently celebrated its 250th anniversary but for us 64 years has been a long journey. It has been difficult at times. We have made mistakes, sometimes we lost our way but we were determined enough to wheel and come again. We have never forgotten that we have a rich legacy to protect and advance – the work and sacrifice of Nanny, Sam Sharpe, Paul Bogle, George William Gordon, Marcus Garvey, Norman Manley, Alexander Bustamante and the countless number of unsung heroes on whose shoulders we stand; the brilliance of Louise Bennett, Bob Marley and Usain Bolt.

Despite whatever setbacks befell us, we have made progress. We are a proud and, sometimes, even feisty people. We are a mature democracy. Lest we forget, the 2016 election was won by only one seat and an overall majority of less than 4,000 votes. Yet, there was a peaceful and orderly change of government. Not a single shot was fired, the PNP didn’t claim that the election was stolen, no mob attacked Gordon House and ransacked the place. People went about their business the next day as if the day before was a normal day. Little as we are, there are some important things that some big and powerful countries can learn from us.

Upon his retirement, Norman Manley said that the mission of his generation was to achieve political independence and he declared “mission accomplished”. The mission of the next generation, he said, was to achieve economic independence. That goal has proven to be elusive.

We have made some important strides over the last 15 years.

• Our national debt that had reached as much as 147 per cent of our Gross Domestic Product has been cut by more than a half…….even after Hurricane Melissa.

• Our Net International Reserves now stand at US$6.5 billion which commands respect in the international financial markets.

• Our unemployment rate is now at a record low of under four per cent. For the first time I have seen “Employees wanted” signs posted on some business places.

• Inflation is running at less than 6% despite the pressures caused by the war in Iran.

• We have a stable exchange rate with annual depreciation of around 1% over the last 5 years.

• Annual tourist arrivals now total over 4 million visitors.

• Our murder rate which I know has caused concern to most of you and which was once as high as over 1,600 a year is now down to less than 600 – still too high but still coming down.

• We have a capable and independent judiciary – we don’t have JLP and PNP judges – and the huge backlog of cases that has plagued our court system is being significantly reduced.

• Despite the pressure on our health services, we managed the Covid crisis better than many other countries. For example, our death toll per 100,000 was 125 compared with 375 here in the United States.

• When Hurricane Melissa hit Jamaica it was a more powerful hurricane than Katrina when it hit New Orleans. It took New Orleans 18 months to restore basic infrastructure and services and 10 years to fully recover. We are only 9 months in and we’re doing better than that.

So, despite the many difficulties that we face, we have a lot to give God thanks for. Our macro-economic fundamentals are in good shape but economic growth remains well below what we need to achieve. Over the past 5 years the economy has grown by an average of less than one per cent per year, due in part to Covid and Melissa but, even then, we have to do much better.

We have to refocus. Low unemployment, healthy foreign reserves, a stable exchange rate and moderate inflation are not sufficient to put us where we want to be. We have to add more value to our output. We have to lift our productivity through education, innovation, upskilling our work force, further upgrading our infrastructure and transforming our business processes. The aim must be for workers to earn better wages and enjoy a higher standard of living. That is our major challenge as we move into our 65th year.

The new challenge facing us

But we are facing an even more pressing and unnecessary challenge at this time. We are an island state but our borders don’t define our circumstances. How we live, how we govern ourselves, how we progress is determined, to a great extent, by the environment in which we live and how we are able to operate within that environment. That environment has always been challenging, testing our mettle and fortitude.

We went through 45 years of the Cold War when we became the bully beef in the sandwich that the two superpowers were fighting over. But I have never witnessed anything like what we are facing now.

We had to adapt to globalization with a set of rules different from what we were accustomed to. The preferential treatment that we enjoyed from the European Union for exporting our sugar and bananas was banned. The protective tariffs and subsidies that we used to help level the playing field for our local manufacturers and farmers had to come down so that foreign goods could more easily enter our markets. We had little say in the design of this new framework but we muscled up to face the new challenges. After all, we had to grow up one day and stand on our own two feet.

But, to our amazement and just as we were learning how to navigate this new landscape, that global order has become topsy-turvy. Established rules are being discarded. New rules are being handed down, not after discussions and negotiations, but unilaterally by social media postings at 2:30 in the morning when most of us are asleep. The long discredited Monroe doctrine has been reincarnated.

New tariffs were imposed last year on our exports to America although America enjoys a huge trade surplus with us. What we export to the United States is less than a quarter of what we import from them.

We have been ordered to send home the Cuban doctors and nurses who have played such a big part in keeping our health services going. Countries and companies that do business with Cuba run the risk of incurring severe penalties. We are being forced to contribute to the strangulation of the Cuban people who have helped us in so many ways, including gifting us the GC Foster College, the Jose Marti Technical High School, the Garvey Maceo High School and the Anchovy High School.

But Cuba is not the only friend we have that we are being told not to keep company with anymore. China has become a major investment partner in Jamaica. It has invested in major highways that have significantly improved our transportation and logistics in. You can now get from the Caymanas to Ocho Rios in less than an hour. The long under-developed parishes of St Thomas and Portland have been opened up because of China’s concessionary loan financing for the South Coast highway. Try buying a piece of land now in St. Thomas and see what you would have to pay.

China invested in our sugar factories when they were on the verge of closure. It is investing almost US$500 million in the revitalization of the Alpart alumina plant. It is heavily involved in the modernization of our port facilities to enable us to better take advantage of our strategic location along a major trade route.

But we are now being told that we must run the Chinese out of Jamaica because they are saddling us with unsustainable debt and threatening America’s influence in Latin America and the Caribbean. The Chinese have never made any indecent request of us or imposed any condition that could be a concern to the United States. What we owe to China is neither a burden nor a debt trap; it is less than four per cent of our total debt and is offered at concessionary rates of two to three per cent – you can’t get rates like that anywhere else! On the other hand, what we owe to American bondholders who account for most of our foreign debt comes at a cost of six to eight per cent.

China thinks long-term, sees potential that investors in countries like the US ignore because it looks too risky and China puts its money where its mouth is. China’s stock of investment in Jamaica now stands at US$2.1 billon – America’s investment is only a fraction of that (US$276 million). But we are being told that we must drive them out of the country!

The most controversial issue in this new hegemonic environment is the requirement for Jamaica to accept Third Country deportees – not Jamaicans whom we are obliged to accept, but persons from various other countries that America wants to get rid of. In our case, we were required to sign an agreement which allows America to send up to 10,000 persons (25 every two weeks) to Jamaica.

We are told that no more than 10 people will be in Jamaica within any 30 day period but no specific arrangements have been provided as to how they will move on or where they go from there. And if it is the case that they will be in Jamaica for such a short time, why bother to send them there? Why not keep them in America for the 30 days and then send them off to wherever they are supposed to go? It just does not make any sense! Or is it America’s unspoken expectation that they will be parked here?

We are not alone in this. Seven Caricom countries have had to sign similar agreements. Please don’t ask me to believe that we entered into these agreements joyfully!

Secretary of State, Marco Rubio, when he visited Jamaica in March 2025, is only the latest highly placed official of the US government who has boasted of the strong, long-standing bond of friendship between Jamaica and the United States. What is being done to us is not friendship. Imposing arbitrary tariffs on us when we are struggling to make our exports competitive in a difficult market is not friendship! Dictating to us who we must do business with is not friendship! Forcing us to accept foreign deportees when we are struggling to look after our own people and trying to recover from Melissa is not friendship!

True friends don’t abuse your friendship; they don’t make unreasonable demands of you; they should be there to help you. Holding a gun to our head and insisting that we must be “reasonable” and do things your way is not friendship! The United States has put us under severe stress – that’s not what friends are for!

There are many at home and abroad who are outraged at what is taking place, who are incensed at the bullying being meted out to us, who are angry that we have not pushed back, that we haven’t stood up like President Lula who declared that “Brazil’s destiny is for Brazilians alone to determine — without foreign interference or subservience”.

But we must pause for a moment to understand who we are and the pickle we are in. Brazil is a large country and provides a US$57B market for American exports. We are not in that league.

We struggle to find markets for our goods. The US market accounts for a half of our total exports. If our exports to the US were slapped with a 50% tariff, our manufacturing sector would fall apart and thousands of persons would lose their jobs.

An airline ticket from Philadelphia to Montego Bay attracts federal taxes of around US$65. Bear in mind that the US accounts for 70% of the tourists who come to Jamaica. If that ticket were slapped with an additional tax of US$200, do you understand what that would do to our tourism industry that is so vital to our economy?

Remittances from the US to Jamaica amounted to more than US$2.6 billion last year. Since January this year a one per cent federal tax was imposed on such remittances. What if the tax on remittances to Jamaica were increased to 25 per cent or disallowed altogether as a form of punishment? We don’t have to pause to wonder what that would mean to thousands of families that cannot survive without it.

Our correspondent bank arrangements are tied to the US financial system. That’s what facilitates transactions between Jamaica and the rest of the world. What if those arrangements were cut off? Our economy would be literally paralyzed.

What if companies that want to do business with us were told that they would be penalized if they did so? What would that do to our investment flows?

Scores of people gather at the US embassy every day hoping to obtain a visa so they can visit their family members in the US or seek better opportunities here. What if the US were to restrict the granting of visas to Jamaicans as has been done to countries like Sierra Leone and Haiti?

And we are not alone in this; all Caribbean countries are at risk and all of us are extremely vulnerable. If our governments say or do anything that the White House finds displeasing, punishment will be meted out to us as sure as night follows day. Tariffs have become the weapon of choice and retribution a foreign policy tool. Canada was recently threatened with a 50 per cent tariff because smoke from wildfires there had drifted into America.

So, when Caribbean governments adopt a measured, cautious approach in dealing with America’s bullying tactics, it is because they understand the pickle we are in. Make a wrong move, defiantly defend the Cuban assistance programmes and our partnership with China and they pay the price. They understand how careful they have to be when their hand is in the mouth of an angry lion.

And, sadly, we have been placed into a position where Caribbean unity is of no avail. Our individual sovereignty and regional leverage are under siege. It is now every man for himself….every country on its own!

Some of us, in the national interest, have to be restrained in what they say; others of us, in the national interest, have to say what needs to be said and I will continue to voice my concerns as to how America’s dictates affect Jamaica and impair the hopes and aspirations of our people. Putting America first should not mean putting Jamaica in jeopardy.

I cautiously cling to the hope that this will pass, that the hemisphere will once again be a neighbourhood of peace, mutual understanding and respect, where true friendship prevails, where all of its people can pursue their own destiny with dignity and purpose and where we can look upon America as a friend indeed.

God bless all of you as you continue to make us proud and keep the black, green and gold flying. God bless the United States of America which, if it is so minded, can hold hands with us in a spirit of true friendship. God bless the land we love – Jamaica – and guide us with His mighty hand through these troubling times.

World.title: Macron’s team seeks Saudi funding for manga theme park near Paris
World.content:
According to one diplomat with contacts in the Gulf, the project would involve Saudi investors acquiring the former Mirapolis site, located some 30 kilometers northwest of Paris, with an eye to turning it into a theme park based on the popular manga series Dragon Ball.

Manga’s explosion in popularity has been felt keenly in France, where comic books and graphic novels are particularly popular.

The expected investment amount is not yet known, but several parties involved in the discussions suggest the deal could exceed €1 billion.

Saudi spinoff

The enterprise is part of Saudi Arabia Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman’s Vision 2030 plan, which aims to diversify the kingdom’s oil-dependent economy with massive investments in tourism and leisure.

The Qiddiya Investment Company is overseeing the construction of the city of Qiddiya — a huge entertainment complex situated some 50 kilometers from Riyadh. The site is set to feature a Formula 1 circuit, a large tennis complex designed to host international tournaments, an amusement park operated by the American chain Six Flags and another theme park based on Dragon Ball.

According to three people familiar with the negotiations, the current plan is to build a smaller-scale Dragon Ball park where Mirapolis once stood.

World.title: Nigel Farage is under siege. That’s just how he likes it.
World.content:
“Farage is facing something of a perfect storm,” said Tim Bale, professor of politics at Queen Mary University of London and an expert on the right in Britain. “But while he’s on the ropes he’s by no means on the floor, let alone out for the count.”

Farage insists he won’t be “cowed” by what he describes as intimidation and says he is preparing for a general election as soon as this autumn, although Burnham has said he has no imminent plans to call one.

It’s an open question whether the Burnham bounce in the polls and the dip in Farage’s fortunes mark a decisive shift in momentum in British politics or merely a blip. What is clear is that the challenges facing Reform are substantial, and growing.

Farage’s side admits that Burnham has lifted the Labour government since he took office on July 20 and hurt Reform with a blizzard of policy pledges and energetic social media videos that have dominated media attention.

Reform’s leader, meanwhile, has been beset by questions over whether he broke parliamentary rules by not declaring a £5 million donation. Last month he quit parliament to trigger a special election in his constituency of Clacton on the east coast of England, vowing to take on the establishment he says is trying to stitch him up over the furor.

But with none of the mainstream parties willing to play ball, the contest has assumed an air of farce: Farage’s only well-known opponent is a candidate who goes by Count Binface, a serial joker who dresses up as a trash can.

World.title: Choppers collide, killing 2, as fires and foreboding grip Greece
World.content:
Another three Greek firefighters died last Wednesday while tackling wildfires in Crete and on the Peloponnese, a rugged peninsula in southern Greece.

While a fire that has been burning since Friday around Porto Germeno on the Gulf of Corinth some 60 ​kilometers northwest of Athens has subsided, on Saturday the flames crossed a mountain to the south, fanned by strong winds of up to 130 kilometers per hour, and reached the settlement of Veniza closer to the capital. According to initial estimates, the fire has destroyed around 200 houses in the area.

On Sunday flames spread rapidly through western Attica, a region that encompasses Athens, threatening communities and an industrial district outside Megara, about 30 kilometers from the capital. Speaking on state TV Ert, the president of the firefighters’ federation, Nikos Lavranos, described it as a “huge front” and a “black blanket covering an area of around [25 acres].”

Dozens of settlements have been evacuated, and firefighters are focusing on preventing the flames from advancing toward Megara, pop. 30,000. Greece’s firefighting service said more than 2,500 people had been evacuated in western Attica by late Sunday afternoon.

“Unfortunately, we have uncontrolled fires in far too many areas. As soon as the fire brigade arrives at one spot, just as the fire is being brought under control, it flares up again in another spot,” Megara Mayor Panagiotis Margetis told Open TV.

Firefighters were also fighting another blaze in the Peloponnese on Sunday as well as on the island of Cephalonia in the Ionian Sea between Greece and Italy. More than 500 firefighters have been deployed across Greece.

World.title: Hungary faces energy crunch as drought shuts down Paks nuclear plant, PM says
World.content:
“Due to the further drop in the Danube’s water level,” Magyar wrote Saturday, “tomorrow it will be completely shut down for the first time in 44 years."

The Soviet-built Paks facility remains the backbone of the country’s power system. The loss of output has triggered national energy-saving measures and offers of support from regional neighbors.

A prolonged outage would cripple Hungary’s electricity supply at a time when temperatures are forecast to rise above 40 degrees Celsius in Budapest next week amid an ongoing heatwave and drought across Europe.

Magyar warned the shutdown could trigger an emergency at a time of high summer demand: “An energy crisis situation may arise from Monday. Coordinated steps and self-restraint will be needed to avoid more severe consequences.”

The government has urged households and businesses to reduce electricity consumption during peak hours between 5 p.m. and 10 p.m., calling on people to limit their use of air conditioning and washing machines. Authorities have also prepared an emergency plan to temporarily restrict consumption at industrial facilities on a rotating basis, while increasing output from other power plants.

The European Commission said Friday it was closely monitoring the situation and was prepared to convene an emergency meeting of its Electricity Coordination Group over the Paks shutdown.

World.title: Trump cancels strikes on Iran, says deal imminent
World.content:
Donald Trump speaks during a Cabinet meeting at Camp David in Maryland, on July 31, 2026. | Aaron Schwartz/ AFP via Getty Images

Tehran has not responded to the U.S. president’s announcement and has not confirmed an agreement to end the Middle East conflict has been reached.

U.S. President Donald Trump said late Saturday that he was canceling planned strikes on Iran pending a rapid agreement with Tehran to end the conflict in the Middle East.

“We have just been asked by Iran, and other Middle Eastern Countries, to hold off any attack in that the perimeters of a deal has been agreed to,” Trump announced in a post on Truth Social.

He said the agreement would include the “Immediate, Complete, and Total OPENING OF THE HORMUZ STRAIT” and “an end to Iran’s nuclear threat.” Trump added that Israel supported his commitment to pause strikes, contingent on “being able to rapidly make a DEAL.”

World.title: Ceuta crisis: 22 EU leaders gang up against Spain’s Sánchez over his migration policy
World.content:
In a letter to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, European Council President António Costa and Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin, the 22 leaders made direct reference to the need for EU-level cooperation on policies such as Madrid’s migrant regularization scheme.

“We have a duty to effectively deter and relentlessly combat illegal migration, by coordinating our action, strengthening our external borders and addressing all policies that can serve as pull factors, such as the regularization of [a] very large number of irregular migrants,” the leaders wrote.

Madrid has pushed back against the claim that the country’s regularization scheme triggered the crisis in Ceuta, and has pointed out that none of the people who illegally entered the exclave would be eligible to benefit from the measure.

“This process is based on very specific conditions, such as proof of residency in Spain before January 1, 2026, and having resided in Spain for five consecutive months at the time of application,” said a spokesperson for the Spanish foreign ministry. Moreover, the deadline for filing applications for the scheme, which was launched in April, was in June.

But those explanations have not appeared to sway the EU leaders who signed the letter to Costa, Von der Leyen and Martin.

“We cannot allow uncontrolled mass crossings, the instrumentalisation of migration or other hybrid threats to create the perception that illegal entry into the European Union is possible. That a migrant’s illegal entry can turn into legal stay,” they went on.

World.title: Labour holds Greater Manchester mayoralty after counting goes to second round
World.content:
Speaking at the Co-Op Live arena to the east of the city, Craig said she stands “ready to serve” her 3 million constituents.

“Every single decision I take as your mayor of Greater Manchester will pass the test of making your life better,” Craig pledged.

The vote was triggered after three-time mayoral contest winner Burnham resigned the job in June to return to Westminster, where he swiftly claimed leadership of the governing Labour Party and became prime minister. There had been concern that Burnham’s move would allow Reform UK — which performed strongly in local elections in England earlier this year — to seize the mayoralty.

Craig will now be have to deal directly with Burnham, who has promised to devolve more powers to England’s mayors as a part of a devolution package. The post currently comes with powers over transport, policing, and housing.

Turnout for the special election was noticeably lower than when Burnham last ran back in 2024, with only 25 per cent of voters heading to the polls this time, compared to 32 per cent at the last vote. POLITICO witnessed some voters on doorsteps Thursday evening learning of the election for the first time.

Counting continued late into the night as the re-instated supplementary voting system took the contest to a second round for the first time ever.

World.title: Morocco reports 11 Ceuta deaths, sharply conflicting  Spanish figures
World.content:
Morocco's interior ministry has issued its first toll for those who died trying to reach Spain's North African enclave of Ceuta last week, saying 11 people had died, which is significantly lower than the number issued by Spain, which was at least 72 people.

 

Tens of thousands of potential migrants crossed into the territory between Wednesday and Friday, sparking diplomatic tension within the European Union as some member states criticised Spain's lack of action and loose migration policies.

Rachid El Khalfi, a spokesman for Morocco's interior ministry, said that of the 11 who died, 10 had drowned, while an eleventh person fell from a rocky area.

Morocco also announced that they were working in coordination with Spain to verify these figures and to identify bodies found on Spanish territory

Meanwhile, the ministry blamed the sudden surge on the "malicious exploitation" of social media and the "spread of misleading information".

But it also cited "misinterpretations of legal provisions", a reference to a July 8 Spanish Supreme Court ruling that migrants arriving by sea should not be returned as quickly as others.

The ministry reported 40,000 attempts to cross into Ceuta unlawfully.

A further 1,135 people sought to illegally enter the Spanish enclave of Melilla, located further east, but were promptly returned to Moroccan territory, the ministry added.

Spain states that over 60,000 people succeeded in entering Ceuta in recent days, though the majority have since returned to Morocco.

The Moroccan Association for Human Rights (AMDH) noted that there were "nearly 130 victims", alongside dozens of others who remain missing.

Prosecutors have launched an official inquiry into the events, according to the ministry.

World.title: Ceuta: more migrants leave but residents still in shock. Far-right leader visits
World.content:
Here at the border between Ceuta and Morocco, the situation is much calmer than in recent days. According to Spanish authorities, the majority of the at least 60,000 people who crossed irregularly at this point on Thursday have already returned.

 

There is still a sporadic but steady stream of people heading back. Most of those returning tell us they entered Spain after receiving social media messages claiming the border was open and that no documentation was required.

Meanwhile, in the city, fear has given way to indignation. Virtually everyone I have spoken to cannot fathom how this situation could have happened and is demanding urgent explanations. It is a tense social atmosphere that is fuelling political debate.

A taxi driver told me:

"I got the feeling that people are very, very angry. I know they’re very angry right now. There are 85,000 of us here, and 60,000 are coming in. So, tell me. What do we do? What are we going to do? We can’t even buy bread. There was no bread. There was nothing. Nothing, nothing. Everything was closed."

While he was reluctant to attribute blame, some residents were more outspoken. Alluding to the initial legal difficulty of sending the migrants back immediately because they came via the sea, a middle-aged man called PM Pedro Sanchez an "accomplice", adding: "this is a disgrace— for me, a disgrace. This has never happened before in my life."

Some Ceutanos do point to a humanitarian duty in connection with the crisis. A 78-year old pensioner told me:

"If there are children there, they need to be given something to drink, they need to be given something to eat. It’s common sense, but that now all of Ceuta, all of Spain—and Spain stands with you—is with you."

However, the situation as a whole he cannot but condemn:

"This is a state of emergency and a declaration of martial law, just to go shopping at Mercadona? I have to pass a soldier every ten meters away from him ten or twenty meters away from him and feed the troops well and the police. That’s a state of siege, and it’s a of national emergency. There’s no question about it."

Santiago Abascal, the leader of Vox, visited the city today, accusing the government of being in thrall to Morocco.

Speaking to the media, Abascal placed the responsibility for what had happened on the government in Rabat and, above all, on Pedro Sánchez himself.

He argued that Morocco acted in the conviction that there would be neither response nor reprisals, because the Spanish prime minister is, in his words, "subservient to the African country".

World.title: Rupert Lowe offers alliance with Nigel Farage to unite Britain's hard right
World.content:
The leader of the UK's hard-right Restore Britain party has offered to partner with Reform UK's Nigel Farage in an effort to defeat Britain's left wing - if Farage agrees to certain conditions.

 

In a video posted to social media on Sunday, Rupert Lowe called on Farage to put "personalities" and "past disagreements" aside and work together to unite what he described as a "hopelessly divided" right.

Lowe, who was a member of parliament for Reform until 2025, when he was kicked out of the party, outlined five points that he said they would have to agree on to be able to find a "common way forward."

Firstly, Lowe said securing Britain's borders must be a priority.

"Ending mass immigration is not enough. The hour is just too late for that. It must be reversed," he said, adding: "Every illegal migrant must be deported."

Lowe's second condition centred on "demographic security" and "reversing the Islamification of Britain."

Lowe cited unspecified projections that he said showed white Britons could one day become a minority in the UK, saying: "Nothing demonstrates the demographic vandalism of mass immigration more than that."

He added that any cooperation between Restore Britain and Reform would hinge on an agreement to ban the burqa, halal and kosher slaughter, and cousin marriage, as well as "Sharia courts" and "mass dominating public Islamic prayer."

The third condition set out by Lowe was a referendum on the reintroduction of the death penalty.

"The British people must be given a full, free, and fair referendum" on the matter, he told Farage.

Britain's Reform UK party leader Nigel Farage speaks during a Reform UK rally in Wymondham, England, Tuesday July 21, 2026. PA

Fourthly, Lowe insisted they would need to commit to "restoring a self-sufficient Britain," which he said could be achieved by controlling spending, cuts to welfare, and tackling inflation.

Lowe warned "enormous cuts" would have to be made to make the plan a reality and that "difficult, unpopular decisions" would need to be taken.

His final condition was an agreement to restore trust in UK politics, as he said the country had "entirely lost faith in Westminster."

"Former Conservative ministers who failed our country and our people in so many important ways must not be part of any future cabinet," he added. "They had their chance".

Concluding his video message, Lowe said he believed that Reform and Restore Britain could find "sufficient common ground" to "destroy the looming left-wing alliance that will finish off what hope remains for this country."

Britain's divided right battles Burnham

Lowe's offer comes as Labour overtook Reform in two opinion polls and drew level in a third at the back end of July, as new UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham made a quick start to life in Downing Street.

Burnham, the former mayor of Greater Manchester, became the UK's seventh prime minister in a decade after taking over from Keir Starmer last month.

Burnham had made a dramatic return to Westminster in June after securing a large majority in the Makerfield by-election, comfortably beating out challengers from Reform UK and Lowe's Restore Britain.

The contest had been predicted to be a closer-run affair between Reform and Labour. However, Restore's stronger-than-expected performance split the right-wing vote - although not by enough to alter the result, with Burnham winning around 55% of the vote.

Since taking office, Burnham has largely focused on domestic affairs, detailing changes to the UK's education system, unveiling plans to overhaul social care, and pushing ahead with devolution pledges.

He has also announced an £8.4 billion investment into the UK's nuclear deterrent and vowed to continue support for Ukraine in its ongoing battle against Russian President Vladimir Putin's invading forces.

World.title: Italian Navy boards tanker from Russian shadow fleet
World.content:
Italian vessel Thaon di Revel boarded a Russian shadow fleet tanker to inspect it in international waters near Pantelleria, an island located between Sicily and Tunisia.

 

The inspection was carried out by the Italian navy on Sunday morning, 2 August, as part of the Operation EUNAVFOR MED IRINI, the European Union mission in the Mediterranean monitoring arms and oil trafficking.

The tanker Toa Payoh, which is subject to European Union sanctions and belongs to the so-called Russian 'shadow fleet', has undergone nationality verification, which for ships is determined by the flag they are authorised to fly. The Toa Payoh is sailing under the declared flag of Cameroon.

The tanker, which left the port of Cotonou in Benin on 16 July bound for Istanbul, was intercepted west of Pantelleria. According to the ministry's account, the tanker's master initially did not provide the requested cooperation. A team of Italian military personnel then reached the vessel by helicopter from the ship Thaon di Revel and carried out the planned checks.

Operation IRINI: ship Thaon di Revel boards tanker belonging to the Russian 'shadow fleet' Ministero della Difesa italiano

"I would like to congratulate the crew of the ship Thaon di Revel and all the service personnel involved in the operation for the professionalism, preparation and resolve they have shown. This activity too is a concrete demonstration of Italy's contribution to the security of the Mediterranean and to the European Union's action," said Defence Minister Guido Crosetto.

How the operation was carried out

The Ministry of Defence reported that the operation, carried out with the support of a Greek ship and a Polish patrol aircraft, lasted around two hours and was concluded routinely and in complete safety.

Operation IRINI: ship Thaon di Revel boards tanker belonging to the Russian 'shadow fleet' Ministero della Difesa italiano

The operation, conducted in international waters under the European mandate, was carried out, the ministry note says, in full compliance with Article 110 of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), which allows a naval vessel, when the conditions laid down are met, to carry out the necessary checks on the nationality of a merchant ship and the flag it is authorised to fly.

At the moment, the Italian authorities are reviewing the information and documentation obtained during the inspection.

World.title: Pentagon UFO files: what role Germany plays
World.content:
Glowing objects in the sky, mysterious military reports and files kept under lock and key for decades: newly released UFO documents offer a glimpse into some of the most baffling cases of recent decades.

 

A key focus of these historical files are reports by Allied pilots from the final months of the Second World War. They described glowing flying objects moving at high speed that accompanied their aircraft over Germany. These phenomena later became known as "Foo Fighters".

In the file (source in German) (source in English), it literally states:

On the night of 22 December 1944, two lights rose from the ground near an aircraft of the 415th Night Fighter Squadron, climbed to its altitude, took up position behind its tail for about two minutes and then 'peeled away again' – according to the crew, always under 'complete control'. Ground radar confirmed that there were no enemy aircraft in the vicinity.

Such encounters were reported repeatedly. Over a period of six weeks, crews of the 415th over Germany and France spoke of red, green, orange and amber-coloured lights that flew in formation with their aircraft, carried out evasive manoeuvres and came as close as around 30 metres. The pilots called these phenomena "Foo Fighters".

The British Air Ministry examined the reports and concluded in a memorandum classified as secret in March 1945 that 'the whole matter still remains something of an enigma'.

Independently of this, pilots also reported sighting an aluminium cylinder roughly 3.6 metres long at an altitude of around 2,700 metres. When fired upon by the aircraft, the object partially lost its shape and showed a red luminous effect, but did not break apart. Intelligence classified it as probably a German 'flak bomb'.

No one was able to provide a clear explanation for the mysterious lights. The file remained classified for 80 years.

1945: A file containing reports from combat pilots Department of War

The military examined several possible explanations. One idea was that they could be previously unknown German secret weapons or experimental aircraft with novel rocket or jet propulsion systems. However, the investigations found no conclusive evidence for this.

Declassified FBI reports, "Nazi UFOs"

The released material also includes historical FBI documents from the 1940s and 1950s, in which reports appear of alleged German developments of disc-shaped flying devices. Some of these references relate to possible secret research projects in the Berlin area and in regions near the Austrian border.

However, these reports do not come from technical investigations or confirmed military files, but are based mainly on statements from informants, rumours and intelligence tips from the immediate post-war period. They therefore primarily reflect which leads the authorities chose to follow at the time.

The documents do not provide evidence that Nazi Germany actually developed operational "flying discs" with extraordinary flight performance. Historians place many of these stories in the context of speculation about German secret weapons, psychological warfare and the Allies' search for advanced German technology.

In the SHAEF and Air Ministry memoranda of 1944/45, there are repeated descriptions of, among other things, red, green, orange and amber-coloured lights that appeared to move in a controlled way, flew in formation with aircraft and in some cases came within short range of them.

Some observers report arrowhead-shaped objects. Despite this variety, certain patterns recur: many of the described craft seem to have no visible wings, rotors or conventional propulsion. They are also said to possess unusual characteristics – such as apparently motionless hovering in the air, sudden bursts of acceleration or flight manoeuvres that are difficult to explain using known technologies.

Glowing shapes, unknown flight manoeuvres

Later investigations such as the US Air Force programme Project Blue Book (1947–1969) also documented a wide range of sighting reports. Observers described, among other things, glowing geometric shapes, disc-shaped or arrow-like objects, as well as phenomena without visible wings, rotors or conventional propulsion systems. Some reports spoke of objects that appeared to hover motionless in the air, accelerate abruptly or perform flight manoeuvres that were hard to reconcile with the aviation technologies known at the time.

Alongside the historical documents, the archives contain numerous files from more recent years. Since the public revelation of the Pentagon programme AATIP (Advanced Aerospace Threat Identification Program) in 2017, the United States has expanded its investigations into so-called UAP (Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena).

The Department of Defense has created new structures for recording and assessing unusual observations by military personnel. The Pentagon has also released several previously classified recordings of unknown flying objects, including videos taken by Navy pilots in 2004 and 2015, whose phenomena could not initially be clearly identified.

In some documents, military personnel also report physical complaints after close encounters, such as nausea, headaches, skin irritation or neurological symptoms. What lies behind these unexplained observations remains disputed to this day. Explanations range from known technological phenomena and misperceptions to far more far-reaching hypotheses.

Recorded by an F/A-18 on 21/01/2015 off the coast of California. The video shows an elongated object flying at high speed against the wind. Navy UAP

This new transparency in the handling of Pentagon files is being closely watched in Europe as well. Security and defence experts are following the US initiatives, as unusual phenomena in airspace are increasingly viewed as a potential security and intelligence issue.

Between history and speculation

The newly released files highlight above all one thing: interest in unusual aerial phenomena goes back a long way and is closely linked to historical events such as the Second World War. Germany does feature in the documents, but the files provide no proof of extraterrestrial spacecraft or secret German "flying discs".

Rather, they document how armed forces and intelligence services have spent decades trying to explain unusual observations – and how enduring myths have grown out of them right up to the present day.

World.title: Fears of wheat price surge amid Ukraine-Russia clashes in the Black Sea
World.content:
Intensifying clashes between Ukraine and Russia in the Black Sea are threatening a crucial trade artery responsible for nearly a third of the world's wheat supply, stoking fears of soaring prices and shortages.

Advertising

Earlier in July, a Russian cruise missile struck the grain carrier Golden Leo, claiming ten lives. This marked the deadliest blow yet in a mounting campaign by both Russian and Ukrainian forces targeting cargo ships in the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov.

"This is a new development in recent months," claims shipping analyst Yoruk Isik, who runs the Istanbul-based Bosphorus Observer consultancy. Isik warns that cargo vessels are caught in a deadly tit-for-tat.

"Ukraine has been targeting Russian seaborne bulkers in particular, the ones transporting stolen grain from the occupied territories of Ukraine," explains Isik, "Russia retaliated and hit Ukraine's civilian port infrastructure in Odesa; a mid-sized vessel carrying corn out of Odesa was totally sunk, other vessels were damaged, and sailors died," he adds.

Turkey’s Shipowners’ Association, having logged 136 incidents involving commercial vessels in recent months, is now urging its members to avoid the Black Sea altogether.

Beyond its role as a key channel for Russian oil, the Black Sea is a lifeline for global grain exports, with Russia and Ukraine among the top suppliers.

"It is very important to note that most of Russia's agricultural commodities are exported through the Black Sea, and that almost all of Ukraine's agricultural commodities are shipped via Ukraine's ports," warns Isik.

Bad timing for harvest

Around a third of the world's wheat moves through these waters. The surge in attacks across the Black Sea and the neighbouring Sea of Azov has brought exports to a near standstill.

"No port is officially closed, but almost no shipowner wants to go there, so trade is close to zero," claims Istanbul-based international grain dealer Can Atbasoglu. "Sellers want buyers to handle the vessels, and buyers want sellers to handle the vessels, but shipowners don't want to risk it."

This deadlock arrives at the worst possible moment: harvest time. "Normally, Russian sellers would have sold all their August cargoes by now; I don't know if anybody has any sales on their books at present," says Atbasoglu.

Turkey agrees deal to clear Black Sea of mines that threaten Ukrainian exports

Wheat prices are already reacting. "The price in Romania is, say, 20-25 percent higher – that's the clearest effect we're seeing. But everybody is waiting for some kind of intervention, and soon," adds Atbasoglu.

Turkey now leads a NATO mission, along with Bulgaria and Romania, to safeguard navigation in the Black Sea. However, former Turkish ambassador and navigation rights expert Mithat Rende believes Ankara will be wary of any effort to enforce passage for commercial ships. "It's very important that the Ukrainian war should not be transformed into a regional war," cautions Rende.

"Where would it stop? Would you fire missiles and intercept Russian missiles in the Black Sea? They (Russia) already accuse all of us of fighting Russia as NATO. It's very important to avoid such operations," he adds.

Full impact yet to be felt

Rende argues Ankara’s priority is diplomacy, having played a pivotal role in brokering the 2022 United Nations-backed grain export deal after Russian forces blocked Ukrainian shipments. "Turkey maintained a dialogue with both the Russian and the Ukrainian sides at the same time," says Rende, "But is there political will for a ceasefire now? I don't see it at present."

Grain trader Atbasoglu warns the full impact of the disruption is not yet reflected in prices. "Buyers are still not fully reacting. It's seen more as an August, or at the latest a September issue, and the markets still want to believe both sides will get together and talk," he says.

However, Atbasoglu cautions that time may be running out. "In 2022, Ukraine was completely closed off, and there was a major panic. We saw the effect: wheat prices jumped 50 percent in 2022, and we could expect something similar if this continues," he concludes.

Africa and the Middle East, which are heavily reliant on Black Sea grain, are beginning to seek pricier alternatives. Europe, too, may soon feel the strain, as drought-hit wheat harvests threaten to push global food prices even higher.

World.title: 5.0 magnitude earthquake strikes Egypt
World.content:
The quake occurred at 3 a.m. local time about 22 miles north ⁠of the Egyptian city of Suez, the US Geological Survey said.

A magnitude 5.0 earthquake struck off Egypt early on Monday, according to the United States Geological Survey.

The quake happened at 3 a.m. local time (0000 ​GMT) and hit an area about 22 miles (36 kilometers) northeast of the seaport city of Suez.

The ​German Research Centre ‌for Geosciences (GFZ) measured the earthquake at magnitude 5.4 and ​recorded the depth of the quake at 6 miles (10 kilometers).

The Egyptian Red Crescent said it had activated ‌its emergency response plan in ‌the governorates where the earthquake was felt.

No immediate reports of damage or injuries

There were no immediate reports of casualties or property damage.

Humanitarian organizations urged residents to avoid buildings showing signs of structural damage.

Damaging earthquakes are uncommon in the northeast African country. The country's deadliest earthquake in modern history struck in October 1992, when a 5.8-magnitude quake shook the capital, Cairo, killing more than 500 people and displacing thousands.
