As the cable enters its final construction phase, regional leaders are once again gathering, this time in Cholpon-Ata for an informal Consultative Meeting of the Heads of State of Central Asia and Azerbaijan, underscoring how cooperation between the countries increasingly extends across transport, energy and digital connectivity.

Nearly two years after Tokayev first identified the project as a strategic priority, it is entering its most tangible phase. Kazakhstan is now carrying out the final stages of the project, with commercial commissioning expected by the end of 2026. The latest phase has shifted from engineering preparation to offshore construction.

According to the Ministry of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development’s release from July 31, regulatory, customs and organizational procedures have been completed, including the approval of equipment required for the offshore works, allowing construction to proceed without administrative delays.

Preparatory work in 2025 included desktop and offshore engineering surveys, selection of the optimal route avoiding anchorage zones and military training areas, environmental approvals from the Mangystau Region authorities, and the production and factory testing in China of a specially armored submarine cable equipped with ROPA optical amplifiers.

With the planning phase complete, attention has shifted from engineering design to execution at sea. The cable, previously delivered from China to the port of Kuryk together with three cable baskets weighing a combined 600 tons, was transported to Baku aboard a specialized logistics vessel. It has now been transferred into the cable tank of the cable-laying vessel, which has departed Baku and is laying the line toward Aktau.

The operation is being carried out by a cable-laying vessel with a displacement exceeding 20,000 tons and equipped with dynamic positioning technology to ensure precise installation on the seabed. Around 70 crew members are involved, including technical supervisors and representatives of Kazakhtelecom. The project is being implemented by CaspiLink B.V., the joint venture established by Kazakhtelecom and AzerTelecom.

A dedicated jointing room has also been installed onboard to allow engineers to repair or reconnect the cable if required during installation. Both the Kazakh and Azerbaijani cable ends have already undergone testing. Subject to favorable weather conditions, installation of the submarine cable is expected to be completed within the next 15 to 20 days, while the overall commissioning process remains on schedule for completion by the end of 2026.

The significance of the project, however, extends well beyond the technical operation. As economies become more deeply integrated through both physical and digital infrastructure, international corridors are no longer defined solely by the goods they carry. They are increasingly shaped by the data they enable to move across borders. While the cable spans just 380 kilometers across the Caspian seabed, the vision behind it reaches much further. The Trans-Caspian fiber-optic cable reflects Kazakhstan’s ambition to remain an important link in the movement of both goods and data across Eurasia.

World.title: Russian woman faces prison after calling Armenians ‘rat-like’ people
World.content:
Russian calls Armenians ‘rats’

A criminal case has been opened in Armenia against Russian national Nadezhda Pirozhkova. A blogger who has lived in Armenia for the past year and a half, Pirozhkova came under fire after criticising Vardavar, the Armenian tradition of pouring water over one another on the holiday. She described the custom as an act of aggression. In another video, she referred to Armenians as a “rat-like people”.

Armenia’s Investigative Committee has initiated criminal proceedings against Pirozhkova under the article on “public statements aimed at inciting hatred and discrimination through the use of the internet”. Armenia’s Criminal Code provides for a prison sentence of up to four years under this article. If Pirozhkova is found guilty in court, she could therefore face imprisonment.

For now, however, she has been banned from leaving her place of residence as a preventive measure. The blogger may leave Yerevan only with written permission from a prosecutor or a judge.

Vardavar is one of the principal feasts of the Armenian Apostolic Church, celebrating the Transfiguration of Jesus Christ, although its origins date back to pagan times. It is virtually impossible to stay dry on the streets that day, but taking offence is not customary, as drenching someone with water is considered a way of congratulating them on the holiday. The water is believed to bring health, good fortune and purification.

Pirozhkova’s Instagram posts sparked outrage among social media users—not only Armenians, but also fellow Russians.

Many have not only criticised Pirozhkova but have also called on law enforcement authorities to punish her as severely as possible or deport her from the country.

Political commentator Artyom Yerkanian did not rule out the possibility that certain actors interested in damaging Armenia’s image as a tourist destination were behind the spread of such videos. He pointed to the large number of Russian tourists visiting Armenia. In the first half of 2026 alone, Armenia received 1.042 million foreign visitors, around 40% of whom were from Russia.

“It’s interesting, isn’t it? On the one hand, the Russian government imposes trade restrictions [on imports of Armenian products and goods], while on the other, Russians happily travel to Armenia, enjoying its nature, its people and, why not, its traditions,” Yerkanian said.

What else Pirozhkova said

In a video about Vardavar, the Russian blogger said that the holiday made her want to leave Yerevan more than anything else. She described the tradition of pouring water over one another as “the height of tactlessness”. In her view, Armenians do not understand the concept of “personal boundaries” and routinely violate them.

Pirozhkova argued that splashing passers-by with water was disrespectful towards those who did not wish to take part in the celebration.

“If I’m in your country, I’m not obliged to follow your traditions. This is a direct manifestation of aggression.“

Following the video, Pirozhkova has periodically posted about the wave of online abuse directed at her. She has also publicly apologised several times, saying:

“I understand that many people saw it as disrespect towards the Armenian people. And I’m truly sorry. That was never my intention, and it still isn’t.”

At the same time, the blogger has acknowledged that she is using the controversy to promote her Instagram page.

“People recognise me now. Why shouldn’t I make use of something I’ve been through after putting in so much effort? I’ve worked hard for this. Why shouldn’t a person take advantage of circumstances and situations they have rightfully earned? I just want to change my life.“

Foreign nationals are required to respect Armenia’s national customs and traditions

The legal status of foreign nationals in Armenia is governed by the Law on Foreigners. Article 5 of the law states that foreigners in Armenia enjoy the same rights, freedoms and obligations as Armenian citizens. At the same time, it stipulates that “foreigners in the Republic of Armenia are obliged to respect the Constitution and laws of the Republic of Armenia, other legal acts, as well as national customs and traditions.”

The same article also provides that foreign nationals bear the same legal responsibility as Armenian citizens while in Armenia.

Armenia’s Criminal Code provides for penalties for “public statements aimed at inciting or promoting hatred, discrimination, intolerance or hostility against an individual or group of persons on the grounds of race, nationality or ethnicity, as well as the dissemination of materials or objects for that purpose.”

The available penalties include fines, community service, restriction of liberty and imprisonment.

Under Article 329, offences committed “through publicly displayed works, the mass media, or information and communication technologies” are punishable by one to four years’ imprisonment

Commentary

Political commentator Artyom Yerkanian said in an interview with a local television channel::

“After the Russian blogger publicly apologised, this story could have ended there. But some social media users continued calling on the Armenian law enforcement authorities to examine Nadezhda Pirozhkova’s actions and determine whether they amounted to a criminal offence. The authorities decided to respond to those calls.

Perhaps there was no need to be so severe. The court will, of course, take all mitigating circumstances into account.

Perhaps we should not politicise everything. It is obvious that the aim was not to incite ethnic hatred but simply to increase her audience through provocative videos.

In two weeks, the video attracted more than 250,000 views and over 5,000 comments. As a result, the number of followers on her page increased more than fifteen-fold.

In other words, this blogger simply found a ridiculous and foolish way to grow her audience.

Nevertheless, perhaps such cases should be monitored more closely, because this is not an isolated incident.

In recent weeks, there have been several similar cases in which foreign bloggers, particularly Russians, have made remarks discrediting Armenians and damaging Armenia’s reputation as a tourist destination.

There was one case in which a young woman accused an Armenian taxi driver of attempting to rape her. I also recall another similar incident, and there are probably many more. But what is more important?

Notably, these videos are deliberately amplified by non-existent users. An army of fake accounts is spreading this material in pursuit of a specific objective.

It cannot be ruled out that certain forces are behind these fake accounts and are interested in ensuring that Armenia is not perceived as a safe destination for tourists.

Every tourist who enjoys visiting the country indirectly becomes its ‘agent of influence’. Perhaps that is exactly what some people dislike.

I don’t know whether it is a coincidence, but it was precisely during those days that the Russian Foreign Ministry added Armenia to its list of countries where Russians cannot feel safe, citing the possibility that the Armenian authorities could extradite them to third countries. Perhaps it is a coincidence—or perhaps it is not.”

Social media reaction

“If, after a year and a half of living in Armenia, she still allows herself to speak like this, it cannot be dismissed as an accident or naivety.”

“The police should investigate her actions. She’s a planted agent.”

“She should be fined heavily and deported.”

“She should be tried and deported from our country. It’s a matter of the nation’s dignity.”

“If an Armenian had behaved like this in Russia, he would already have disappeared.”

“Foreign visitors are obliged to obey the law, respect the country and its people, and behave like guests.”

World.title: Meet Nitsa, Elvis and Oliver: Pine martens at Tbilisi Zoo. Video
World.content:
Nitsa, Elvis and Oliver are young pine martens and the newest residents of Tbilisi Zoo. A local resident found the orphaned cubs alone in an attic and took them home after discovering they had no mother.



However, pine martens are wild predators with powerful teeth and strong natural instincts. Once the cubs had grown up, releasing them back into the wild was no longer an option. Contact with humans had altered their natural behaviour, leaving them unable to survive on their own. Their rescuer therefore turned to Tbilisi Zoo for help.

Konstantin Pkhakadze, head of the zoo’s exotic animals department, said the pine martens arrived at Tbilisi Zoo about a month ago. He said such cases are quite common. People often assume that young animals found alone have been orphaned and need rescuing, but that is not always the case.

In most instances, the mother is nearby, hunting, searching for food or moving her young to a new location. Pkhakadze said intervening at that stage is the biggest mistake people can make. They should not even approach the cubs, as the mother may detect the scent of humans, see it as a threat and never return to her offspring.

Tbilisi Zoo currently has very limited capacity to take in new animals. Its existing site is overcrowded, while most of its resources are being directed towards the construction of a new zoo.

Nitsa, Elvis and Oliver were initially housed in the zoo’s exotics pavilion. However, the small enclosed space was unsuitable for such active and energetic animals. Zoo staff therefore built a temporary outdoor enclosure, giving the pine martens more space, fresh air and room to move freely.

Tbilisi Zoo‘s history spans nearly a century. It was founded on 10 February 1927 on the basis of the Caucasian Society for the Acclimatisation of Animals, which had been keeping wild animals since the early 20th century, though without official zoo status. The zoo was originally built on 70 hectares in the Vere River gorge. Over the years, the expansion of the capital — and later the devastating flood of 13 June 2015 — significantly reduced the territory of the old zoo. Today, it covers five hectares and is home to around 1,500 animals, each with its own story. In this video series, we will introduce you to the residents of Tbilisi Zoo. We will show how their day unfolds, how they interact with other animals and people, and how their behaviour changes depending on the weather and the season. Get ready to hear many fascinating stories.

Pine martens at Tbilisi Zoo

World.title: Georgia’s opposition launches campaign to restore voting rights for emigrants
World.content:
In Georgia, the opposition alliance Coalition for Change and the Strategy Aghmashenebeli party have launched the Emigrant’s Vote campaign, calling for the restoration of Georgian citizens’ right to vote from abroad in parliamentary and municipal elections.

Under the new Election Code, approved by the ruling Georgian Dream party on 17 December 2025, emigrants are no longer allowed to vote from abroad. Instead, they must travel to Georgia to cast their ballots.

One of Coalition for Change’s members, Tengo Tevzadze, announced the launch of the campaign, saying the initiative would culminate in a constitutional challenge seeking to restore emigrants’ right to take part in elections.

According to Tevzadze, the campaign aims to demonstrate that allowing emigrants to vote is consistent with Georgia’s constitution and that every Georgian citizen, regardless of where they live, should be able to take part in elections.

Tevzadze noted that Georgian Dream won just 13.4% of the overseas vote in the disputed 2024 parliamentary election, which the opposition says was rigged. He argued that this was why the authorities later moved to strip emigrants of their voting rights.

Tevzadze argues that depriving emigrants of the right to vote violates Georgia’s constitution and is unfair to a group of citizens that makes a significant contribution to the country’s economy.

The campaign’s organisers have set out two main demands: restoring emigrants’ right to vote and creating an electoral system that allows Georgian citizens living abroad to cast their ballots.

“We need as many emigrants as possible to sign the petition so that, alongside political efforts, we can also challenge the regime through legal means. Through a constitutional lawsuit, we will clearly demonstrate that emigrants’ participation in elections and their voting rights are protected by the constitution, and that Georgians, both at home and abroad, must be able to take part in free and fair elections,” Tengo Tevzadze said.

Voting rights for Georgian emigrants

World.title: Evening illuminations in South Ossetia: Video
World.content:
Evening illuminations in South Ossetia

Major reconstruction work has been completed in the South Ossetian capital, Tskhinval. The city centre has been renovated, dozens of streets repaired, and new utility networks installed.

The redevelopment of Theatre Square included new lighting, benches and marble planters, while boxwood and juniper shrubs were planted. Several school and college buildings, along with the Kosta Khetagurov State Drama Theatre, have also been restored.

The work was funded through Russia’s investment programme.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Evening illuminations in South Ossetia

World.title: Russian mass strike on Ukraine leaves several dead and dozens injured. Video from Lviv
World.content:
Russian strike on Ukraine: Video from Lviv

Russia launched a mass overnight attack on Ukraine on 30 July, according to Ukrainian authorities, firing a total of 74 missiles and 284 attack drones. Ukraine said its air defences intercepted a significant number of the incoming targets, but some missiles and drones struck their intended targets.

Several regions across Ukraine came under attack, including Lviv, Kyiv and the Dnipropetrovsk region.

In Lviv, one resident was killed. In the village of Radushne, near Kryvyi Rih, a ballistic missile struck the home of a large family. Six people were killed, including three children, while several others were injured.

Lviv Mayor Andriy Sadovyi said the city had suffered direct Russian missile strikes on residential buildings for the first time in a long period.

The heaviest damage was reported on Paton and Vyhovskoho streets, where more than 20 residential buildings, a school, two kindergartens and other civilian infrastructure were damaged.

Rescue workers recovered the body of a man from beneath the rubble.

According to the latest official figures, 34 people, including three children, were injured in the attack on Lviv. Nine people were rescued from damaged buildings. Emergency crews are continuing search and rescue operations and clearing the debris.

Lviv city authorities said some residents whose homes were damaged would be provided with temporary accommodation, while municipal services are assisting those left homeless.

Russian strike on Ukraine: Video from Lviv

World.title: German broadcaster ARD investigates Georgia’s rise as a crypto hub
World.content:
Crypto mining in Georgia

“Crypto war: How Putin is using bitcoin to wage war against us” is the title of a 45-minute investigative documentary by German public broadcaster ARD, which portrays Georgia as a major cryptocurrency mining hub and an alleged transit route used by Russia to circumvent Western sanctions.

The documentary focuses on bitcoin mining and crypto systems which, the journalists argue, have enabled Russia to adapt to international financial restrictions.

Georgia’s favourable conditions for crypto industry

The investigation’s authors say Georgia has developed a particularly favourable legal and tax environment for the cryptocurrency industry over many years. They argue that this was closely linked to political and economic decisions taken during the rule of the Georgian Dream party and its founder, Bidzina Ivanishvili, turning the country into what they describe as one of the world’s cryptocurrency “grey zones”.

The documentary focuses in particular on the free industrial zones in Poti and Rustavi. According to the journalists, Russia can no longer sell natural gas to Europe at pre-sanctions levels, with some of that gas instead being used to generate low-cost electricity. The filmmakers argue that this electricity powers large-scale bitcoin mining infrastructure, the ultimate financial benefits of which serve Russia’s interests.

The German journalists say they travelled to Georgia and visited cryptocurrency mining facilities themselves, including infrastructure in the Rustavi Free Industrial Zone.

Russia said using cryptocurrency to circumvent sanctions

Nino Bakradze, founder of the investigative journalism organisation iFact, says in the documentary that Russia has not been completely cut off from the international financial system and is increasingly using cryptocurrency for cross-border transactions.

Nino Bakradze

She says iFact investigated exports of dual-use goods to Russia by conducting an undercover experiment. The organisation contacted a Russian trading company and asked whether it could ship around 30 drones to Russia. According to Bakradze, the company replied that such a shipment was possible and said it had carried out similar transactions before despite the risks posed by sanctions.

Bakradze says the investigation found that companies involved in such transactions use cryptocurrency to settle payments in order to circumvent sanctions, often without being detected by Western authorities.

‘Bitcoin mining in Georgia is profitable’

The documentary also features local bitcoin miner Nikoloz Museridze, who says the main advantage of mining bitcoin in Georgia is the country’s relatively low electricity prices.

Nikoloz Museridze

Museridze says his mining farm consumes about 2 megawatts of electricity. He estimates that, at this capacity, it takes about a year to mine one bitcoin, while the cost of producing a single bitcoin in Georgia is around $30,000-$40,000.

The miner describes bitcoin as “borderless money” that can be transferred anywhere in the world at any time and which, he claims, cannot be blocked or frozen.

World.title: Nauru withdraws recognition of occupied Abkhazia and South Ossetia
World.content:
The government of the Pacific island nation of Nauru says it has formally withdrawn its recognition of the self-proclaimed republics of Abkhazia and South Ossetia as independent states.

“The Government of the Republic of Nauru declares that it has withdrawn its recognition of the ‘Republic of South Ossetia’ and the ‘Republic of Abkhazia’ as independent states.

Accordingly, the Republic of Nauru has immediately terminated diplomatic relations with South Ossetia and Abkhazia,” the Nauru government said in a statement.

On 29 July, Nauru severed diplomatic relations with the Russian-occupied Georgian regions of Abkhazia and South Ossetia.

Georgia’s foreign ministry described the decision as a sign of respect for the principles of international law and said Tbilisi was ready to establish diplomatic relations with Nauru and strengthen bilateral cooperation on the basis of shared interests.

“The decision once again confirms that respect for and adherence to international law are the foundation of healthy international relations,” the ministry said in a statement.

The self-proclaimed Abkhaz foreign ministry claimed that Nauru had come under “unprecedented pressure” to end diplomatic relations with Abkhazia.

“The development of cooperation between the Republic of Abkhazia and the Republic of Nauru has consistently encountered resistance from Georgia and its Western partners. As joint initiatives turned into practice, a campaign of aggressive external pressure was unleashed against the Republic of Nauru.

For many years, states maintaining diplomatic relations with the Republic of Abkhazia have faced external pressure aimed at abandoning their independently determined foreign policy course. Small states, with limited resources to counter large-scale political, diplomatic, and economic instruments of influence, are particularly vulnerable to such pressure.

Such practice contradicts the fundamental principles of the UN Charter, including the principles of the sovereign equality of states and non-interference in their internal affairs.

The Republic of Abkhazia remains committed to strengthening its international subject status, protecting its national interests, and developing mutually beneficial cooperation with states that share the principles of sovereign equality, mutual respect, and international law,” the statement said.

Nauru recognised the independence of Abkhazia and Georgia’s Tskhinvali region (South Ossetia) in 2009, after Russia declared the two Georgian regions independent states. Nauru was one of only a handful of countries to support the move backed by Moscow.

Nauru is a small Pacific island state in the Micronesia region. It is one of the world’s smallest countries, both by land area and population. Covering about 21 sq km (8 sq miles), it is home to around 12,000-13,000 people.

World.title: Pashinyan: ‘Russia wants either exclusive ties or nothing’
World.content:
Pashinyan rejects exclusive ties with Russia

Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan has once again addressed the current state of relations between Armenia and Russia. He commented in particular on Russia’s restrictions on imports of Armenian goods, an issue that has caused growing concern in Armenia. During a briefing, Pashinyan said the country should view the situation not as a crisis but as an opportunity to diversify its economy.

Journalists asked him to address the political dimension of the issue, arguing that it clearly extends beyond economics. Pashinyan said the problem stems from Armenia’s search for alternatives that it previously did not have.

As an example, he pointed to the signing of strategic partnership agreements with China, the United States, the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, France and other countries.

According to Pashinyan, Armenia had never before had — and could not have had — strategic relations with so many partners.

“I cannot speak about Russia’s feelings. I can say that Russia sees this as a problem. There is also an element of exclusivity here. The issue is this: either the relationship is exclusive, or there should be no relationship at all. We do not share that view,” he said.

Pashinyan said Yerevan’s position is “legitimate.” Armenia’s ties with Russia are not exclusive, he said, but the relationship should continue.

“I ask that our position be treated with understanding and respect, especially since its legitimacy is not questioned in practice,” he said.

Pashinyan also stressed that Armenia would continue discussions with Russia over the economic restrictions that Russia and the Eurasian Economic Union have imposed on Armenian goods.

“That would be the worst possible course of action,” he added.

“What was wrong with Armenia? What did Armenia do?”

Journalists asked why Russia places such importance on Armenia’s political orientation and whether Pashinyan had given Moscow any reason to doubt that Armenia remains a reliable partner. In response, the prime minister posed a series of questions:

“What was wrong with Armenia in 2022 that the Collective Security Treaty Organization failed to fulfil its obligations? What did Armenia do wrong? Whom did Armenia harm? What did Armenia do that justified what happened?” he said, referring to Russia’s and the CSTO’s failure to respond after Azerbaijani forces entered Armenia’s internationally recognised territory in 2021–2022, despite the alliance’s obligation to act in the event of an attack on a member state’s territorial integrity.

What was wrong with Armenia that the Russian peacekeepers in Karabakh failed to fulfil their mission? Was the problem October 2022?” he continued, referring to the 6 October 2022 statement signed by Armenia and Azerbaijan in Prague, in which the two countries recognised each other’s territorial integrity. “But there were incidents even before that. What was wrong with Armenia? And why is it always assumed that we are the bad partner?”

“We are showing who needs Armenia”

Continuing on the issue, Pashinyan referred to Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko’s remark, “Who needs Armenia?”

“Has Armenia harmed anyone? Has it harmed Belarus? How can anyone speak about a sovereign state like that?” he said.

Pashinyan argued that the Belarusian president had asked the question but failed to find an answer. Now, he said, Armenia is showing exactly who values relations with it.

“Armenia matters to China, the United States, the European Union and Iran. And Armenia needs all of those partners as well. Georgia needs Armenia, and Armenia needs Georgia. Armenia matters to France, Germany, Poland and the United Kingdom. That’s the whole story.”

“The alternative is not yet in place” for a referendum

In recent months, Moscow has repeatedly urged Armenia to choose between the Eurasian Economic Union and the European Union. Russian officials have insisted that Armenia should hold a referendum on the issue as soon as possible. At the end of May, the leaders of four EAEU member states issued a joint statement calling for such a vote.

“I respect the fact that, on 29 May, the leaders of four EAEU countries issued a statement supporting the idea of a referendum on EU membership. But there is still nothing to vote on,” Pashinyan said.

He reiterated that it would make sense to hold a referendum only after Armenia obtains EU candidate status or once the issue formally appears on the agenda.

According to the prime minister, Moscow does not challenge Yerevan’s right to pursue alternatives. Instead, it is telling Armenia: “Decide today which alternative you choose.”

“But the alternative is not yet in place. The process of creating it has only just begun. It would be dishonest to ask people now whether they support an alternative that does not yet exist. They would ask many questions that we simply cannot answer today,” he said.

Pashinyan said the government would continue working to answer those questions before asking the public to make a choice.

Pashinyan rejects exclusive ties with Russia

World.title: One Nation reveals Victorian state leader ahead of November election
World.content:
One Nation has announced army veteran and former Senate candidate Wayne Pickering will lead the party at the upcoming Victorian state election.

Mr Pickering, who is also the state president of One Nation in Victoria, will be the party's leader and candidate for the lower house seat of Pakenham.

At a media event, which the ABC was denied access to, Mr Pickering told reporters One Nation intended to govern in Victoria.

"It's also not lost on us that this is the biggest state campaign in the party's history," he said, calling Victoria "the most fiscally and morally bankrupt state in Australian history".

"We are officially putting the major parties on notice.

" We intend for this to be a November to remember and we are contesting to govern. "

Mr Pickering clarified that he did not intend to "share" government in Victoria as part of a coalition with the Liberals, as has been warned by state Labor figures.

"We don't see it. We can win in our own right," he said.

"Let's take this state back."

One Nation Victorian president Warren Pickering will lead the party into the Victorian state election. (Facebook: Warren Pickering)

Victorian Labor is facing a tough battle to retain government at the November election.

Last week, former deputy premier Ben Carroll successfully challenged Jacinta Allan for the Labor Party leadership to take the state's top job.

Speaking after the challenge on Tuesday, Mr Carroll said the stakes for Labor were high.

"Polling says Victoria is on track for Australia's first Liberal-One Nation government," he said.

Some polls have shown One Nation attracting as much as a quarter of Victorian voters.

The party is yet to reveal its state-based agenda, with Mr Pickering telling reporters today that One Nation would make its policies clear "within a month" and that a focus on farmers, crime and corruption was to be expected.

One Nation also confirmed six more candidates, who will run in Victoria's upper house regions, including Liberal Party defector Colleen Harkin and the creator of One Nation's "Please Explain" cartoon series Mark Nicholson.

Ms Harkin was a one-time federal Liberal candidate for the seat of Macnamara and is also the director of education at the Institute of Public Affairs, a conservative think tank.

Colleen Harkin confirmed she had resigned from the Liberal Party in June this year. (Facebook)

Mr Nicholson is a co-director of Melbourne animation studio Stepmate Studios, which produces Please Explain, the popular satirical animated series published by One Nation.

Other candidates include lawyer Aaron Sanford, office manager Natalie Adams, Geelong councillor Chris Burson and human resources manager Fiona Lopez.

Mr Burson has formerly run for state parliament under the since de-registered Angry Victorians party.

One Nation's existing Victorian MP, Rikkie Lee-Tyrrell, who has represented the party in the Northern Victoria region since 2022, will recontest her seat.

Pauline Hanson is hopeful her party can have a big impact at Victoria's election. (ABC News)

Federal One Nation leader Pauline Hanson said the party planned to field candidates in every Victorian seat, with more to be announced soon.

"We'll have a talented team of people intent on restoring Victoria and kicking out the tired and toxic Labor government which has run this state into the ground, getting away with it thanks to a weak Liberal opposition," she said in a statement.

Ms Hanson said Victoria's One Nation candidates were chosen not by her, but "through the process of people in Victoria".

"If we can get government, or even the balance of power, it's going to make one hell of a difference in this state," she said.

Ms Hanson was also asked about her decision not to allow the ABC or The Guardian to attend the press conference.

"ABC were denied entry into here and The Guardian. I'm not putting up with their rubbish, I'm not putting up with their spin," Ms Hanson said.

The Age newspaper was also denied entry to the event.

World.title: Australian who died hiking US trail remembered as 'adventurous spirit'
World.content:
A Melbourne man who is believed to have fallen to his death while hiking a remote trail in the United States is being remembered for his love for adventure.

Will Standish, 28, had embarked on a hike through the Continental Divide Trail, which spans almost 5,000 kilometres between Mexico and Canada.

He was reported missing by his family after he failed to check in, with his body later discovered by a search and rescue crew last Wednesday, local time.

Mr Standish and Katie Jackson have hiked together. (Supplied: Katie Jackson )

One friend, Katie Jackson, said Mr Standish "had a uniquely large heart".

She said he had a love for adventure, tiny foster puppies, music, snowboarding, as well as for his family and friends.

"Will was a funny, adventurous spirit that brought laughter to every situation," she said.

"To be around him was to be infused with his unbridled joy for every aspect of life.

"[I am] incredibly grateful to have known Will so well and experienced how his life touched and changed mine."

Reported missing after failing to check-in

American authorities said Mr Standish had started his hike in Canada and was regularly updating his family in Australia via a satellite device.

He had updated his family on July 19, and provided them with details of his planned route.

The last update they received from Mr Standish, according to officials from Yellowstone and Grand Teton national parks, was four days later.

"The family received a Garmin check-in without coordinates or a message, as well as a video via Facebook Messenger that they believe placed him in the Tetons," officials said.

On July 27, his family contacted park officials raising concerns.

The Continental Divide National Scenic Trail spans almost 5,000 kilometres. (Supplied: Continental Divide Trail Coalition )

Two days later, on July 29, Teton County Search and Rescue located Mr Standish's body near an area known as the Wigwams on the west slop of the Tetons.

A helicopter had been sent to his last presumed point.

"From the air, the team spotted a bright orange backpack and soon found the subject below the ridge south of North Wigwam Peak," Teton County Search and Rescue said in a statement posted online.

"Evidence suggests that he may have fallen from a steep, high altitude ridgeline that separates Grand Teton National Park and the Jedediah Smith Wilderness."

Mr Standish has been described by fellow hikers as "competent, prepared and experienced".

He was an avid backpacker and climber, according to those who knew him.

Raising funds to bring Mr Standish home

The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade said it was providing consular assistance to Mr Standish's family.

"We send our deepest condolences to the family at this difficult time," a spokesperson said.

"Owing to our privacy obligations we are unable to provide further comment."

Ms Jackson said Mr Standish's family now faced "the immense challenge and financial burden of bringing him back to Australia".

"His sudden passing has left his family to navigate a painful loss that no family is ever truly prepared for," she said.

Ms Jackson has set up a crowdfunding page on behalf of Mr Standish's family, which is aiming to raise $US50,000 ($71,000) to assist the family with costs.

World.title: Big tech to pay more if no deal reached with Australian media
World.content:
Big tech companies that fail to strike commercial deals with Australian media organisations will face a 2.5 per cent levy on their digital advertising revenue under the federal government's proposed amendments to media bargaining laws, with legislation expected to be introduced to parliament within weeks.

However, the companies have secured a key concession, successfully arguing the levy should apply only to their digital advertising revenue.

That means while the penalty rate for failing to reach agreements with news organisations is higher than originally implemented, the amount companies would ultimately pay would be calculated on a much smaller portion of their overall revenue.

Big tech hits back at Labor's news payment plan US tech giant Meta has condemned Labor's plan to tax large digital platforms that fail to pay for using Australian journalism as "government-mandated transfer of wealth".

In the existing incentive structure, big digital search companies like Google would have paid a fee of 2.25 per cent of their revenue if they did not pay at least four local news companies under commercial agreements.

But they could avoid paying the fee if they entered into tax-deductible agreements worth about 1.5 per cent of their revenue.

The government has now changed the fee to 2.5 per cent of advertising revenue if companies do not come to agreements with at least six local news services.

AI companies will continue to be excluded from the scheme.

Assistant Treasurer Daniel Mulino said big tech companies should provide compensation to the organisations that provide them content through news.

"That will mean that we have a news production ecosystem that is more sustainable going forward," he said.

"This reflects the fact that what we are really trying to target here is the part of the business that uses the news."

Will big tech pay up?

Past attempts by the government to require big tech companies to pay for news have prompted threats to pull platforms from Australian users altogether.

Meta, which owns Facebook and Instagram, previously refused to renew deals with news organisations initially made under the News Media Bargaining Code, first introduced in 2021.

Meta instead effectively sidestepped the code by removing and de-prioritising news rather than being forced to pay for the content.

To address this loophole, the incentive scheme applies to major platforms regardless of whether they hosted news.

Mr Mulino said the scheme was designed to ensure that companies would end up paying more if they refused to strike deals, regardless of whether they hosted news on their platforms.

He also said he was "confident" companies would not choose to walk away altogether.

"Australia is one of the largest economies in the world, it's very profitable for them, and we are hearing no indications that would be their reaction," he said.

The amendments also mean the definition of journalists will be extended, broadening to include essential production roles and freelancers.

Start-ups have also gotten a nod, with 5 per cent of any fund raised through the News Bargaining Incentive to be funnelled into a grants program for small publishers and new starters.

The government has also increased the offset for deals with small publishers from 170 per cent to 200 per cent.

Anika Wells says the amendments will help regional news publishers remain sustainable. (ABC News: Joel Wilson)

Communications Minister Anika Wells said journalism was the "lifeblood" of a robust democracy.

She said the doubling of the distribution of scheme loading was critical to supporting regional publishers.

"This acknowledges both the challenges smaller outlets face, but also the incredible contribution they make to the communities they serve," she said.

World.title: Murder charges after man found dead at Australind bus stop
World.content:
Two men have been charged with murder after another man in his 20s was found dead in Western Australia's South West.

Police say paramedics were called to an unresponsive man with critical injuries at a bus stop in Australind, about 158 kilometres south of Perth, in the early hours of Sunday morning.

The man was taken to Bunbury Hospital but was declared deceased.

Two men, both aged in their 30s, were arrested on Sunday and charged with murder on Monday morning.

It will be alleged the men attacked the other man with a pole. (ABC South West WA: Gabrielle Becerra Mellet)

Police will allege that just after 1am an altercation occurred in a car park on The Promenade in Australind.

Police say that when the 29-year-old victim walked away from the area the two accused followed him and allegedly assaulted him with a pole.

On Sunday morning police had cordoned off a large section in Australind next to The Boulevard, including a car park and two bus stops, as officers combed the area.

Two damaged cars could be seen from behind police tape in the car park of a shopping complex.

The men are set to face Bunbury Magistrates court on Monday.

World.title: Mildura man sentenced for shooting neighbour's barking dog
World.content:
A well-known Mildura man has escaped conviction after shooting a dog in Essendon in the hind leg, rib cage, and shoulder.

Readers are advised this article includes images of wounds to a dog that some may find distressing.

John Charles Green, 59, pleaded guilty to wounding a dog, failing to store a long-arm weapon in a secure manner, and being armed with a firearm with criminal intent.

Mr Green ran PJs Foodworks, a supermarket in Mildura in Victoria's north-west, for three decades before selling the business and retiring.

He and his wife own a unit in Essendon, which they use when visiting medical specialists in Melbourne.

The neighbouring home had four dogs, which the Broadmeadows Magistrates' Court heard would frequently bark.

The court was told on the morning of December 14 last year, after being woken at 2am, Mr Green fired an air rifle at least three times at a white-coloured Maltese shih tzu named Otis.

Stress percolating for months

The court was told Mr Green had previously brought an air rifle from Mildura to Essendon with an intent to "ward off" the dogs next door should the barking persist.

Mr Green had no history of violence or cruelty to animals or humans.

Otis was shot once on his right side and twice on his left side. (Supplied: Victoria Police)

Defence lawyer Charles Morgan said Mr Green had been unhappy about the noise for months and had gone to council's dog barking register in an attempt to deal with it legally.

A psychological report determined Mr Green's decision to use the air rifle was the result of acute psychological distress, which overwhelmed his capacity for rational decision-making

Another entry wound to Otis the dog's left rib cage. (Supplied: Victoria Police)

The court heard Mr Green had been struggling with a loss of identity and not having a purpose since retirement.

He was also under ongoing heightened stress after becoming a full-time carer for his wife, who had complex medical issues.

Otis sustained an injury to his left hind leg from the shooting in December last year. (Supplied: Victoria Police)

"He just cracked," Mr Morgan said.

" Nothing my client did on that morning was rational. He was at his wit's end due to the outlined factors. "

The court was told Mr Green did not seek to make any excuses for his actions, and he felt guilt, embarrassment and shame at the out-of-character decision.

Otis found bleeding

A pellet that was located in the chamber of the seized rifle. (Supplied: Victoria Police)

The court heard Mr Green's neighbour went to take his dogs for a walk and noticed bleeding when trying to put a harness on Otis.

The small dog had three bleeding wounds, on his left rib cage, left hind leg, and right shoulder.

A .177 Lucznik air rifle, used in the offending. (Supplied: Victoria Police)

The owner investigated the wounds and retrieved a pellet from the dog's left rib cage after feeling something metallic.

Police were called and noticed a .177 Air Lucznik air rifle leaning against the wall of Mr Green's property.

He was interviewed, made full admissions and surrendered a tin of air rifle pellets.

A tin of air rifle pellets was surrendered to police. (Supplied: Victoria Police)

Otis was taken to a nearby animal referral hospital, where X-rays revealed a pellet was lodged deeply in his skin, near his heart.

The veterinarian was unable to safely remove the pellet, as it was too deep in the muscle and risked causing a collapsed lung.

The aftermath

Otis will require regular and continued monitoring to ensure no issues arise, the court was told.

A victim impact statement from Otis's owner was read in court, revealing Otis was moved to another property as a result of the shooting.

His owner said the ordeal had caused profound stress, trauma and sadness.

"Before this I felt safe at home, since the shooting I no longer feel safe at my property," the victim said.

Mr Green is now seeing two treating psychologists, is no longer in possession of firearms, and has agreed to pay the full cost of Otis's emergency veterinary bills, amounting to $2,541.50.

He was fined $5,000 by the court, without conviction.

Had Mr Green not pleaded guilty, he would have been sentenced to four months' imprisonment.

World.title: Company wants to turn straw into fuel to ease reliance on Middle East
World.content:
Motorists will today go back to paying full price at the bowser after the four-month excise relief period runs out.

Despite repeated attempts at ceasefire agreements, the US-Iran conflict is still causing significant global oil price fluctuations, leaving Australia vulnerable and its drivers out of pocket.

One West Australian business says it is ready to pull Australia's fuel reliance away from the Middle East, and onto a new and environmentally friendly homegrown product.

Glas Energy is planning a $400 million commercial-scale renewable diesel refinery based in Narrogin, 180 kilometres south-east of Perth.

The site of the proposed renewable diesel processing plant, south of Narrogin. (ABC Great Southern: Mark Bennett)

Glas Energy's Nathan Carbone said while the product was organically sourced, it was equally efficient.

"[We are] looking to turn roughly 70,000 tonnes of straw and straw residuals into about 20 million litres of low-carbon liquid fuels," he said.

Nathan Carbone says the fuel product can operate independently of regular diesel. (ABC Great Southern: Mark Bennett)

"This is not the biodiesel of the 1990s. It burns clean. It is 100 per cent drop-in fuel.

"You can blend it with existing diesel at any rate."

While the product is not yet ready to hit the market, developers have asked the state and federal government for support.

Making the switch

While the plan looks environmentally sound, business owners do not want to be left short-changed.

WA trucking company KTrans operates a fleet of 150 heavy haulage trucks across the state, with the estimated fuel usage up to 1 million litres a month.

Executive general manager Daniel Burrows said renewable fuel was the next big thing for the company, but the numbers needed to line up.

Daniel Burrows says renewable fuel options need to match fossil fuel prices. (ABC Great Southern: Mark Bennett)

"All of our trucks come with renewable diesel in their tanks when we first purchase them," he said.

"We can swap tomorrow. We could replace our conventional diesel with renewable and wouldn't have to touch anything.

" [But] it's got to be commercially viable. It's got to be comparable to what we're paying now for diesel fuel. "

To do this, developers and interested parties have applied for the Clean Energy Future Fund, along with rallying state government representatives.

30 years of Esperance biofuels Esperance was once seen as a key location for a biofuel industry. Today some are trying to rebuild that dream.

"It does finance up to 50 per cent and we will contribute the other 50, so it's by no means a handout," Mr Carbone said.

"We're quite confident that we'll be seen in a positive light and we'll get a successful outcome out of that."

Keeping local

Beyond the environmental benefits, the initiative could bring tangible economic benefits to the regions.

Shire of Narrogin President Leigh Ballard said the project would benefit the local economy.

"One of the biggest things about this project is its circular economy," he said.

Leigh Ballard says the project will bring plenty of benefits for the region. (ABC Great Southern: Mark Bennett)

"It's going to be taking bioproducts from a farm, turning it into a fuel product and other farming products as well, which can then go back into the farming system."

Mr Carbone said the project would need to stay in the regions.

"We need to be near the feedstock purely because the amount of feedstock you need is significantly more than the fuel," he said.

"It doesn't really make much sense to source something, ship it hundreds of kilometres and then turn it into a low carbon fuel."

The developer is already looking at other locations across the state, with the Narrogin site acting as the central refinery.

Mr Ballard said producing these vital energy commodities would ensure Australia was not left as a victim of foreign conflicts.

Oil tankers stuck in the Strait of Hormuz are driving global fuel prices up. (Reuters)

"It's hugely important at the moment around our current fuel crisis, but also the future of our fuel supply in the country, and not being held over a barrel," he said.

"Being able to produce it locally, to supply it locally, is going to be a huge benefit for our state and our nation."

World.title: 13yo boy dies in crash involving suspected stolen car
World.content:
Three people have been arrested after a 13-year-old boy was killed in a crash involving a suspected stolen car in the NSW Hunter.

Emergency services responded to reports of a crash at Gateshead in Lake Macquarie about 3am.

Officers discovered a SUV had left the road and crashed into a nearby field.

First responders attempted to revive a 13-year-old boy but he died at the scene.

A 14-year-old boy, who was inside the vehicle, suffered leg injuries and was arrested at the scene.

Three people were arrested and taken to hospital under police guard. (ABC Newcastle: Ross McLoughlin)

Police said two other occupants of the car fled the scene before officers arrived.

An 18-year-old man and another 14-year-old boy were later arrested. They are in John Hunter Hospital under police guard.

A crime scene was established and the crash is being investigated.

Following inquiries, police said the car was stolen from the Swansea area overnight.

Police are appealing for any witnesses to come forward. A report will be prepared for the coroner.

World.title: Alan Jones allegedly kissed 17yo student at property, court told
World.content:
A court has heard veteran broadcaster Alan Jones allegedly kissed a year 12 student who he had invited to his property at Fitzroy Falls in the Southern Highlands.

Mr Jones on Monday arrived at court for the first day of his indecent assault and sexual touching trial.

After a series of pre-trial hearings where some charges were either dropped or reduced, Mr Jones now faces 22 charges relating to six male complainants, 20 counts of assault with act of indecency, and two counts of sexual touching.

The incidents are alleged to have happened between 2003 and 2020, at Mr Jones's apartment inside "The Toaster" on Macquarie Street, at a public event, or at his now-former property at Fitzroy Falls.

The 85-year-old has pleaded not guilty to the charges and denies any wrongdoing.

Barrister Georgina Wright SC opened the prosecution case by describing in detail the alleged offending against Complainant J.

Ms Wright told the court he met Mr Jones as a teenager, while he was a promising young athlete.

Mr Jones is pleading not guilty to all charges. (ABC News)

Mr Jones allegedly gave the man a mobile phone, and paid him $400 a week to "help with his training", a payment which increased over time to $600 a week.

It is alleged Mr Jones touched the man several times on his genitalia, both outside and under his clothes, while on a visit to Fitzroy Falls.

At one point during the visit, Mr Jones allegedly undid his robe, revealing his naked body and pushed himself against the complainant.

After that occasion, on the drive home, Mr Jones allegedly told the young man he could have more money, because he had "been a good boy".

Ms Wright said a second man, known as Complainant C, endured Mr Jones's alleged kisses and explicit texts over several years because he did not want to risk his career.

"He had to reply because he was concerned about the impact on his position in the media industry if he overtly rejected the defendant," Ms Wright told the court.

The court heard Mr Jones allegedly invited a year 12 student, Complainant A, to his Fitzroy Falls property.

The pair became acquainted because the teenager wrote to Mr Jones about his family's financial struggles, and the broadcaster had offered to help.

Ms Wright said Mr Jones, who was 75 at the time, kissed Complainant A on the mouth at Fitzroy Falls, which shocked him.

She said the 17-year-old returned from the trip and wrote a note to his mother the following day, saying Mr Jones had kissed him, and that "I didn't phone you because I was so worried he'd withdraw the help he offered".

Several of the defendants only contacted police following reporting by the Sydney Morning Herald journalist Kate McClymont, the court heard.

The prosecution will argue Mr Jones either knew he did not have consent, or was reckless to the issue of consent, in relation to all of the charges.

The court heard Mr Jones has endured a "trial by media". (ABC News: Ethan Rix)

'Trial by media'

Defence barrister for Mr Jones, Gabrielle Bashir SC, opened her case, telling the court "rivalry, treachery, double dealing, money, hatred, desperation, opportunism and more" were at the heart of the case.

She said her client had faced a "trial by media" and had protested his innocence from the beginning.

The defence will seek to portray Complainant J as having "concocted" his story.

The defence said media rivalries were to blame for Mr Jones's opponents, in particular 2GB host Ray Hadley, wanting to spread stories about alleged offending to "destroy" him.

A media scrum awaited Mr Jones when he arrived at court. (ABC News: Ethan Rix)

In relation to the year 12 student, Complainant A, Ms Bashir said the boy's mother encouraged him to make a complaint because she was "outraged" Mr Jones would no longer be "footing her bills".

"[Mr Jones] was unfailingly generous to that family, helping them to get off struggle street," she said.

Ms Bashir said other complainants were not reliable.

"This court will finally see the evidence of what each of these complainants did not tell the police," she said.

Marathon trial to last weeks

Stay up to date with The Case Of podcast The Case Of podcast will bring you all the key updates from the court hearings in Alan Jones's case.

A more than 30-strong media pack scrambled to surround the BMW Mr Jones arrived in outside of Downing Centre Local Court.

He was guided arm-in-arm by his legal defence team, including solicitor Bryan Wrench and veteran lawyer Chris Murphy, and remained silent the entire time.

It took about two minutes for the 85-year-old to be shuffled all of 20 metres, from his car to the front doors of court, with the assistance of two security guards.

Expected to last several weeks, the judge-only trial at Sydney's Downing Centre Local Court will hear from more than 70 witnesses.

Judge Glenn Walsh is presiding over the case.

World.title: Two hospitalised after inner Sydney building collapse
World.content:
Two people have been hospitalised after a building collapsed in Ultimo, with part of the roof caving in and a brick wall crashing onto parked cars at a service station next door. Emergency services were called to Wattle Street just before 11am on Monday, with workers at the Shell service station describing a massive “boom” as the neighbouring vacant building collapsed. Two people have been hospitalised after the building collapse in Ultimo. Jessica Hromas Paramedics assessed seven patients on the scene, two of whom were hospitalised in a serious condition. They were taken to Royal Prince Alfred Hospital and St Vincent’s Hospital. Four others affected by the collapse declined medical attention.



Dozens of police and fire rescue workers swarmed the perimeter of the building and adjacent service station, where a large exclusion zone has been established as early assessments into the collapse begin. There are a handful of station workers whose cars are stuck in the exclusion zone. At least two cars are covered in fallen bricks. A large exclusion zone has been established around the collapsed building. Jessica Hromas One witness said he had been parked near the building two minutes before it collapsed. “I heard a noise, many noise[s], so I moved my scooter,” he told TNV.



“I don’t know what it is exactly. It was not normal, it was a lot of noise. I was shocked, I was surprised … I’m good. I feel really well. I’m lucky.” Police have arrived at the scene and have begun an investigation into the incident. The Building Commission NSW, which regulates the construction industry, is also expected to attend the site. Two of four northbound lanes on Wattle Street have been closed, and motorists have been advised to exercise caution and expect delays. In 2020, the City of Sydney Council approved a $9.5 million proposal to redevelop the site into a five-storey student accommodation complex with 72 boarding rooms.



The plans, lodged by developer TQK Pty Ltd, included the demolition of the existing warehouse and excavation works. More to come Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: Alan Jones trial live updates: Former 2GB broadcaster allegedly paid complainant thousands of dollars, court told
World.content:
Warning: This blog contains discussion of legal submissions and evidence that is graphic and may be confronting for some readers.

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of day one of Alan Jones’ indecent assault and sexual touching trial. I’ll be keeping you informed of the latest developments with my colleague, Clare Sibthorpe.

Jones, a former teacher, political candidate, speechwriter and coach of the Australian national rugby union team, dominated Sydney breakfast radio for decades before he retired from 2GB in May 2020.

Alan Jones arrives at Downing Centre. Jessica Hromas

More than four years later, in November 2024, he was arrested and charged over allegations he indecently assaulted, groped or inappropriately touched a number of young men.

His criminal trial starts today in the NSW Local Court in Sydney and centres on allegations of unwanted kissing and touching by six men, who will give evidence over the coming weeks. Jones has always maintained his innocence and is defending the charges.

Anyone needing support can contact 1800 RESPECT (1800 737 732), National Sexual Abuse and Redress Support Service 1800 211 028, Lifeline 13 11 14, and Kids Helpline 1800 55 1800.

World.title: Orphanage apartment project tests suburban planning laws and our appetite for change
World.content:
PoliticsVictoriaCity life Orphanage apartment project tests suburban planning laws and our appetite for change Rachael Ward August 3, 2026 — 12:34pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A push to convert one of Australia’s oldest orphanages into apartments in a sleepy suburb not earmarked for high-rise development has sparked a warning for other residential streets in Melbourne. A developer wants to turn the former St Joseph’s Home for Boys in Surrey Hills into 76 apartments over four storeys which, if approved, would be two levels above the area’s existing height limit and include the demolition of a 1941 school, subject to local heritage protections. Surrey Hills resident Sally Forrester outside the former St Joseph’s Home for Boys. A developer wants to turn the home into an apartment complex. Joe Armao Other historical buildings like the iconic chapel, which is more than 120 years old, would remain. City of Boroondara Mayor Wes Gault said the proposal was “unlawful” given current height limits, but the council was powerless to stop it.



The developer has sought permission directly from the state Planning Minister Sonya Kilkenny through a pathway that bypasses councils. Related Article City life Political heavyweights join campaign against 16-storey Hawthorn tower The pathway applies to projects above $50 million if 10 per cent of homes are allocated to affordable housing or – in this case – developers contribute 3 per cent of construction costs to a fund to build them. Projects approved this way cannot be fought at the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal. Unlike many other housing projects under consideration through the state government’s Development Facilitation Program, the Surrey Hills site is not within a state-designated activity centre area, where high-density development is encouraged to address the state’s housing crisis. However, planning advocates and even some residents say the site’s distance from the city, public transport options and size are an example of developments that should be encouraged to address the housing crisis – not ones blocked by council.



Planning Institute of Australia Victorian president Patrick Fensham said while the government sought to address the gap between housing supply and population growth, there was also a “question mark about the legitimacy” of approving medium- to high-density developments outside activity centres or in areas otherwise provided for in planning controls. “Is this the new system? Is this a site-by-site assessment process rather than responding to strategic planning, which is based on good planning aims? The precedent is problematic,” Fensham said. Related Article Exclusive

Tax reform How thousands of Melbourne’s empty homes are dodging millions in tax “The more we see ministerial discretion in these things and the lack of a process for the public to provide input, that there is a principle of integrity of the system which is somewhat at risk.” Professor Andrew Butt, from RMIT University’s Centre for Urban Research, supports greater housing density in spots with good access to services such as transport. But he is concerned existing rules around height and setbacks could be waived, particularly as a community’s appeal rights diminish, and believes the public should be able to trust existing controls will be upheld.



“If you’re testing the limits of those controls and, in fact, breaking them, what faith would we have in the controls anywhere? This could happen anywhere,” Butt said. Sally Forrester is among many Surrey Hill residents who lodged objections to the plans for the St Joseph’s site, and is concerned the development would overwhelm mostly single-storey heritage homes nearby. “It’s time that it gets developed,” Forrester said. “But in short, the current proposal is far too large, too intense, and it’s too inconsistent with the preferred neighbourhood character of the precinct.”



Some residents fear the school building will be demolished. Joe Armao Boroondara Heritage Group committee member Christina Branagan worries about the potential loss of the school building. Not only was it a significant structure and enhanced the area’s character, she said, but it was vital to uphold the broader principle of protecting heritage assets for future generations. However, other residents are broadly in favour, including Jocelyn, who asked for her surname to be used. She has lived nearby for two decades and said the proposed height wasn’t a concern as the chapel was already tall, and she was relieved older heritage buildings would be restored. Her concern is how the narrow surrounding streets might cope with an influx of cars. “As long as it looks the same and the features are preserved, it doesn’t worry me,” Jocelyn said.



There is a bus stop on the same street as the former boys’ home, and Chatham train station is about 500 metres away. Some housing advocates argue many local planning rules are restrictive as they prevent more homes – including affordable apartments – from being built, particularly in inner-city areas. A planning report prepared for Antipodean Land Developments, the company behind the proposed development, says the building would respond to housing demand, add to the diversity of homes available in the area and breathe life into underutilised land through a design by award-winning architects. An artist’s render of the development proposed in Surrey Hills. Woods Bagot The report cites “extensive pre-application engagement” with the state’s development program, while a heritage impact report has also been released.



Related Article Property development Beloved Kew supermarket site headed to Supreme Court over controversial development Gault, the mayor, described the plans as inappropriate for the site and said it would be “unlawful for council to approve a building of this size”. “We want to see housing growth in Boroondara which is respectful of significant and irreplaceable heritage properties and doesn’t see oversize development in residential areas,” he said. Antipodean Land Developments declined to discuss the proposal. Critics of the current planning rules for the area argue they are restrictive and prevent more housing from being built.



A Victorian government spokesperson said the planning system was being overhauled to ensure more homes were built. Related Article Planning Melbourne has Australia’s least restrictive planning zones, but these suburbs remain ‘locked down’ “Boroondara Council is working overtime to block new homes – locking out workers, families and young Victorians from living in these well-connected areas,” the spokesperson said. “Any proposal will be considered on its merits and in accordance with the relevant planning scheme including heritage overlays.” Former orphanages and children’s homes across Melbourne have varied uses.



The former St Vincent’s Boys’ Orphanage in South Melbourne is now occupied by child welfare agency MacKillop Family Services, and the Blackhall mansion, previously occupied by the Catherine Booth Girls’ Home in Kew East, is owned by Carey Baptist Grammar School. The Box Hill Boys Home is part of a retirement village, and Abbotsford Convent, now an arts and cultural precinct, used to include an orphanage. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Matt King to take over as NSW coach as Laurie Daley confirms Origin exit
World.content:
Updated SportNRLNRL 2026 Matt King to take over as NSW coach as Laurie Daley confirms Origin exit Chris Barrett and Christian Nicolussi Updated August 3, 2026 — 12:30pm ,first published August 2, 2026 — 4:31pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

NSW and Sydney Roosters assistant Matt King will take over as the Blues’ State of Origin coach following Laurie Daley’s decision earlier on Monday to stand aside. King was Daley’s senior assistant as NSW captured the interstate series against the odds this year with a famous victory in game three at Suncorp Stadium. Matt King is set to be given a two-year deal as NSW’s Origin coach. NRL Photos The former Blues outside back was Daley’s favoured successor and has also won over top brass at the NSW Rugby League. Sources not authorised to speak publicly on the matter confirmed the news on Monday. King, who previously worked on Michael Maguire’s coaching staff at South Sydney, has been with the Roosters for a decade and is regarded as a future NRL head coach. He played nine Origins for NSW and won 10 Kangaroos caps in a playing career that took in stints at Melbourne and South Sydney, and Warrington in the Super league.



It is expected he will be handed a two-year contract with NSW. It is unclear if King will continue full-time with the Roosters next season, but there is no rule against being an assistant at club level and an Origin coach at the same time. Loading Daley gave his endorsement to the 45-year-old after saying it was “just the right time” to walk away from the NSW post. As reported by this masthead on Sunday afternoon, Daley confirmed on Monday morning via his Sky Sports Radio Big Sports Breakfast program that he would not renew his Origin deal.



He had been frustrated last week by a News Corp report that he had quit due to health concerns, which he quickly denied – but only after several family members had become concerned and contacted him. Daley was glad he got to bow out with a series win that was sealed with a victory on Queensland soil. Blues head coach Laurie Daley (right) speaks to his assistant Matt King (left). Getty “I feel like now is the right time for someone else to have the opportunity to lead this great state and this great team,” Daley said. “It’s just the right time. “You always have to be careful that you don’t make decisions based on emotion. You have to think things through. When we won game three, you sit back, reflect, which is why I didn’t want to make the announcement straight away.



“Over the last couple of weeks, from where I was going into the series to where I was after the game, it hadn’t changed. I knew my commitment to the team was for that two-year period. “I felt like it was the best time to leave – it was the best time to pass the baton onto someone else.” Laurie Daley’s time as NSW Blues coach is over. NRL Photos The NSWRL has not yet commented on Daley’s replacement, but it is set to announce King’s appointment by Wednesday. Daley said King was a first-grade coach in waiting who was “ready to go”.



Related Article NRL 2026 Penrith premiership winner not due back until finals in blow to NRL title bid King has excellent communication skills, is popular with the players and has been a part of the Blues’ coaching set-up since being brought on board by Maguire for the 2024 series. Penrith’s Ivan Cleary will finish at the Panthers at the end of 2027 and has spoken of his desire to move into coaching representative teams, but he had already ruled himself out of the NSW job for next year. Brisbane coach Maguire was rumoured to have put his name forward, despite still being contracted to the Broncos, but NSWRL officials confirmed there had been no contact from the man who led the Blues to a come-from-behind series triumph two years ago. The Origin series will feature a game in New Zealand for the first time in 2027. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: ‘What drugs do you want?’: How betting companies lured Luke Bateman into gambling more
World.content:
PoliticsFederalGambling ‘What drugs do you want?’: How betting companies lured Luke Bateman into gambling more Natassia Chrysanthos Updated August 3, 2026 — 12:29pm ,first published 12:01pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Former rugby league player turned BookTok influencer Luke Bateman has described being flown to interstate race days by betting companies, where he was plied with alcohol and supplied with his choice of drugs, including in the presence of senior gambling company executives. As he told a Senate inquiry about the tactics betting companies used to induce him into gambling more money, Bateman said he would also steal from his mother, partner and siblings so he could redeem the $1000 worth of free bonus bets that he would be offered after losing everything. Luke Bateman during a hearing into Labor’s gambling bill. Alex Ellinghausen “The inducements really destroyed my life because that’s what kept you coming back... when you wanted to get out,” Bateman said. “But it also destroyed the lives of the people who loved me as well.” The 31-year-old was one in a lineup of gambling reform advocates, including former Victorian MP Russell Northe, who outlined how they were wooed by betting companies while in the depths of addiction. Star Casino, Tabcorp and SportsBet were named in witness testimony about gamblers being offered free hotel rooms, escorts, drugs and grand final tickets as part of “VIP” programs.



The Albanese government’s contentious gambling package does not ban betting inducements, despite full prohibition being recommended by the Murphy report in 2023. Related Article Good Weekend How Luke Bateman became Australia’s most unlikely book influencer “On Wednesdays and Saturdays, which are your two main race days, I would receive direct offers customised for me that basically said if you deposit $1000, we will give you $1000 in bonus bets,” Bateman said on Monday, saying those messages came through text messages and emails. “Even if you didn’t put on a bet for one weekend, the next Wednesday and Friday, you would receive those promotions and inducements once again ... directly targeted, to motivate you into gambling.” Asked by ACT Senator David Pocock to describe the most “gobsmacking examples” of inducements, Bateman said: “There were times where I would be flown interstate and taken to race days, put in marquees with alcohol and food provided all day, things like that.



“Before getting there, the VIP manager would offer: hey mate, what drugs do you want? Do you want a couple of bags for this weekend? We’ll organise that for you. We’ll have that ready for you when you get here.” Another time, Bateman said he was hosted at an exclusive event on the canals of the Gold Coast. “And the entire C-suite of the company was there. All the management team administration, and they were all in a backroom doing drugs together. And I was out in this room doing drugs with all of them. This is like the CEO, the founders, the VIP managers,” he said. “I would have been, you know, 23 years old. So while I was absolutely ... I would put my hand up and say I was a willing participant of that. These are men in positions of power with influence who should be looking out for your welfare.” Asked whether the presence of C-suite executives meant these companies knew how the system worked, Bateman said: “Well, not only did they know, they were participating in it.”



Luke Bateman in 2017, during his time as an NRL player. Getty Images Bateman said there were many times when his gambling was extremely erratic, and showed signs of extreme harm – turning over hundreds of thousands of dollars in a single day, on hundreds of races. But there were never any welfare checks. Instead, companies drew him in further. Bateman has previously described being in hundreds of thousands of dollars of debt and unable to buy groceries. Star Casino, TAB, Sportsbet named in evidence A bipartisan report helmed by the late Peta Murphy in 2023 had recommended a total gambling advertising blackout, ban on inducements and national regulator. The witnesses to Monday morning said these were glaring omissions in Labor’s final legislation. Chief gambling advocate Tim Costello said Prime Minister Anthony Albanese had set himself three tests with this gambling legislation: to delink gambling and sport, protect children and reduce the saturation of gambling ads.



“We think this legislation in its present form fails those tests,” he said. “This legislation has some good aspects ... However, it’s line ball whether it’s actually better than the status quo.” Costello shared the story of one man who would soon plead guilty to criminal offences – a financial adviser who stole $12.3 million from his company in 17 months. “In that time, he was given free accommodation at Star Casino. He had to leave each week so they could technically say he wasn’t living there and come back the next morning,” Costello said. “He was the TAB’s biggest customer in that time. They were giving him $50,000 bonus bets. He was also Sportsbet’s biggest customer. They were flying him to grand finals. They were offering him escorts, drugs, whatever he wanted. He was doing turnover of more than $20 million a month.” Costello said the question for the inquiry was: “How do licensed bookmakers, who we are told are regulated, get away with this? The answer is the first recommendation of the Murphy report. We don’t have a national regulator – that’s how they’re getting away with this.”



Northe also pleaded with the inquiry to consider a national regulator. His own political career collapsed under the weight of gambling addiction – he served a year in prison after the Victorian County Court heard he falsely claimed more than $170,000 in parliamentary expenses during 2018 and 2019, while losing more than $223,000 through gambling over the same period. Related Article Exclusive

Gambling Labor’s millions in gambling donations revealed amid last-ditch push for reform “From my own experience, what happened to me quite regularly was I would open and close accounts on a regular basis, and that was a cry for help for me – closing an account, trying to get out,” he told the inquiry. “But during that period where I was stopped gambling and I had closed an account, I would be targeted, contacted by the gambling companies to reopen [an] account again with inducements and incentives. “Recommendation 16 of the Murphy report: it says to ban inducements without delay. Here we are what 1132 days down the track and it’s still happening. What carnage has been caused in that time?”



Another advocate, Mark Kempster, said he was working with one family who had lost $500,000 in 30 days after being given $55,000 worth of bonus bets – the person had been allowed on a betting app in one part of the country, despite being self-excluded in another. “Those types of things that happen across nearly all the major VIP programs that I’ve seen,” he said. TAB and Responsible Wagering Australia, the peak body for gambling companies, have been contacted for comment. Both Albanese and Communications Minister Anika Wells have defended the package, saying it is stronger than current settings. Wells on Monday addressed the issue of inducements by saying people could sign up to the self-exclusion register, BetStop.
