Latest data shows 40,000 people had active exclusions with BetStop as of June; advocates say about 2 million Australians are at risk.



“I would say to people who are either suffering from gambling harm or … who have been advocating in the space of inducements, to assist the cause by making sure that people who might benefit from BetStop are aware of BetStop,” Wells told reporters in Canberra. Albanese said last month. “I think we’ve got the balance right … It actually, in some ways, goes further than [the Murphy] report went. It’s a comprehensive approach.” Related Article Gambling ‘How can it be?’ Church leader turns Albanese’s words against him Witness Kate Seselja was brought to tears as she described her frustration at Albanese’s insistence that the government’s legislation had gotten “the balance right”. “It just was so horrible to hear him say those words when there is absolutely no balance to this equation,” she said. “The stories of people harmed by this industry: when is enough? Like when is it enough? How many of us have to line up and say this is not okay?”



Another advocate, Anne Bardsley, said it was “beyond frustrating” to know that the government had been handed a blueprint for reform with the Murphy inquiry. “This bill is all we get, and frankly, it’s piss weak – it’s a piss weak response to a public health crisis.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. World.title: Australia news LIVE: Hanson bars media outlets from Melbourne press conference over ‘character assassination attempts’; Government to provide bird flu update
World.content:
Nine Entertainment and News Corp have criticised the federal government’s late changes to its News Bargaining Incentive, warning the revised scheme risks weakening the pressure on tech platforms to pay for Australian journalism.

The government confirmed on Monday it would narrow the charge to digital advertising revenue while lifting the rate from 2.25 per cent to 2.5 per cent, and require platforms to strike deals with at least six publishers.

Nine chief executive Matt Stanton said the changes, made late in the process, required closer scrutiny “to ensure it continues to meet its fundamental purpose: compelling these platforms to negotiate fairly for the journalism they benefit from”. Nine Entertainment is the owner of this masthead.

News Corp Australasia executive chairman Michael Miller went further, saying the changes “gut the incentive for tech platforms to strike fair deals with Australian media, right when those rules need strengthening, not softening”. Miller called for full revenue transparency backed by “severe, non-negotiable penalties” for platforms that flout local law.

Professional networking site LinkedIn has also been added to the scheme, which the government expects will generate more than $250 million a year for the local media industry.

Meta, TikTok and Google declined to comment.

World.title: Say goodbye to bubble wrap: The new products popping the plastic bubble
World.content:
EnvironmentSustainabilityRecycling Say goodbye to bubble wrap: The new products popping the plastic bubble Caitlin Fitzsimmons August 3, 2026 — 11:59am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

If you walk into a hardware store, you can now find rolls of “bubble wrap” made from paper. The product has the same performance as plastic for about the same price, but the rolls are a lot thinner because it has a honeycomb design rather than air bubbles. Yet the real beauty of it, says Visy chief executive Mark De Wit, is what happens when you are finished with it. Visy chief executive Mark De Wit with a roll of the paper-based alternative to bubble wrap. Dominic Lorrimer “We’ve all had bubble wrap before … it’s a soft plastic so it ends up in landfill, and somewhere between 500 and 1000 years later, it might disintegrate into microplastics,” De Wit said. “This [paper bubble wrap] can go in your recycle bin, and we’ll turn it back into a box within a few weeks of it being collected from your house.” This is just one of a host of innovations in consumer products and packaging that has occurred in the past five years, since this masthead and Visy started hosting an annual recycling roundtable with business leaders and the federal environment minister of the day.



Other examples from Visy alone include cardboard replacements for the plastic protective sheets used by painters and renovators, fruit and vegetable punnets made from recycled cardboard, new insulated material made from reused cardboard to replace polystyrene. Asahi Beverages has replaced the plastic shrink wrap around Carlton Dry six-pack bottles with innovative fibre-board packaging. The company’s Australian primary packaging (excluding caps and labels) was 100 per cent recyclable, reusable or compostable for the first time last year. Nu-Pure has decreased the volume of plastic resin in its water bottles. The company’s 600ml round PET bottle produced in NSW now weighs just 8.59 grams, plus 1.3g for the lid, making it one of the lightest still water bottles in Australia. Several companies are now supplying disposable coffee cups to cafes where the cup and lid are made entirely out of compostable and biodegradeable fibre to Australian standards. Another achievement is that Australian-produced glass now contains 54 per cent recycled content. For Visy, it had increased from 30 per cent to 64 per cent and was expected to reach 70 per cent by next year once the company’s new facility in Yatala, Queensland was complete. This put Australia on par with Germany and New Zealand “and a country mile ahead of everyone else”.



But the failure of the federal and state governments to agree on national packaging standards has stymied growth. Last week, Suzanne Toumbourou, chief executive of the Australian Council of Recycling, put out a statement decrying the lack of federal government action. “Australians are doing their part,” Tomoubourou said. “Recyclers have invested. But the Australian government is betraying that effort by delaying the packaging rules it promised, while more plastic goes to waste and Australian recycling capacity shrinks.” Asahi Beverages chief executive Amanda Sellers and Environment Minister Murray Watt at the 2026 recycling roundtable. Dominic Lorrimer Australians use more than 1.3 million tonnes of plastic packaging every year, but only 19 per cent is collected for recycling, leaving more than one million tonnes to wind up as landfill or litter. Yet Toumbourou said about 320,000 tonnes of Australian plastic reprocessing capacity was standing ready, much of it sitting idle, awaiting the government reforms. This left recyclers in severe commercial peril with some plants facing closure, she said. The industry has been saying for several years that mandatory national standards for packaging are needed so that companies can invest with confidence. The Albanese government has talking about legislation since 2022, but former environment minister Tanya Plibersek and current Environment Minister Murray Watt say the problem has been getting the states and territories to agree.



“When I discuss these things with states, some are completely on board,” Watt said at the roundtable on Friday. “Some are very concerned about what might be quite minimal cost increases for consumers.” Related Article Perspective

Plastic Tooth powder and blocked drains: My week without single-use plastic Watt said packaging would be on the agenda at the next meeting of the federal, state, and territory environment ministers in September. One option for Watt could be using national policy payments to states to encourage them to come on board with national standards. De Wit said the economics of glass, cardboard and aluminium recycling made sense because they were a comparable cost to virgin material. That was not true for hard plastics – including the PET bottles such as water and soft drinks and the HDP bottles such as cloudy milk bottles – because the recycled resin had fixed costs based on collection and processing, while the virgin product was tied to the price of oil and fluctuated wildly. “As a producer of this recycled resin, we see the sales go strong when the virgin price is up here, and then drop off when they’re down here because a lot of companies buy the cheapest, whatever that is, virgin or recycled,” De Wit said.



“What I would like to see is what they’ve done in the 27 EU countries, in the UK, in California, Washington State, New Jersey, where they’ve said because of this exact issue, there has to be 25 per cent minimum recycled content in every plastic bottle.” De Wit said the additional cost would between half and one cent per bottle, so it would “not contribute one iota to a cost of living crisis”. Visy chief Mark De Wit showing an imported drink bottle with a PVC wrapper that contaminates plastic recycling. Dominic Lorrimer Another issue requiring government action was that imported drinks were not held to Australian standards. A plastic drink bottle produced in Australia had to have a wrapper that could be recycled with the bottle. But imported drinks such as those found in Asian supermarkets had PVC wrappers that contaminated the waste stream – one 3g wrapper would contaminate 150 kilograms of PET plastic recycling, which meant 7500 bottles could no longer be processed into food-grade packaging. Arnott’s chief executive George Zoghbi at the recycling roundtable hosted by Visy and this masthead. Dominic Lorrimer



George Zoghbi, chief executive of Arnott’s Biscuits, said he had two things on his wish list. “One is curbside collection for everything, including soft plastic because if you can do that at scale, it changes the game for everybody, and it makes the cost of recycling significantly cheaper, and the take-up rate significantly higher,” Zoghbi said. “The second one is that it’s very hard for consumers to look at these chemical symbols and say which colour bin you should use. Instead, you could put dots on the packaging that matches the colour of the bin – if it’s a red dot, it goes in the red bin; if it’s yellow, it goes in a yellow bin.” This would require states and territories to harmonise their bin collection systems. Get to the heart of what’s happening with climate change and the environment.

World.title: Fool’s gold: Trump’s promise to America is not going to plan
World.content:
BusinessThe economyTrump's America Opinion Fool’s gold: Trump’s promise to America is not going to plan Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist August 3, 2026 — 11:58am

August 3, 2026 — 11:58am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Who would have thought it? The eurozone, derided by Donald Trump as a declining economy that was heading in the wrong direction, outpaced the US economy in the June quarter. The eurozone economy grew at an annualised rate of 1.8 per cent that quarter, while the US economy grew at 1.5 per cent. Canada, hit hard by Trump’s tariffs, grew its economy over the quarter at an annualised rate of 3.4 per cent. US President Donald Trump, along with his Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, have repeatedly promised a “Golden Age” would arrive this year for the US economy. AP Europe’s growth rate was its fastest in more than a year, despite continuing energy shocks emanating from Trump’s war in the Middle East and his tariffs. In the United States, growth slowed from 2.1 per cent rate in the first three months of the year, despite the continuing boom in artificial intelligence-related investment, lower oil and petrol prices during the ceasefire in the war on Iran and a surge in spending by wealthier Americans (with some assistance from the World Cup) in June.



So much for an economic “Golden Age” for the US that Trump, his Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick have repeatedly promised would arrive this year. So far, the only gold is to be found in the White House, or on Washington’s monuments, where Trump has been gilding anything and everything he can, or in the wealth being accumulated by the Trump family and their associates. Related Article Trump's White House ‘I don’t have inside information’: How Donald Trump Jr is cashing in on dad’s presidency The US economy would probably be running a lot hotter if not for the war in the Middle East and the global war on trade that Trump keeps trying to establish a legal basis for. Along with the data on GDP that was published late last week, the Commerce Department put out personal consumption expenditures (PCE) data for June that showed the US Federal Reserve Board’s preferred measure of inflation, the PCE index, fell 0.1 per cent in June to be 3.7 per cent higher than it was in the same month last year.



While that’s well below the 4.1 per cent May-on-May rate, it is still way above the Fed’s inflation target of 2 per cent. Even stripped of energy and food prices, “core” PCE inflation was 3.3 per cent. In July, hostilities in the Middle East resumed, and oil prices, which had fallen back below $US72 ($102) a barrel in June, spiked again after the brief ceasefire. They surpassed $US100 a barrel last month, before again falling, to about $US84 a barrel at present, as talks appear to have resumed. The US economy would probably be running a lot hotter, if not for the war in the Middle East and the global war on trade that Trump keeps trying to find a legal basis for. Bloomberg US petrol and diesel prices remain well above their prewar levels – petrol about $US1 a gallon higher and diesel about $US1.60 a gallon higher – and will continue to feed into the inflation rate. It is inflation, a declining savings rate, and the fact that much of the equipment required for the boom in AI is imported (and therefore subtracts from GDP) that are weighing on US growth.



For various reasons – not least the stop-start ways in which the trade war, and the real war, have been waged – their impact on the inflation rate and economic growth hasn’t been as significant as most outside the administration had expected. With another newly imposed round of global tariffs on 99.4 per cent of America’s imports, and the war in the Middle East dragging on without any obvious clean conclusion, their effects on the economy and the inflation rate might have been stretched out and delayed, rather than avoided. Related Article Opinion

Interest rates As the Fed sits tight on interest rates, investors take action Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Rather than a one-off shock before prices stabilised, they might still be bleeding into prices and the economy in a fashion that means they may not be “transitory” and therefore can’t be dismissed as such by the Fed, which left its policy rate unchanged – for the fifth successive time – after last week’s meeting. With the Fed’s new Trump-appointed chairman, Kevin Warsh, creating an information vacuum by withdrawing any guidance on interest rates, the bond market has taken matters into its own hands.



The 10-year bond yield is now 4.74 per cent, compared with its pre-meeting level of 4.61 per cent. The 30-year yield has jumped 18 basis points to a 19-year high of 5.27 per cent. Those yields, if sustained, will choke spending and investment and raise the borrowing and refinancing costs on the US government’s debt, which is rapidly nearing $US40 trillion ($57 trillion). So far, the only gold is to be found in the White House, or on Washington’s monuments, where Trump has been gilding anything and everything he can, or in the wealth being accumulated by the Trump family and their associates. Eurozone data shows that its economies – despite being battered by energy-related shocks that began with the war in Ukraine and are continuing with the war in the Middle East, and having to deal with a tide of cheap Chinese imports that has swelled since Trump started building his tariff wall around the US market – are more resilient than expected. All the major economies – Germany, France, Italy and Spain – grew solidly, if not spectacularly, in the quarter, and Ireland, a beneficiary of the AI boom, bounced back from a sharp contraction in the first quarter to growth of 3.9 per cent in the second.



Like most of the rest of the world (China and Canada being the exceptions), while it did threaten action, the eurozone didn’t respond to the US tariffs with retaliatory tariffs – taxes on its consumers – of its own. It’s the US, thanks to the tariffs and the impact of the war-driven higher oil prices on domestic petrol and diesel prices, that is hitting its own businesses and consumers and its own growth hardest. A 1.5 per cent growth rate isn’t a disaster, but it’s hardly the “Golden Age”. The 5 or 6 per cent growth rates that Trump said his policies could generate haven’t materialised (which is no surprise), and neither have the trillions of dollars of foreign investment in the US manufacturing sector that he also said would flow. The Trump family and their associates are accumulating vast amounts of wealth during Donald’s second term. AP Real wages for US workers are declining, manufacturing sector jobs have shrunk, and it is the AI boom and those wealthiest households who benefited most from the tax cuts in Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act and who have gained most from the AI-driven sharemarket wealth effects that are generating the reasonably solid but unspectacular economic growth rate.



If something were to disrupt the AI boom – and investors are getting nervous about the sustainability of the vast amounts of capital being poured into it, by increasingly negative cashflow-generating companies, relative to the cheaper Chinese alternatives and the returns in prospect – the implications for the sharemarket and economy would be threatening. Related Article Opinion

Trump's White House The lyin’ king Trump is the kind of leader the nation’s father feared and reviled Maureen Dowd New York Times columnist Trump and those in his team regularly denigrate the Europeans and their economies, saying the economies are over-regulated, stagnating or declining, being swamped by illegal migrants and effectively subsidised by the US (or leeching off it via unfair terms of trade). Some of those criticisms might be valid, but the Trump alternative of aggressive deregulation, trade barriers and extortion, draconian crackdowns on undocumented migrants and immigration more broadly and a war in the Middle East that is delivering nothing but humiliation and higher energy costs make it difficult for the administration to claim the US, or at least this particular administration, has the superior economic or governance model. World.title: Two hospitalised after inner Sydney building collapse
World.content:
Two people have been hospitalised after a building collapsed in Ultimo, with part of the roof caving in and a brick wall crashing onto parked cars at a service station next door. Emergency services were called to Wattle Street just before 11am on Monday, with workers at the Shell service station describing a massive “boom” as the neighbouring vacant building collapsed. Two people have been hospitalised after the building collapse in Ultimo. Jessica Hromas Paramedics assessed seven patients on the scene, two of whom were hospitalised in a serious condition. They were taken to Royal Prince Alfred Hospital and St Vincent’s Hospital. Four others affected by the collapse declined medical attention.



Dozens of police and fire rescue workers swarmed the perimeter of the building and adjacent service station, where a large exclusion zone has been established as early assessments into the collapse begin. There are a handful of station workers whose cars are stuck in the exclusion zone. At least two cars are covered in fallen bricks. A large exclusion zone has been established around the collapsed building. Jessica Hromas One witness said he had been parked near the building two minutes before it collapsed. “I heard a noise, many noise[s], so I moved my scooter,” he told TNV.



“I don’t know what it is exactly. It was not normal, it was a lot of noise. I was shocked, I was surprised … I’m good. I feel really well. I’m lucky.” Police have arrived at the scene and have begun an investigation into the incident. The Building Commission NSW, which regulates the construction industry, is also expected to attend the site. Two of four northbound lanes on Wattle Street have been closed, and motorists have been advised to exercise caution and expect delays. In 2020, the City of Sydney Council approved a $9.5 million proposal to redevelop the site into a five-storey student accommodation complex with 72 boarding rooms.



The plans, lodged by developer TQK Pty Ltd, included the demolition of the existing warehouse and excavation works. More to come Be the first to know when major news happens.

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of day one of Alan Jones’ indecent assault and sexual touching trial. I’ll be keeping you informed of the latest developments with my colleague, Clare Sibthorpe.

Jones, a former teacher, political candidate, speechwriter and coach of the Australian national rugby union team, dominated Sydney breakfast radio for decades before he retired from 2GB in May 2020.

Alan Jones arrives at Downing Centre. Jessica Hromas

More than four years later, in November 2024, he was arrested and charged over allegations he indecently assaulted, groped or inappropriately touched a number of young men.

His criminal trial starts today in the NSW Local Court in Sydney and centres on allegations of unwanted kissing and touching by six men, who will give evidence over the coming weeks. Jones has always maintained his innocence and is defending the charges.

World.title: Orphanage apartment project tests suburban planning laws and our appetite for change
World.content:
PoliticsVictoriaCity life Orphanage apartment project tests suburban planning laws and our appetite for change Rachael Ward August 3, 2026 — 12:34pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A push to convert one of Australia’s oldest orphanages into apartments in a sleepy suburb not earmarked for high-rise development has sparked a warning for other residential streets in Melbourne. A developer wants to turn the former St Joseph’s Home for Boys in Surrey Hills into 76 apartments over four storeys which, if approved, would be two levels above the area’s existing height limit and include the demolition of a 1941 school, subject to local heritage protections. Surrey Hills resident Sally Forrester outside the former St Joseph’s Home for Boys. A developer wants to turn the home into an apartment complex. Joe Armao Other historical buildings like the iconic chapel, which is more than 120 years old, would remain. City of Boroondara Mayor Wes Gault said the proposal was “unlawful” given current height limits, but the council was powerless to stop it.



The developer has sought permission directly from the state Planning Minister Sonya Kilkenny through a pathway that bypasses councils. Related Article City life Political heavyweights join campaign against 16-storey Hawthorn tower The pathway applies to projects above $50 million if 10 per cent of homes are allocated to affordable housing or – in this case – developers contribute 3 per cent of construction costs to a fund to build them. Projects approved this way cannot be fought at the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal. Unlike many other housing projects under consideration through the state government’s Development Facilitation Program, the Surrey Hills site is not within a state-designated activity centre area, where high-density development is encouraged to address the state’s housing crisis. However, planning advocates and even some residents say the site’s distance from the city, public transport options and size are an example of developments that should be encouraged to address the housing crisis – not ones blocked by council.



Planning Institute of Australia Victorian president Patrick Fensham said while the government sought to address the gap between housing supply and population growth, there was also a “question mark about the legitimacy” of approving medium- to high-density developments outside activity centres or in areas otherwise provided for in planning controls. “Is this the new system? Is this a site-by-site assessment process rather than responding to strategic planning, which is based on good planning aims? The precedent is problematic,” Fensham said. Related Article Exclusive

Tax reform How thousands of Melbourne’s empty homes are dodging millions in tax “The more we see ministerial discretion in these things and the lack of a process for the public to provide input, that there is a principle of integrity of the system which is somewhat at risk.” Professor Andrew Butt, from RMIT University’s Centre for Urban Research, supports greater housing density in spots with good access to services such as transport. But he is concerned existing rules around height and setbacks could be waived, particularly as a community’s appeal rights diminish, and believes the public should be able to trust existing controls will be upheld.



“If you’re testing the limits of those controls and, in fact, breaking them, what faith would we have in the controls anywhere? This could happen anywhere,” Butt said. Sally Forrester is among many Surrey Hill residents who lodged objections to the plans for the St Joseph’s site, and is concerned the development would overwhelm mostly single-storey heritage homes nearby. “It’s time that it gets developed,” Forrester said. “But in short, the current proposal is far too large, too intense, and it’s too inconsistent with the preferred neighbourhood character of the precinct.”



Some residents fear the school building will be demolished. Joe Armao Boroondara Heritage Group committee member Christina Branagan worries about the potential loss of the school building. Not only was it a significant structure and enhanced the area’s character, she said, but it was vital to uphold the broader principle of protecting heritage assets for future generations. However, other residents are broadly in favour, including Jocelyn, who asked for her surname to be used. She has lived nearby for two decades and said the proposed height wasn’t a concern as the chapel was already tall, and she was relieved older heritage buildings would be restored. Her concern is how the narrow surrounding streets might cope with an influx of cars. “As long as it looks the same and the features are preserved, it doesn’t worry me,” Jocelyn said.



There is a bus stop on the same street as the former boys’ home, and Chatham train station is about 500 metres away. Some housing advocates argue many local planning rules are restrictive as they prevent more homes – including affordable apartments – from being built, particularly in inner-city areas. A planning report prepared for Antipodean Land Developments, the company behind the proposed development, says the building would respond to housing demand, add to the diversity of homes available in the area and breathe life into underutilised land through a design by award-winning architects. An artist’s render of the development proposed in Surrey Hills. Woods Bagot The report cites “extensive pre-application engagement” with the state’s development program, while a heritage impact report has also been released.



Related Article Property development Beloved Kew supermarket site headed to Supreme Court over controversial development Gault, the mayor, described the plans as inappropriate for the site and said it would be “unlawful for council to approve a building of this size”. “We want to see housing growth in Boroondara which is respectful of significant and irreplaceable heritage properties and doesn’t see oversize development in residential areas,” he said. Antipodean Land Developments declined to discuss the proposal. Critics of the current planning rules for the area argue they are restrictive and prevent more housing from being built.



A Victorian government spokesperson said the planning system was being overhauled to ensure more homes were built. Related Article Planning Melbourne has Australia’s least restrictive planning zones, but these suburbs remain ‘locked down’ “Boroondara Council is working overtime to block new homes – locking out workers, families and young Victorians from living in these well-connected areas,” the spokesperson said. “Any proposal will be considered on its merits and in accordance with the relevant planning scheme including heritage overlays.” Former orphanages and children’s homes across Melbourne have varied uses.



The former St Vincent’s Boys’ Orphanage in South Melbourne is now occupied by child welfare agency MacKillop Family Services, and the Blackhall mansion, previously occupied by the Catherine Booth Girls’ Home in Kew East, is owned by Carey Baptist Grammar School. The Box Hill Boys Home is part of a retirement village, and Abbotsford Convent, now an arts and cultural precinct, used to include an orphanage. World.title: Matt King to take over as NSW coach as Laurie Daley confirms Origin exit
World.content:
Updated SportNRLNRL 2026 Matt King to take over as NSW coach as Laurie Daley confirms Origin exit Chris Barrett and Christian Nicolussi Updated August 3, 2026 — 12:30pm ,first published August 2, 2026 — 4:31pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

NSW and Sydney Roosters assistant Matt King will take over as the Blues’ State of Origin coach following Laurie Daley’s decision earlier on Monday to stand aside. King was Daley’s senior assistant as NSW captured the interstate series against the odds this year with a famous victory in game three at Suncorp Stadium. Matt King is set to be given a two-year deal as NSW’s Origin coach. NRL Photos The former Blues outside back was Daley’s favoured successor and has also won over top brass at the NSW Rugby League. Sources not authorised to speak publicly on the matter confirmed the news on Monday. King, who previously worked on Michael Maguire’s coaching staff at South Sydney, has been with the Roosters for a decade and is regarded as a future NRL head coach. He played nine Origins for NSW and won 10 Kangaroos caps in a playing career that took in stints at Melbourne and South Sydney, and Warrington in the Super league.



It is expected he will be handed a two-year contract with NSW. It is unclear if King will continue full-time with the Roosters next season, but there is no rule against being an assistant at club level and an Origin coach at the same time. Loading Daley gave his endorsement to the 45-year-old after saying it was “just the right time” to walk away from the NSW post. As reported by this masthead on Sunday afternoon, Daley confirmed on Monday morning via his Sky Sports Radio Big Sports Breakfast program that he would not renew his Origin deal.



He had been frustrated last week by a News Corp report that he had quit due to health concerns, which he quickly denied – but only after several family members had become concerned and contacted him. Daley was glad he got to bow out with a series win that was sealed with a victory on Queensland soil. Blues head coach Laurie Daley (right) speaks to his assistant Matt King (left). Getty “I feel like now is the right time for someone else to have the opportunity to lead this great state and this great team,” Daley said. “It’s just the right time. “You always have to be careful that you don’t make decisions based on emotion. You have to think things through. When we won game three, you sit back, reflect, which is why I didn’t want to make the announcement straight away.



“Over the last couple of weeks, from where I was going into the series to where I was after the game, it hadn’t changed. I knew my commitment to the team was for that two-year period. “I felt like it was the best time to leave – it was the best time to pass the baton onto someone else.” Laurie Daley’s time as NSW Blues coach is over. NRL Photos The NSWRL has not yet commented on Daley’s replacement, but it is set to announce King’s appointment by Wednesday. Daley said King was a first-grade coach in waiting who was “ready to go”.



Related Article NRL 2026 Penrith premiership winner not due back until finals in blow to NRL title bid King has excellent communication skills, is popular with the players and has been a part of the Blues’ coaching set-up since being brought on board by Maguire for the 2024 series. Penrith’s Ivan Cleary will finish at the Panthers at the end of 2027 and has spoken of his desire to move into coaching representative teams, but he had already ruled himself out of the NSW job for next year. Brisbane coach Maguire was rumoured to have put his name forward, despite still being contracted to the Broncos, but NSWRL officials confirmed there had been no contact from the man who led the Blues to a come-from-behind series triumph two years ago. The Origin series will feature a game in New Zealand for the first time in 2027. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: ‘What drugs do you want?’: How betting companies lured Luke Bateman into gambling more
World.content:
PoliticsFederalGambling ‘What drugs do you want?’: How betting companies lured Luke Bateman into gambling more Natassia Chrysanthos Updated August 3, 2026 — 12:29pm ,first published 12:01pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Former rugby league player turned BookTok influencer Luke Bateman has described being flown to interstate race days by betting companies, where he was plied with alcohol and supplied with his choice of drugs, including in the presence of senior gambling company executives. As he told a Senate inquiry about the tactics betting companies used to induce him into gambling more money, Bateman said he would also steal from his mother, partner and siblings so he could redeem the $1000 worth of free bonus bets that he would be offered after losing everything. Luke Bateman during a hearing into Labor’s gambling bill. Alex Ellinghausen “The inducements really destroyed my life because that’s what kept you coming back... when you wanted to get out,” Bateman said. “But it also destroyed the lives of the people who loved me as well.” The 31-year-old was one in a lineup of gambling reform advocates, including former Victorian MP Russell Northe, who outlined how they were wooed by betting companies while in the depths of addiction. Star Casino, Tabcorp and SportsBet were named in witness testimony about gamblers being offered free hotel rooms, escorts, drugs and grand final tickets as part of “VIP” programs.



The Albanese government’s contentious gambling package does not ban betting inducements, despite full prohibition being recommended by the Murphy report in 2023. Related Article Good Weekend How Luke Bateman became Australia’s most unlikely book influencer “On Wednesdays and Saturdays, which are your two main race days, I would receive direct offers customised for me that basically said if you deposit $1000, we will give you $1000 in bonus bets,” Bateman said on Monday, saying those messages came through text messages and emails. “Even if you didn’t put on a bet for one weekend, the next Wednesday and Friday, you would receive those promotions and inducements once again ... directly targeted, to motivate you into gambling.” Asked by ACT Senator David Pocock to describe the most “gobsmacking examples” of inducements, Bateman said: “There were times where I would be flown interstate and taken to race days, put in marquees with alcohol and food provided all day, things like that.



“Before getting there, the VIP manager would offer: hey mate, what drugs do you want? Do you want a couple of bags for this weekend? We’ll organise that for you. We’ll have that ready for you when you get here.” Another time, Bateman said he was hosted at an exclusive event on the canals of the Gold Coast. “And the entire C-suite of the company was there. All the management team administration, and they were all in a backroom doing drugs together. And I was out in this room doing drugs with all of them. This is like the CEO, the founders, the VIP managers,” he said. “I would have been, you know, 23 years old. So while I was absolutely ... I would put my hand up and say I was a willing participant of that. These are men in positions of power with influence who should be looking out for your welfare.” Asked whether the presence of C-suite executives meant these companies knew how the system worked, Bateman said: “Well, not only did they know, they were participating in it.”



Luke Bateman in 2017, during his time as an NRL player. Getty Images Bateman said there were many times when his gambling was extremely erratic, and showed signs of extreme harm – turning over hundreds of thousands of dollars in a single day, on hundreds of races. But there were never any welfare checks. Instead, companies drew him in further. Bateman has previously described being in hundreds of thousands of dollars of debt and unable to buy groceries. Star Casino, TAB, Sportsbet named in evidence A bipartisan report helmed by the late Peta Murphy in 2023 had recommended a total gambling advertising blackout, ban on inducements and national regulator. The witnesses to Monday morning said these were glaring omissions in Labor’s final legislation. Chief gambling advocate Tim Costello said Prime Minister Anthony Albanese had set himself three tests with this gambling legislation: to delink gambling and sport, protect children and reduce the saturation of gambling ads.



“We think this legislation in its present form fails those tests,” he said. “This legislation has some good aspects ... However, it’s line ball whether it’s actually better than the status quo.” Costello shared the story of one man who would soon plead guilty to criminal offences – a financial adviser who stole $12.3 million from his company in 17 months. “In that time, he was given free accommodation at Star Casino. He had to leave each week so they could technically say he wasn’t living there and come back the next morning,” Costello said. “He was the TAB’s biggest customer in that time. They were giving him $50,000 bonus bets. He was also Sportsbet’s biggest customer. They were flying him to grand finals. They were offering him escorts, drugs, whatever he wanted. He was doing turnover of more than $20 million a month.” Costello said the question for the inquiry was: “How do licensed bookmakers, who we are told are regulated, get away with this? The answer is the first recommendation of the Murphy report. We don’t have a national regulator – that’s how they’re getting away with this.”



Northe also pleaded with the inquiry to consider a national regulator. His own political career collapsed under the weight of gambling addiction – he served a year in prison after the Victorian County Court heard he falsely claimed more than $170,000 in parliamentary expenses during 2018 and 2019, while losing more than $223,000 through gambling over the same period. Related Article Exclusive

Gambling Labor’s millions in gambling donations revealed amid last-ditch push for reform “From my own experience, what happened to me quite regularly was I would open and close accounts on a regular basis, and that was a cry for help for me – closing an account, trying to get out,” he told the inquiry. “But during that period where I was stopped gambling and I had closed an account, I would be targeted, contacted by the gambling companies to reopen [an] account again with inducements and incentives. “Recommendation 16 of the Murphy report: it says to ban inducements without delay. Here we are what 1132 days down the track and it’s still happening. What carnage has been caused in that time?”



Another advocate, Mark Kempster, said he was working with one family who had lost $500,000 in 30 days after being given $55,000 worth of bonus bets – the person had been allowed on a betting app in one part of the country, despite being self-excluded in another. “Those types of things that happen across nearly all the major VIP programs that I’ve seen,” he said. TAB and Responsible Wagering Australia, the peak body for gambling companies, have been contacted for comment. Both Albanese and Communications Minister Anika Wells have defended the package, saying it is stronger than current settings. Wells on Monday addressed the issue of inducements by saying people could sign up to the self-exclusion register, BetStop. Latest data shows 40,000 people had active exclusions with BetStop as of June; advocates say about 2 million Australians are at risk.



“I would say to people who are either suffering from gambling harm or … who have been advocating in the space of inducements, to assist the cause by making sure that people who might benefit from BetStop are aware of BetStop,” Wells told reporters in Canberra. Albanese said last month. “I think we’ve got the balance right … It actually, in some ways, goes further than [the Murphy] report went. It’s a comprehensive approach.” Related Article Gambling ‘How can it be?’ Church leader turns Albanese’s words against him Witness Kate Seselja was brought to tears as she described her frustration at Albanese’s insistence that the government’s legislation had gotten “the balance right”. “It just was so horrible to hear him say those words when there is absolutely no balance to this equation,” she said. “The stories of people harmed by this industry: when is enough? Like when is it enough? How many of us have to line up and say this is not okay?”



Another advocate, Anne Bardsley, said it was “beyond frustrating” to know that the government had been handed a blueprint for reform with the Murphy inquiry. “This bill is all we get, and frankly, it’s piss weak – it’s a piss weak response to a public health crisis.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. World.title: Australia news LIVE: Hanson bars media outlets from Melbourne press conference over ‘character assassination attempts’; Government to provide bird flu update
World.content:
Nine Entertainment and News Corp have criticised the federal government’s late changes to its News Bargaining Incentive, warning the revised scheme risks weakening the pressure on tech platforms to pay for Australian journalism.

The government confirmed on Monday it would narrow the charge to digital advertising revenue while lifting the rate from 2.25 per cent to 2.5 per cent, and require platforms to strike deals with at least six publishers.

Nine chief executive Matt Stanton said the changes, made late in the process, required closer scrutiny “to ensure it continues to meet its fundamental purpose: compelling these platforms to negotiate fairly for the journalism they benefit from”. Nine Entertainment is the owner of this masthead.

News Corp Australasia executive chairman Michael Miller went further, saying the changes “gut the incentive for tech platforms to strike fair deals with Australian media, right when those rules need strengthening, not softening”. Miller called for full revenue transparency backed by “severe, non-negotiable penalties” for platforms that flout local law.

Professional networking site LinkedIn has also been added to the scheme, which the government expects will generate more than $250 million a year for the local media industry.

Meta, TikTok and Google declined to comment.

World.title: Say goodbye to bubble wrap: The new products popping the plastic bubble
World.content:
EnvironmentSustainabilityRecycling Say goodbye to bubble wrap: The new products popping the plastic bubble Caitlin Fitzsimmons August 3, 2026 — 11:59am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

If you walk into a hardware store, you can now find rolls of “bubble wrap” made from paper. The product has the same performance as plastic for about the same price, but the rolls are a lot thinner because it has a honeycomb design rather than air bubbles. Yet the real beauty of it, says Visy chief executive Mark De Wit, is what happens when you are finished with it. Visy chief executive Mark De Wit with a roll of the paper-based alternative to bubble wrap. Dominic Lorrimer “We’ve all had bubble wrap before … it’s a soft plastic so it ends up in landfill, and somewhere between 500 and 1000 years later, it might disintegrate into microplastics,” De Wit said. “This [paper bubble wrap] can go in your recycle bin, and we’ll turn it back into a box within a few weeks of it being collected from your house.” This is just one of a host of innovations in consumer products and packaging that has occurred in the past five years, since this masthead and Visy started hosting an annual recycling roundtable with business leaders and the federal environment minister of the day.



Other examples from Visy alone include cardboard replacements for the plastic protective sheets used by painters and renovators, fruit and vegetable punnets made from recycled cardboard, new insulated material made from reused cardboard to replace polystyrene. Asahi Beverages has replaced the plastic shrink wrap around Carlton Dry six-pack bottles with innovative fibre-board packaging. The company’s Australian primary packaging (excluding caps and labels) was 100 per cent recyclable, reusable or compostable for the first time last year. Nu-Pure has decreased the volume of plastic resin in its water bottles. The company’s 600ml round PET bottle produced in NSW now weighs just 8.59 grams, plus 1.3g for the lid, making it one of the lightest still water bottles in Australia. Several companies are now supplying disposable coffee cups to cafes where the cup and lid are made entirely out of compostable and biodegradeable fibre to Australian standards. Another achievement is that Australian-produced glass now contains 54 per cent recycled content. For Visy, it had increased from 30 per cent to 64 per cent and was expected to reach 70 per cent by next year once the company’s new facility in Yatala, Queensland was complete. This put Australia on par with Germany and New Zealand “and a country mile ahead of everyone else”.



But the failure of the federal and state governments to agree on national packaging standards has stymied growth. Last week, Suzanne Toumbourou, chief executive of the Australian Council of Recycling, put out a statement decrying the lack of federal government action. “Australians are doing their part,” Tomoubourou said. “Recyclers have invested. But the Australian government is betraying that effort by delaying the packaging rules it promised, while more plastic goes to waste and Australian recycling capacity shrinks.” Asahi Beverages chief executive Amanda Sellers and Environment Minister Murray Watt at the 2026 recycling roundtable. Dominic Lorrimer Australians use more than 1.3 million tonnes of plastic packaging every year, but only 19 per cent is collected for recycling, leaving more than one million tonnes to wind up as landfill or litter. Yet Toumbourou said about 320,000 tonnes of Australian plastic reprocessing capacity was standing ready, much of it sitting idle, awaiting the government reforms. This left recyclers in severe commercial peril with some plants facing closure, she said. The industry has been saying for several years that mandatory national standards for packaging are needed so that companies can invest with confidence. The Albanese government has talking about legislation since 2022, but former environment minister Tanya Plibersek and current Environment Minister Murray Watt say the problem has been getting the states and territories to agree.



“When I discuss these things with states, some are completely on board,” Watt said at the roundtable on Friday. “Some are very concerned about what might be quite minimal cost increases for consumers.” Related Article Perspective

Plastic Tooth powder and blocked drains: My week without single-use plastic Watt said packaging would be on the agenda at the next meeting of the federal, state, and territory environment ministers in September. One option for Watt could be using national policy payments to states to encourage them to come on board with national standards. De Wit said the economics of glass, cardboard and aluminium recycling made sense because they were a comparable cost to virgin material. That was not true for hard plastics – including the PET bottles such as water and soft drinks and the HDP bottles such as cloudy milk bottles – because the recycled resin had fixed costs based on collection and processing, while the virgin product was tied to the price of oil and fluctuated wildly. “As a producer of this recycled resin, we see the sales go strong when the virgin price is up here, and then drop off when they’re down here because a lot of companies buy the cheapest, whatever that is, virgin or recycled,” De Wit said.



“What I would like to see is what they’ve done in the 27 EU countries, in the UK, in California, Washington State, New Jersey, where they’ve said because of this exact issue, there has to be 25 per cent minimum recycled content in every plastic bottle.” De Wit said the additional cost would between half and one cent per bottle, so it would “not contribute one iota to a cost of living crisis”. Visy chief Mark De Wit showing an imported drink bottle with a PVC wrapper that contaminates plastic recycling. Dominic Lorrimer Another issue requiring government action was that imported drinks were not held to Australian standards. A plastic drink bottle produced in Australia had to have a wrapper that could be recycled with the bottle. But imported drinks such as those found in Asian supermarkets had PVC wrappers that contaminated the waste stream – one 3g wrapper would contaminate 150 kilograms of PET plastic recycling, which meant 7500 bottles could no longer be processed into food-grade packaging. Arnott’s chief executive George Zoghbi at the recycling roundtable hosted by Visy and this masthead. Dominic Lorrimer



George Zoghbi, chief executive of Arnott’s Biscuits, said he had two things on his wish list. “One is curbside collection for everything, including soft plastic because if you can do that at scale, it changes the game for everybody, and it makes the cost of recycling significantly cheaper, and the take-up rate significantly higher,” Zoghbi said. “The second one is that it’s very hard for consumers to look at these chemical symbols and say which colour bin you should use. Instead, you could put dots on the packaging that matches the colour of the bin – if it’s a red dot, it goes in the red bin; if it’s yellow, it goes in a yellow bin.” This would require states and territories to harmonise their bin collection systems. Get to the heart of what’s happening with climate change and the environment.

World.title: Fool’s gold: Trump’s promise to America is not going to plan
World.content:
BusinessThe economyTrump's America Opinion Fool’s gold: Trump’s promise to America is not going to plan Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist August 3, 2026 — 11:58am

August 3, 2026 — 11:58am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Who would have thought it? The eurozone, derided by Donald Trump as a declining economy that was heading in the wrong direction, outpaced the US economy in the June quarter. The eurozone economy grew at an annualised rate of 1.8 per cent that quarter, while the US economy grew at 1.5 per cent. Canada, hit hard by Trump’s tariffs, grew its economy over the quarter at an annualised rate of 3.4 per cent. US President Donald Trump, along with his Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, have repeatedly promised a “Golden Age” would arrive this year for the US economy. AP Europe’s growth rate was its fastest in more than a year, despite continuing energy shocks emanating from Trump’s war in the Middle East and his tariffs. In the United States, growth slowed from 2.1 per cent rate in the first three months of the year, despite the continuing boom in artificial intelligence-related investment, lower oil and petrol prices during the ceasefire in the war on Iran and a surge in spending by wealthier Americans (with some assistance from the World Cup) in June.



So much for an economic “Golden Age” for the US that Trump, his Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick have repeatedly promised would arrive this year. So far, the only gold is to be found in the White House, or on Washington’s monuments, where Trump has been gilding anything and everything he can, or in the wealth being accumulated by the Trump family and their associates. Related Article Trump's White House ‘I don’t have inside information’: How Donald Trump Jr is cashing in on dad’s presidency The US economy would probably be running a lot hotter if not for the war in the Middle East and the global war on trade that Trump keeps trying to establish a legal basis for. Along with the data on GDP that was published late last week, the Commerce Department put out personal consumption expenditures (PCE) data for June that showed the US Federal Reserve Board’s preferred measure of inflation, the PCE index, fell 0.1 per cent in June to be 3.7 per cent higher than it was in the same month last year.



While that’s well below the 4.1 per cent May-on-May rate, it is still way above the Fed’s inflation target of 2 per cent. Even stripped of energy and food prices, “core” PCE inflation was 3.3 per cent. In July, hostilities in the Middle East resumed, and oil prices, which had fallen back below $US72 ($102) a barrel in June, spiked again after the brief ceasefire. They surpassed $US100 a barrel last month, before again falling, to about $US84 a barrel at present, as talks appear to have resumed. The US economy would probably be running a lot hotter, if not for the war in the Middle East and the global war on trade that Trump keeps trying to find a legal basis for. Bloomberg US petrol and diesel prices remain well above their prewar levels – petrol about $US1 a gallon higher and diesel about $US1.60 a gallon higher – and will continue to feed into the inflation rate. It is inflation, a declining savings rate, and the fact that much of the equipment required for the boom in AI is imported (and therefore subtracts from GDP) that are weighing on US growth.



For various reasons – not least the stop-start ways in which the trade war, and the real war, have been waged – their impact on the inflation rate and economic growth hasn’t been as significant as most outside the administration had expected. With another newly imposed round of global tariffs on 99.4 per cent of America’s imports, and the war in the Middle East dragging on without any obvious clean conclusion, their effects on the economy and the inflation rate might have been stretched out and delayed, rather than avoided. Related Article Opinion

Interest rates As the Fed sits tight on interest rates, investors take action Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Rather than a one-off shock before prices stabilised, they might still be bleeding into prices and the economy in a fashion that means they may not be “transitory” and therefore can’t be dismissed as such by the Fed, which left its policy rate unchanged – for the fifth successive time – after last week’s meeting. With the Fed’s new Trump-appointed chairman, Kevin Warsh, creating an information vacuum by withdrawing any guidance on interest rates, the bond market has taken matters into its own hands.



The 10-year bond yield is now 4.74 per cent, compared with its pre-meeting level of 4.61 per cent. The 30-year yield has jumped 18 basis points to a 19-year high of 5.27 per cent. Those yields, if sustained, will choke spending and investment and raise the borrowing and refinancing costs on the US government’s debt, which is rapidly nearing $US40 trillion ($57 trillion). So far, the only gold is to be found in the White House, or on Washington’s monuments, where Trump has been gilding anything and everything he can, or in the wealth being accumulated by the Trump family and their associates. Eurozone data shows that its economies – despite being battered by energy-related shocks that began with the war in Ukraine and are continuing with the war in the Middle East, and having to deal with a tide of cheap Chinese imports that has swelled since Trump started building his tariff wall around the US market – are more resilient than expected. All the major economies – Germany, France, Italy and Spain – grew solidly, if not spectacularly, in the quarter, and Ireland, a beneficiary of the AI boom, bounced back from a sharp contraction in the first quarter to growth of 3.9 per cent in the second.



Like most of the rest of the world (China and Canada being the exceptions), while it did threaten action, the eurozone didn’t respond to the US tariffs with retaliatory tariffs – taxes on its consumers – of its own. It’s the US, thanks to the tariffs and the impact of the war-driven higher oil prices on domestic petrol and diesel prices, that is hitting its own businesses and consumers and its own growth hardest. A 1.5 per cent growth rate isn’t a disaster, but it’s hardly the “Golden Age”. The 5 or 6 per cent growth rates that Trump said his policies could generate haven’t materialised (which is no surprise), and neither have the trillions of dollars of foreign investment in the US manufacturing sector that he also said would flow. The Trump family and their associates are accumulating vast amounts of wealth during Donald’s second term. AP Real wages for US workers are declining, manufacturing sector jobs have shrunk, and it is the AI boom and those wealthiest households who benefited most from the tax cuts in Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act and who have gained most from the AI-driven sharemarket wealth effects that are generating the reasonably solid but unspectacular economic growth rate.



If something were to disrupt the AI boom – and investors are getting nervous about the sustainability of the vast amounts of capital being poured into it, by increasingly negative cashflow-generating companies, relative to the cheaper Chinese alternatives and the returns in prospect – the implications for the sharemarket and economy would be threatening. Related Article Opinion

Trump's White House The lyin’ king Trump is the kind of leader the nation’s father feared and reviled Maureen Dowd New York Times columnist Trump and those in his team regularly denigrate the Europeans and their economies, saying the economies are over-regulated, stagnating or declining, being swamped by illegal migrants and effectively subsidised by the US (or leeching off it via unfair terms of trade). Some of those criticisms might be valid, but the Trump alternative of aggressive deregulation, trade barriers and extortion, draconian crackdowns on undocumented migrants and immigration more broadly and a war in the Middle East that is delivering nothing but humiliation and higher energy costs make it difficult for the administration to claim the US, or at least this particular administration, has the superior economic or governance model.
