World.title: In-school teacher training programmes get funding boost
World.content:
In-school teacher training programmes are a "disruptor" that will help improve initial teacher education, says the education minister.

The government has announced it will increase the number of funded places from 528 this year to 660 next year and 704 every year from 2028.

Education Minister Erica Stanford said the increase would cost $21.7m over five years and the funding was redirected from a relocation grant for foreign early childhood teachers.

Students on the School Onsite Training Programme are placed three days a week in a host school and are paid a $19,930 stipend while they complete a one-year teaching qualification.

Stanford said it was a good option for students straight out of university and for career-changers.

Asked if the government wanted the model to become the dominant or preferred form of teacher education, Stanford said it would depend on the programme's success.

"We do need to do an evaluation at a later date, once we've had a few years under our belt. But it is certainly proving to be very successful," she said.

"All of the schools I talk to absolutely love it. They love the teachers who come out the other end because they're so much more prepared to teach in the classroom.

"So it is something I would like to keep investing in if the statistics show that it is working."

Universities recently told RNZ they felt out of favour because non-universities were allocated significant increases in funded places under the scheme, but they were not.

"They are not out of favour," Stanford said.

"There's a criteria. Meet the criteria and you'll get places. It's as simple as that."

But Stanford said initial teacher education needed a shake-up, citing a 2024 Education Review Office report that said many new teachers were not well-prepared for their job.

Universities have [https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/education/516698/universities-reject-ero-criticism-of-teacher-training-courses

criticised the report], saying it was completed after Covid lock-downs disrupted many students' classroom placements and the principals unhappy with the quality of graduates were not a representative sample.

"You will have seen ERO's report into the ability of teachers to manage classroom behaviour and be ready to teach, and they have made many comments about the state of initial teacher education," she said.

"There isn't a day of the week that I don't go into a school and have a principal say to me that they lament the state of initial teacher education in this country. I make no apologies that this is a system disruptor.

"It's part of the reason I'm taking the initial teacher education standard setting function off the teaching council, putting it with the Ministry of Education because we want to up the standards to make sure that the graduates are coming out and it's to be fair to them as well.

World.title: Inquest begins into 'plainly unlawful' carbon monoxide death of 12-year-old Jesse Samuel
World.content:
The mother of an Otago boy who died from carbon monoxide poisoning in a shower has told a coronial inquest she will never think of his death as an accident because it was preventable.

At an inquest in Queenstown, coroner Mary-Anne Borrowdale is examining what she calls the "plainly unlawful" circumstances of Jesse's death and what could be done to prevent something similar happening in future.

Jesse's mother Justine Walker told the court her son had his whole life ahead of him and it had been eight long years waiting for the inquest.

"I know today will never give Jesse his life back, his future, his dreams, his goals. It will not give me my life back and it will not give my children their childhood or their lives back but from today, I wish those involved are made accountable and acknowledged and that changes are made," she said.

Walker described her son as a dedicated athlete, a fabulous big brother and a truly caring soul.

"What I admire most about him was his passion for life. He never missed a moment or an opportunity. He was going to make the most of everything and give it his all," she said.

The inquest follows the 2021 sentencing of gasfitter Michael Cartwright and the company Laser Plumbing Alexandra who pleaded guilty to charges under the Plumbers, Gasfitters and Drainlayers Act.

Cartwright signed off on his co-worker Gary Hale's installation of the water heater despite never seeing the work.

Cartwright and the company were fined more than $120,000.

Borrowdale said Jesse died on a freezing, wet day when the bathroom window was "understandably closed".

The heater was not meant to be used in a bathroom, she said.

"When Jesse showered, the little shower unit filled with carbon monoxide gas. Carbon monoxide is odourless, colourless and tasteless, but it is deadly poisonous," she said.

"When Jesse was found he was unable to be revived."

Borrowdale said the inquest would focus on the certification of the appliance, the sufficiency of current training for gas fitters and the regulatory systems in place to prevent dangerous installations.

Gasfitting expert David Whitfield told the inquest that Cartwright made a "rudimentary error" signing a safety certificate for the work.

He said supervising gasfitters were not required to visit every single site but Hale and Cartwright were both working at the Haast property.

Whitfield said Cartwright did not perform any tests or ask Hale for the specifics of what he had done.

The wrong type of ventilation - a flue pipe - was used, while a label on the gas heater showed that it should not be installed in a bedroom, bathroom, toilet or sleeping area, Whitfield said.

He told the inquest it was likely that Hale saw the safety warnings on the gas heater but was not fully aware of the risk.

It had been a long time since Hale was trained, Whitfield noted.

"A person who only does gas burning work infrequently can over time forget some of the fundamental knowledge of the specific regulation or specific part of the standards," he said.

"In my experience, it is common for gas burners to make mistakes if they gas burn as a small percentage of their work."

Whitfield said gasfitters should be required to upload photos and test results of their work to a database.

Such a system would allow regulators to identify and fix dangerous installations before anyone came to harm, he said.

Whitfield said the licensing board - the Plumbers, Gasfitters, and Drainlayers Board - should also have "more teeth" and be allowed to force gasfitters to undertake competency reviews.

The coroner is also expected to hear from Michael Cartwright, Jesse's uncle Brendan Walker, and representatives from WorkSafe, the heating appliance maker Bosch, and the Ministry of Business Innovation and Employment.

World.title: Person found dead, police cordon off property in Palmerston North
World.content:
Police have cordoned off a property in Palmerston North's Highbury on Monday.

Officers were trying to find a couple of people when a person was found dead on Wilson Crescent, police at the scene said.

RNZ / Jimmy Ellingham

Investigations were now underway, including from the coroner.

A tow truck has taken away a white car, while a hearse arrived at the scene about 2pm.

RNZ / Jimmy Ellingham

World.title: Ex-Fiji Rugby executive says anti-corruption agency 'not fit for purpose' after court victory
World.content:
A former Fiji Rugby Union executive and longtime journalist believes the country's anti-corruption agency is "not fit for purpose".

Charlie Charters, a British-Fijian national, made the comments after the Fiji High Court in Suva permanently stayed the criminal proceedings against him a fortnight ago.

In March, the Fiji Independent Commission Against Corruption (FICAC) charged Charters with two counts of aiding and abetting an unidentified whistleblower to unlawfully disclose official information about the organisation.

However, the Fiji High Court, on 24 July, dismissed the charges, ruling that FICAC violated his constitutional rights and abused the court process.

In his ruling, Justice Pita Bulamainaivalu found that Charters' "right under Section 13 of the Constitution 2013 was violated by FICAC", adding that his "right to freedom of speech, expression, thought, opinion and publication under Section 17 of the Constitution 2013 including not to divulge the sources of his journalistic information was violated by FICAC".

Charters said the ruling was a victory for him and everyone who believed in justice.

He said Fiji needed to take "a long hard look at how it wants to fight corruption".

He added that if successful corruption prosecutions were the yardstick of success then "FICAC is not fit for purpose".

"I was grateful that the High Court decision sent as loud and crystal-clear a message as it did in the ruling but it should not have come to this and that FICAC broke very basic prosecution rules," he said.

"Everyone came to understand that this was how FICAC operated under Bainimarama (former Prime Minister Frank Bainimarama), a way to take out regime enemies or political opponents.

FICAC is Fiji' anti-corruption agency. ABC/Supplied

He said that was why Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka campaigned in 2022 to close FICAC and fold its resources into the police.

"But FICAC has continued to operate in the same fashion today - tying up government opponents in ultimately unsuccessful prosecutions like myself," the 57-year-old said.

"If the same outcome happens with the cases against Manoa Kamikamica and Professor Biman Prasad (former deputy prime ministers), every citizen should be outraged that literally nothing has changed between the Bainimarama and Rabuka governments.

"It's like Bainimarama created the weapon, the Rabuka government told everyone they would get rid of the weapon. But when they got into office, Rabuka's government found the weapon was actually quite useful.

"You could just imagine someone saying, 'Maybe, we will use the weapon a little bit ourselves'."

Both Kamikamica and Prasad currently have cases against FICAC.

Charters was represented by lawyers Juleen Fatiaki and Seforan Fatiaki, while Justice Bulamainaivalu had granted FICAC 30 days to appeal to the Fiji Court of Appeal.

World.title: Inquest into Pauline Hanna's death 'not a trial of Dr Polkinghorne'
World.content:
An inquest into the death of Pauline Hanna has begun in Auckland - with a reminder that her husband is not on trial.

The inquest will attempt to determine how Hanna died and the circumstances surrounding her death.

Polkinghorne attended Monday's hearing, but was not expected to give evidence until next week.

Pauline Hanna's brother, Bruce Hanna. RNZ / Marika Khabazi

Hanna's brother Bruce Hanna, his wife Shelley and son Jacob were also there. They set up a framed photo of Hanna and a small bunch of flowers from the family garden in a white vase at the front of the court.

They were wearing white ribbons on their shirts.

Coroner Tania Tetitaha. RNZ / Marika Khabazi

In her opening remarks, Coroner Tania Tetitaha noted an inquest was to try to determine how Hanna died.

Even though some of the evidence overlapped with the trial, the purpose of the inquest was very different, she said.

"I remind everyone that this is not a trial of Dr Polkinghorne," she said.

Pauline Hanna's husband, retired eye surgeon Philip Polkinghorne, was found not guilty of her murder at a trial in 2024. NZME/Michael Craig

She would only consider evidence about him if it was directly related to determining the cause of Hanna's death, she said.

"No person is on trial, there is no prosecution, there is no defence, there is no burden of proof," she said.

Coroner Tetitaha said she would try to determine what happened, on the balance of probabilities.

Alysha McClintock. RNZ / Marika Khabazi

Crown solicitor (in court as counsel for police) Alysha McClintock acknowledged the case was not a trial, but said there was still a major question about whether Hanna's death was self-inflicted or whether it was inflicted by someone else.

Suppressions meant media were not able to report anything about the mechanism of Hanna's death.

In her opening, McClintock said there was a question about whether Hanna was the victim of an assault. There was evidence a struggle had taken place, including that Hanna's room was dishevelled, she said.

The day before her death Hanna had gone to see her personal trainer, had made a meal for some sick friends and had gone to the rubbish dump, she said. There was no suicide note and no search on her personal devices regarding suicide, McClintock said.

She asked the coroner to consider that some of Polkinghorne's initial account when he called police to report finding Hanna was at odds with what police found at the scene.

There was evidence he had been active during the night, and a few days later he searched how to delete search history from iCloud.

Polkinghorne's lawyer Ron Mansfield said the police were still obsessed with the idea Hanna died as a result of homicide. They were fixated on Polkinghorne's lifestyle, and that made them prejudiced against him, he said.

Mansfield said the police had a "voyeuristic fascination" with Polkinghorne and Hanna's lifestyle that was clouding their judgement.

McClintock had been the prosecutor at the trial and seemed to be reverting to that role at this hearing, even though her role in the inquest was to assist the coroner with finding answers, Mansfield said.

The suggestion that homicide was behind Hanna's death needed to be viewed with scepticism, he said.

Her messy room was merely because her bed had been slept in, he said.

Philip Polkinghorne's lawyer Ron Mansfield. RNZ / Marika Khabazi

Bruce Hanna addressed the court, saying there were still many unanswered questions about his sister's death.

"That terrible day, 5th of April 2021, was the worst day of my life," he said. "Not only was I devastated by Pauline's death but what I was told on that day I do not believe and I still do not believe five years later."

He said he believed Polkinghorne was on meth the night Hanna died and that should be a major part of the inquest.

"There have been many tall stories, misconceptions, lies, absolute garbage that I have heard and read. I hope these will be exposed in the coming days and weeks."

The inquest will likely take about two weeks, with more detailed evidence from police, and a pathologist and pharmacologist from Australia.

Where to get help:

World.title: ACT policy on class disruption 'simplistic' but has a point - Education Minister Erica Stanford
World.content:
The education minister has offered tentative support for ACT's plan allowing teachers to physically force students from classrooms, saying it is heading in the right direction.

ACT wants to give teachers the legal power to use reasonable force to remove seriously or persistently disruptive students.

Education spokesperson Paul Henry said it would regain order over "little shits" in the classroom.

Erica Stanford told Midday Report ACT had picked up on something that was a known problem.

"They do have a point... that it has become very unclear through the legislation and the guidance and the training about what teachers can and can't do in a classroom.

"I would argue that their approach is probably a little bit overly simplistic, but heading in the right direction."

The law already allowed for teachers to remove children from classrooms, Stanford said.

"The training that I've identified that they get is woeful and the guidance is poor, so there's a huge grey area about what they can and can't do.

"So while they have the legal ability, they're not using it."

The coalition was looking at improving that training and guidance, she said.

"There's a huge bureaucracy around it, you've got to fill in a million pieces of paperwork, and then [it's] just not clear on the situations where they can and can't do things."

Labour education spokesperson Ginny Andersen said ACT's policy would make classrooms less safe.

World.title: 'Something is very wrong': Samoa rugby split deepens with launch of rival union
World.content:
A new rugby union has been launched in Samoa, despite efforts by the sport's global governing body to mediate a resolution to the current impasse between the Samoan government and Lakapi Samoa.

Media reports out of Apia says the new Samoa Rugby Football Union (SRFU), a rival organisation to Lakapi Samoa, was launched at the Sheraton Samoa Aggie Grey's Hotel on Friday evening.

At the same time, there are reports that Lakapi Samoa chairman Afioga Namulauulu Papali'i Leota Sami Leota and his board members have stepped aside pending a review.

The new body was launched just two days after the Samoan government anounced it was withdrawing support for Lakapi Samoa, throwing the future of the sport in the country into disarray.

Both the Samoa Observer and the Talamua Online News reported the new body was launched over the weekend.

SRFU secretary Tafafunai Aialii Anapu stated the organisation remained committed to its establishment and its vision of uniting Samoa's rugby community.

RNZ Pacific sources says World Rugby had given conditions given to government, although World Rugby has denied giving an ultimatum, stating it was "in dialogue with all parties in a mediator role".

The Pacific Rugby Players Welfare (PRPW) said in a Facebook post that Lakapi Samoa board chairman Afioga and his board members have stepped aside pending a review.

"A caretaker Board to be appointed in the interim," the PRPW said.

"Tough times but excited what lies ahead for Samoan rugby. A total reset was required."

Lakapi Samoa has not responded to RNZ Pacific's questions about Lakapi Samoa board resignations.

But Talamua Online News said the new union is led by former Manu Samoa representative Matafeo George Latu as chairman.

It reported the new union is supported by 16 sub-unions, which were represented by their respective presidents at the launch.

Matafeo told attendees at the launch the new union was initiated due to the current status of the sport that is impacting negatively on the future of Samoan rugby, the lack of innovation by the board and management, the lack of trust by district rugby unions of Lakapi Samoa and the lack of accountability.

"Something is very wrong with Samoa rugby," Matafeo said at the launch.

"What saddens me more is lack of accountability for the underperformance of our teams with the blame being put on the players, on the coaches, and even on the government for not providing enough funds.

"Not once have I heard those that govern rugby in Samoa own up or take responsibility for the dire state of Samoan rugby."

Matafeo added that sports and politics cannot mix.

"There is a real danger that politicians on sports board can, and have, used sports to further their own political agendas."

Prime Minister La'auli Leuatea Schmidt had publicly revealed that he was not supportive of Lakapi Samoa's board, including former PM Tuilaʻepa Saʻilele Malielegaoi, who was board chairman until he resigned earlier this year.

La'auli had threatened to start a rival union.

World.title: Luxon plans chat with Peters about 'racist' remarks 'at some point', says they've both 'been on the road'
World.content:
The prime minister is yet to pick up the phone to Winston Peters after his tirade towards a Chinese-born MP in Parliament last week, saying he will talk to the foreign minister "at some point".

New Zealand First's leader responded to heckling in the House on Wednesday by attacking the Greens' Lawrence Xu-nan, telling him to go back to his own country.

Christopher Luxon on Monday told Morning Report the comments were racist, but he had not yet spoken with Peters about it.

"This is him talking in his New Zealand First capacity," Luxon said.

Weekly interview with Prime Minister, Christopher Luxon Morning Report Download MP3 9m

Multiple international media outlets have published Peters' comments, referring to him as New Zealand's foreign minister.

Luxon said he had made his position clear in previous comments to the media.

"I will talk to him at some point, I'm sure, about it. But the point is I've been on the road, he's been on the road," he said.

"I have a strong view about it. It is racist and offensive. That's it."

Luxon said he was calling out Peters' game-playing.

"It is deliberate attention seeking to push buttons to get the attention on himself... rather than issues that matter to Kiwis."

Luxon was asked whether he would rule out forming another coalition with NZ First.

"There's a lot of hypotheticals - at the moment, I don't want to work with anyone," he said.

"My ideal situation is 20 National ministers in Cabinet would be the very best outcome for New Zealand."

But Luxon said National had proven it could find common ground with coalition partners, ACT and NZ First, despite disagreeing with them on some things.

That was the nature of MMP politics, he said.

Untenable as foreign minister - Opportunity

Quilae Wong rules out working with Peters as Foreign Minister Midday Report Download MP3 5m

The Opportunity Party, which National had already ruled out working with, has itself ruled out working with a government that has Peters as foreign minister.

The party has never been in Parliament before, but says it is willing to find common ground with anyone, including NZ First.

Qiulae Wong. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

But leader Qiulae Wong told Midday Report that Peters' position as foreign minister had become untenable.

"Given that this is repeated behaviour, we've seen these kinds of comments happen multiple occasions, I don't think that it's the kind of behaviour that we should expect, particularly of a foreign minister, and we wouldn't want to be part of a government that was putting him in that position."

She said Opportunity was aligned with NZ First on matters like shaking up the supermarket and energy sectors, but Peters' language was "not conducive" to a country that needed to come together and move forward.

World.title: Quick hits: Delta stuns with Aussie classic, 76yo claims history-making gold
World.content:
Delta Goodrem belts out an Aussie classic, a 76-year-old makes Commonwealth Games history and a cycling star is proud to have not thrown up on the podium.

Here are the quick hits from day nine of the Commonwealth Games.

1. Delta makes it a hat-trick with Aussie classic

Delta Goodrem produced a breathtaking performance in the closing ceremony. (Getty Images: Mattia Ozbot)

It was a closing ceremony featuring some serious Australian star power, with Delta Goodrem headlining proceedings.

It was the third time, after Melbourne 2006 and Gold Coast 2018, that Goodrem had performed at a Commonwealth Games, and the Australian icon was in fine form at the Hydro indoor arena in Glasgow.

Goodrem was revealed to the crowd in dramatic fashion, lit by a spotlight and sitting at a grand piano, belting out her classic Born To Try, before rising from her seat and welcoming the athletes into the venue with an inspired medley of her hits.

And the performance reached a real crescendo when she welcomed Scottish pop star Cammy Barnes to the stage for a rendition of the most classic of Aussie classics, John Farnham's You're the Voice.

Goosebumps in Glasgow.

2. 76-year-old creates Games history

Louise Hoskins made history on the final day of competition. (Getty Images: Adam Pretty)

Louise Hoskins, 76, made history on the final day of competition in Glasgow, becoming the oldest medal winner in Commonwealth Games history.

She, along with partner Serena Bonnell, won gold in the women's Para bowls, defeating New Zealand in a classic.

It was Bonnell who provided the winning moment for the Aussies, conjuring a sublime shot late in the second set to secure the win.

The oldest competitor in Glasgow, Hoskins was struggling to wrap her head around the enormity of the achievement.

"It is incredible. I'm still pinching myself," she said.

"I never thought I'd ever get [a gold medal] at my age. Get out there and have a go, and never give up."

Asked how she planned to celebrate, Hoskins noted Bonnell still owed her a few drinks.

What will it be then?

"Whatever Serena's going to give me," Hoskins laughed.

3. Cycling star proud not to spew on podium

Leigh Hoffman looked far from comfortable on the podium. (Getty Images: Rob Casey/SNS Group)

Australian Leigh Hoffman won four medals in a packed track cycling program, including a gold on the final day of competition.

He was the second-last rider in the men's 1,000m time trial, so had a truncated warm-down before climbing onto the podium to receive his gold medal.

And he looked far from comfortable on the top step.

"You don't feel human," he says.

"You're just so cooked, my legs are still burning right now, I think it's been a solid hour. There's no pain like it for sprint and endurance – 1 kilometre all-out sprint, 58 seconds of pure pain. I'm still feeling it.

"I made sure to eat about four hours out so my stomach was pretty empty. I'm proud I didn't spew."

This is the sprint and keirin specialist's first 1km time trial in six years, but he says he has no plans to keep riding them at world titles, although he may go again in Amdavad in four years' time.

4. Aussie chef de mission gets ink

Loading...

Australia's chef de mission Petria Thomas loves the Friendly Games — and understandably so.

She was a nine-time Commonwealth gold medallist during her decorated swimming career and has just overseen a Games in which Australia claimed 70 golds, 41 more than the next best nation, England.

On the final day of competition, Thomas was seen out in Glasgow getting herself a permanent testament to the event for which she has so much affection.

She said the Games have a special place in her heart, and now a special place on her body.

"I've thought about it for a long time and the Commonwealth Games has been such a big part of my life, as big a part as the Olympics. So I thought why not get the Commonwealth Sport mark as well, and I'll wear it very proudly," Thomas said.

"The Commonwealth Games has played such an important part of my life and I wanted to get something to remember that."

5. Scottish athletes win fashion stakes

Scottish athletes had some fun at the closing ceremony. (AP: Kin Cheung)

Scottish athletes were hard to miss at the closing ceremony.

The host nation's contingent wore traffic cones on their heads as they took part in the festivities inside The Hydro.

Loading Instagram content

It's common practice for Glaswegians to put traffic cones on the heads of statues around the city.

Arguably the most famous example is the Duke of Wellington statue outside the Gallery of Modern Art.

A statue in Boston could not escape the Glaswegian tradition during the FIFA World Cup. (Getty Images: Craig Williamson/SNS Group)

The ritual was celebrated at the recent FIFA World Cup, with Scottish fans decorating statues in Boston in their customary way.

You can never suggest Scots don't know how to poke fun at themselves.

ABC/AAP

World.title: Blues pay tribute to 'hero' Daley as he stands down as coach
World.content:
Laurie Daley has ended speculation about his future by stepping down as NSW State of Origin coach after a series victory over Queensland.

After much speculation about his future, Daley took the expected step and announced the move in a statement from the NSWRL.

"I've always considered it an absolute honour and privilege to be involved with the NSW Blues State of Origin team, whether that was as a player or a coach, and I've always been ready to answer the call for my state whenever they needed me," Daley said.

Daley slams 'hidden agendas' after NSW Origin win Laurie Daley has the last laugh over critics who hounded him ahead of the State of Origin decider at Lang Park.

"We faced plenty of challenges in the 2026 series and I'm proud of the way the players banded together to overcome them and save their best performance for Game Three in Brisbane to secure a memorable series win.

"I thank the fans for their passion and their support, and I can't think of a better way to move on with the Shield back where it belongs in NSW."

The NSWRL paid tribute to Daley for his time with the team.

"NSWRL owes a massive debt of gratitude to Laurie for the service he has given to his state as both a player and a coach," NSWRL chief executive David Trodden said.

"He is widely regarded as one of the greatest players to have ever pulled on a sky blue jumper, becoming the first NSW captain to lead his state to three consecutive series wins in 1992-94.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"He has also led NSW to arguably two of the greatest Origin series wins of all time as a coach, after ending Queensland's eight-year winning streak in 2014 and overcoming adversity to steer the Blues home in 2026.

"Those wins transcended football. They lifted and reinvigorated the whole state. He deserves to leave the NSW Origin arena as the hero that he is."

After sealing the State of Origin series win, Daley delivered a scathing rebuke to his critics, suggesting there were "hidden agendas" that attempted to undermine his NSW camp.

Daley, hammered publicly and privately over the Blues' form through the first two games of the series, had the last laugh as NSW secured a 30-12 victory at Lang Park.

World.title: Commonwealth Games don't need to mean anything to you to mean the world
World.content:
You see a lot of Olympic rings tattoos on athletes.

They feature a lot in the pool and the track, as you'd expect, but you'll catch them on NRL and NRLW players too from time to time, thanks to the recent inclusion of rugby sevens.

Petria Thomas got them on her right ankle 30 years ago and, after Glasgow, she's had the 2026 Commonwealth Games logo inked on the other side.

"The Commonwealth Games has been such a big part of my life, as big a part as the Olympics, so I thought why not?" the eight-time Olympic medallist said.

"I'll wear it very proudly."

Loading...

Thomas, who won nine golds across three Commonwealth outings, said the 1994 Games were the springboard for her career, just as they will be for so many athletes in Glasgow.

"For many athletes, this is their first experience in a multi-sport environment and there's nothing that can compare to going into those sorts of environments," she said.

"So to have the opportunity to do it here in Glasgow has been incredible and for so many of our Australian athletes, the Commonwealth Games is their launching pad."

The 2026 Games will forever mark the coming out party for debutant athletes as varied as 14-year-old Mia Hogan, a girl who made the final of the women's 100m freestyle S13 on the first night of the swimming program, and 76-year-old Louise Hoskins, Australia's oldest gold medallist after para pairs bowls victory in the final hours of competition.

At 76, Games debutant Louise Hopkins is Australia's oldest gold medallist. (Getty Images: Adam Pretty)

For the rising athletics team, this was a combination of a coming of age and a coming out, with the middle-distance, long-distance and field stars reaffirming their brilliance, and the newly minted sprint stars shining at an international meet for the first time.

Even in the swimming team, with so many established stars who regularly speak about the Commonwealth Games as a stepping stone, there were people like Jenna Forrester and Sam Williamson and Meg Harris getting their moments in the sun.

At times it felt like an unfair fight.

Shayna Jack, Meg Harris and Mollie O'Callaghan made just one of the podium sweeps for the Australian team. (Gety Images: Ross MacDonald/SNS Group)

In the end, Australia led the overall medal tally by a cool 61 medals, winning more than twice as many golds as England and more than triple Canada's after topping the swimming, cycling and athletics.

It's true that some of the best sporting nations weren't here and of those that were, some of the superstars didn't turn up, but you can only beat the ones who do.

"We're just good at our sport. Everyone likes an underdog. We're the same in Australia," Thomas said.

"Australians really value Commonwealth Games, it's always been an important competition for us and our sports know how important it is for athlete development and career progression. We really have prioritised Commonwealth Games and that's really shown here."

And try telling Peter Bol that these Games don't matter as he cheered on Luke Boyes and Peyton Craig on their way to the 800m final.

It mattered to Peter Bol. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Try telling Paul Trainor not to worry as he processed being battered by Dimeji Shittu in their heavyweight semifinal.

It mattered to Paul Trainor. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Try telling Kiana Elliott to cheer up after her third clean and jerk left her fourth for a second straight Games.

It mattered to Kiana Elliott. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Try telling Georgia Baker her spectacular Games weren't worth anything as she burst into tears when receiving the news she was the closing ceremony flag-bearer.

It mattered to Georgia Baker. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

These Games can mean government waste to Victorians, they can mean occasional traffic inconveniences to Glaswegians, they can mean late nights or early mornings on a blog or stream for many of you.

But they can also mean a new beginning, for athletes young and old, and for the Games as a whole.

Ironically, the event that Thomas credits for kickstarting her international career 32 years ago, was held in Victoria, albeit the one in Canada. This time around, the Australian version's withdrawal led to Glasgow picking up the baton.

Fans gather near Glasgow's Finnieston Crane between Games events. (Getty Images: Euan Cherry)

Limited and imperfect, it was a decision that saved a concept on life support.

"We're just grateful to be here," Thomas said, getting choked up.

"After what occurred, there was a time where we didn't know whether there would ever be another Commonwealth Games."

Commonwealth Sport has pledged to keep the Games alive.

It wants to engage with athletes to make them fit for purpose and sustainable, economically and environmentally.

Amdavad in India has pledged to deliver a full slate of events in 2030, with prospective hosts allegedly expressing interest in taking on 2034.

Who knows if that will come to fruition, but for 10 days of inclement weather and imperfect organisation, we saw a glimpse of Australia's future, and that's got to be worth something.

World.title: Cronulla coach's belief grows as Sharks surge towards NRL finals
World.content:
Cronulla is promising no let-up after extending its league-best winning streak to five matches, sparking talk that an elusive second NRL premiership is in the offing for the surging Sharks.

Rarely has understated coach Craig Fitzgibbon been more bullish about his belief in the team than after Sunday's dazzling 32-16 dispatch of South Sydney.

"I've never felt any different about the group in the last five years, to be honest, but maybe I believe in them more than they believe in themselves," he said.

With Nicho Hynes back to the vintage form that earned him the Dally M Medal and the Sharks a top-two finish in 2022, and his halves partner, Braydon Trindall, in career-best touch, the Sharks are flying with nine wins from their past 10 outings.

Michael Ennis, the club's 2016 grand final-winning hooker-turned-analyst, believes the Sharks will go all the way again a decade on from breaking the longest and most infamous title drought in premiership history.

It's 10 years since the Sharks beat the Storm in the NRL grand final and the club is shaping up to scale the heights again. (Getty Images: Mark Kolbe)

"We're working hard towards something and we've been building that for a little bit," Fitzgibbon said.

"And then sometimes you get things go your way, sometimes they don't. But at the moment, it's going our way.

"There's still plenty more. We'll have a hiccup here and there and there'll be turbulence, but you won't challenge me on how much I believe in them."

Sitting fourth and certain not to face any more top-eight opposition until the finals, the Sharks are well placed to snatch an all-important top-two spot.

But skipper Blayke Brailey says the Sharks won't be taking their foot off the pedal, with the side's immediate focus on Sunday's derby with St George Illawarra.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

The Dragons may be wooden spoon-bound but the Sharks won't be taking their arch rivals lightly, especially with points differential between the top teams looking increasingly important.

"A derby clash, no matter where you're sitting on the table, it's a tough contest," Brailey said.

"Those derby games are tough, no matter the form you're in."

After the Dragons at Kogarah, the Sharks face Canberra at home, the Titans on the Gold Coast, Parramatta away and Melbourne in a potentially crucial last-round battle at Shark Park.

AAP

World.title: Lorena Wiebes sprints to second straight win at Tour de France Femmes
World.content:
Lorena Wiebes again sprinted to victory in the second stage of the Women’s Tour de France.

The Dutch rider of SD Worx-Protime won the flat 147.9-kilometre stage from Aigle to Geneva, the second on Swiss territory, in 3 hours, 42 minutes, 8 seconds on Sunday.

Wiebes went ahead with some 250 metres to go and claimed her seventh overall victory at the tour.

Wiebes also won the opening stage on Saturday in the same dominant fashion.

Lidl-Trek rider Elisa Balsamo finished second and Marianne Vos of Team Visma-Lease a Bike was third.

Wiebes leads Kim Le Court Pienaar by 14 seconds overall, with the 2023 Tour champion Demi Vollering another two seconds back in third.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Monday's 156.5km (97.2-mile) hilly stage starts in Geneva before the riders cross the border to France to finish in Poligny.

This edition of the race, the fifth of the Women’s Tour, covers 1,175km (730 miles) over nine days.

Amanda Spratt is the leading Australian in the race, in 68th place, 3 minutes and 20 seconds behind Wiebes.

Tadej Pogacar won his fifth men's Tour de France title last weekend.

AP/ABC

World.title: Diamonds win bronze medal with an eye to greater things for netball
World.content:
There's a sentiment in team sports at multi-sport events like the Commonwealth Games that you lose silver and win bronze.

The bronze medallists get to climb on the podium having won their last match, while second place is coming off a heartbreaking loss, having let gold slip through their grasp.

For the Diamonds, bronze at the 2026 Commonwealth Games is a complicated celebration.

Less than 20 hours after Jamaica ripped their hearts out in the semifinal, the Aussie netballers were back on court at 9am in Glasgow for the first centre pass of their first-ever bronze-medal match.

Diamonds fumble Australia's most anticipated gold medal The Diamonds will miss the Commonwealth Games gold medal match for the first time after a shock semifinal loss to Jamaica in front of a crowd baying for Australia's downfall.

It was hard to bounce back from the loss but they did so against England, winning 65-80.

"We had such a quick time to process what happened, I think a lot of us still feel quite numb," defender Jo Weston said.

"Then you go out and have a game like we did, we're so proud and we know all of Australia have been behind us, so it's been a real rollercoaster of emotions in a very short time frame. But I think the overwhelming feeling is pride and a lot of love for each other.

"It's immensely challenging for us having that mental fortitude to come back out. We have very high expectations of ourselves and we want to do our country proud.

The Diamonds rediscovered their flow to keep their medal-winning streak alive. (AP: Andrew Milligan/PA)

"They always say Diamonds are made under pressure and I think that really showed in us today. Although it's not the colour we were after we're really proud about it."

Coach Stacey Marinkovich said the night between the games was about leaving space for team members to "be vulnerable".

There was no point pretending they weren't gutted, that the loss was anything other than gut-wrenching, but once they left the meeting room it was about moving forward.

"It was very emotional last night, it was still probably lingering today a little bit, so to be able to mentally switch in showed our culture isn't words on a wall," she said.

There were complicated emotions for Australia's bronze medallists. (Getty Images: James Fearn)

"That took a lot of grit to be able to go out there and get that result."

Adding another layer of emotion for these stewards of the game, constantly fighting for eyeballs and recognition, is the more objective flip-side of the loss.

That is those celebrations of the Sunshine Girls after the semifinal.

For the first five Commonwealth Games, only Australia and New Zealand won gold and silver. In 2018, England stunned the Diamonds on their home patch for the Gold Coast title. Four years ago Jamaica beat the Aussies in their group match and made their first final. And in Glasgow, they went even better to take the Diamonds down in a knockout match to fight New Zealand for gold.

"International netball is the best it's ever been, which is so good for the sport, it's what we want to see," Weston said.

Four countries is not an enormous range of winners or even contenders, but in every event around the world there are dominant forces.

It wasn't the colour they wanted or expected, but a medal's a medal. (Getty Images: James Fearn)

With six years to the Brisbane Olympics and a push for the sport's inclusion, the Diamonds' bronze may have been the best thing for game.

"It's great for the sport because we always want the game to grow. Gone are the days where it's just one or two nations really dominating," Kiera Austin said.

"It's disappointing for us to have not gotten to that point ... but Jamaica were far too good on the day and that's great going into Brisbane hopefully getting netball into the Olympics.

"It's a sport we absolutely love, a sport we think deserves a great platform on the international stage and if it means a greater competition, then winning that gold medal whenever we get the chance to again is going to be all that much sweeter."

World.title: Delta Goodrem brings Australia's golden Commonwealth Games to a close
World.content:
Delta Goodrem shone on a saltire-shaped stage as Glasgow waved farewell to the Commonwealth Games in spectacular style by the banks of the River Clyde.

As a packed Hydro crowd roared with Scottish rock band Simple Minds and fireworks lit up the River Clyde waterfront, lingering fears were momentarily set aside.

The Commonwealth Games, having been on life support, are alive and kicking.

The Australian athletes were led out by Georgia Baker, who earned flagbearer honours by adding two gold medals in Glasgow to take her record-equalling cycling tally to five.

Glasgow's cut-price "Friendly Games" were inescapably cheerful and run with good humour throughout, even through persistent summer rain, in tribute to a proud city that picked up the pieces when Victoria pulled out.

Delta Goodrem brought the house down at the Hydro for the closing ceremony. (Getty: Euan Cherry)

Eleven days of competition — which produced 171 medals for table-topping Australia — came to a close in a celebration of athletic performances as Glasgow 2026 formally passed the baton to Amdavad 2030.

It came with an unmistakable message from Scotland's gritty cultural hub, its people and the headline act: Don't you forget about me.

Scottish singer-songwriter Sandi Thom, shimmering in a sequined saltire dress, kicked off the closing ceremony with her reworked football anthem Proud to Be from Scotland.

Australian pop princess Delta Goodrem also shone on the saltire-shaped stage, opening with Born To Try and belting out a cover of John Farnham's You're the Voice with Scottish country and folk singer-songwriter Cammy Barnes.

Goodrem's presence was designed as a metaphor for an extension of Scotland's hand of friendship to the country that was originally to have staged the Games.

Australian chef de mission Petria Thomas expressed gratitude to Glasgow for taking on hosting duties after Victoria pulled out.

"The Commonwealth Games is a really critically important event," Thomas said.

"If this had not been on it would have left a huge hole in our in the calendar, and for many athletes this is their first experience in a multi-sport environment.

"There's nothing that can compare to going into those sort of environments, so to give them the opportunity to do it here in Glasgow has been incredible.

"For so many of our Australian athletes, the Commonwealth Games is their launching pad."

What the Commonwealth Games mean is up to you Australian chef de mission and eight-time Olympic medallist Petria Thomas cried as she spoke about the importance of the Commonwealth Games to her, so it doesn't really matter if it felt too easy for Australia at times.

Goodrem's medley led into a "festival of connection" supported by musicians in Highland dress and the appearances of Glasgow-based rapper Bemz and neo-traditional folk band Elephant Sessions.

Scotland's dual gold medallist Melanie Woods — who won the 400m T54 and 1500m T54 races — was handed the David Dixon Award for fair play and contribution to the Games.

Glasgow 2026 organising committee chair George Black hailed the city for putting on an "unforgettable" event.

"Together we have achieved something extraordinary and I am extremely proud of Glasgow," Black said in his address.

" Once again this city has shown the world who we are. "

The 2030 hosts, Amdavad, also known as Ahmedabad, gave a vision of the celebration to expect in four years' time.

The colourful and extravagant showcase was dubbed "The world is one family", and included performances by Indian artists Rashmika Mandanna and Shankar Mahadevan, amid a cast of about 200 dancers.

The Glasgow crowd was given a taste of Amdavad at the closing ceremony. (Getty: Mattia Ozbot)

Prince Edward, Duke of Edinburgh, formally closed the event, thanking athletes for their efforts.

"You have brought the spirit and values of the Commonwealth to life," the Duke said.

"You have inspired us and, hopefully, future generations. You have also demonstrated what unites us."

UK street dance group Diversity lit up the stage, bringing the crowd to its feet and another troupe performed a traditional Gaelic ceilidh with a modern twist.

But local lads Simple Minds had the final say, bringing down the curtain on Glasgow 2026 as fireworks lit up the sky from the Finnieston Crane to Govan Docks.

World.title: Australia's Rhiannan Iffland becomes greatest cliff diver of all time
World.content:
Australia's Rhiannan Iffland has officially become the greatest cliff diver of all time after winning the penultimate event of the season in Mostar, in southern Bosnia and Herzegovina.

The 34-year-old from Newcastle arrived at the historic bridge knowing that victory on Saturday local time from the 21m platform would seal her 10th World Series title in a row and 48th victory of her career.

An estimated 23,000 fans turned out across three days of competition to see Iffland tally 363.20 points, finishing ahead of Canada's Molly Carlson (361.60) and Australian Xantheia Pennisi (345.80) to again lift the King Kahekili Trophy.

Pennisi's 10th career podium came thanks to a personal best total score, while Stella Forsyth (276.15), the third Australian participating, came 10th in the 12-woman field.

Rhiannan Iffland is now a commanding 27 points ahead of her nearest rival in the standings. (Getty Images: Dean Treml)

"I'm super stoked, and I guess it's time to process and then celebrate," said Iffland, who entered the final round just 1.6 points ahead of Carlson in sweltering conditions.

"I knew deep down in my heart that it wasn't going to be an easy one today. I knew Molly wasn't going to leave without putting up a good fight."

Iffland's triumph — her 48th in 59 stops — moved her to 77 points after four of the five stops on tour, an unassailable 27 clear of Carlson, with compatriot Pennisi (35) fifth.

The win — thanks to a stunning inward three somersaults half twist tuck dive into the Neretva River — also moved Iffland ahead of Englishman Gary Hunt on the all-time wins list.

It is the third time she has wrapped up the title with a stop to spare.

Romania's Constantin Popovici (right) joined Australia's Rhiannon Iffland in celebrations after winning the men's event in Mostar. (Getty Images: Romina Amato)

"Forty-eight out of 50-something starts, it's nuts," the five-time high diving world champion added.

"But I guess the recipe really comes down to passion, and drive and hard work. There is no secret recipe to being so consistent. Practice, practice, practice, and it paid off for me."

The men's event was won by Romania's Constantin Popovici, who edged out Britain's Aidan Heslop and James Lichenstein of the United States.

Heslop leads the standings on 68 points, followed by Lichtenstein (57) and Popovici (55).

Divers now have an extended two-month break before the final event of the 2026 calendar takes place in Polignano a Mare, Italy — the home of European cliff diving — from September 27.

Tech.title: Rachika Nayar’s Heaven Come Crashing is an instrumental epic of desperate longing
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Two minutes and thirty seconds into the title track of Rachika Nayar’s Heaven Come Crashing, an absolutely massive drum and bass beat drops. As a fan of Nayar’s debut record Our Hands Against The Dusk, it caught me off guard. That album has no percussion on it at all. Heaven Comes Crashing is almost entirely drum-free, too. There are some rapid-fire mechanical hi-hats on the second track, “Tetramorph,” and the back half of track six, “Gayatri,” has what sounds like a snare buried deep in the mix. But it isn’t until track seven that Nayar delivers an unexpected drum explosion, before immediately retreating to the soothing wash of “Sleepless,” just one song later.

Nayar’s unique brand of guitar-heavy ambient-adjacent music plays almost like a version of M83 from an alternate universe. One where instead of turning to ‘80s pop music for inspiration, Anthony Gonzalez mined his instrumental epics for every last drop of emotion. Heaven Comes Crashing is as emotionally heavy as the title would imply but uses surprisingly few words to get there. The only vocals come courtesy of Maria BC, who floats over the title track and the stunning album closer “Our Wretched Fate,” where she worldlessly belts out her laments.

There are lyrics on “Heaven Comes Crashing,” but they’re almost indecipherable as Maria BC whispers beneath an ocean of flailing guitar lines and sparkling drones:

Is it morning? I don’t remember going to sleep How can we face the day Like this? You throw down your arms and count to see How deep it is

Instead of words, Nayar turns to heavily processed guitar, lonesome textures, and the occasional burst of trance chords to capture the desperate longing at the album’s core. But the album is also an indictment of the sort of abandon that often accompanies unbridled passion. It’s bookended by “Our Wretched Fantasy” and “Our Wretched Fate,” betraying a certain disgust for its own emotional recklessness. Track three isn’t “Death and Love”; it’s “Death and Limerence” — opting to spotlight unhealthy romantic obsession rather than fulfilling emotional partnership, through U2-esque guitar lines that eventually drown beneath heavily reverbed and out-of-tune tremolo-picked notes.

That’s followed by the unease of “Nausea,” which builds from an unsteady drone to maximalist panic of ‘90s synths and one of the simplest and prettiest guitar melodies on the record. The ambient emo of “Promises” follows, leading into “Gayatri,” which ratchets up the energy and serves as a bridge to the explosive title track.

Rachika Nayar’s Heaven Comes Crashing is available on Bandcamp and most major streaming services, including Apple Music, Spotify, YouTube Music, Qobuz, and Deezer.

Tech.title: Fender’s CEO seems to think your bandmates are just analog AI
Tech.content:
Cole’s philosophy is that AI in music is nothing new. “I think AI has existed in music as long as there’s been recorded music,” he says. While the biggest barrier to playing guitar is the time it takes to learn the instrument, it’s the second barrier, writing songs, where he believes AI plays a part.

“I actually believe cover music has been sort of analog AI for a long time,” says Cole. Those that don’t yet have the skills to write their own songs can play the songs written by their favourite artists instead. “I listened a lot to REM, U2, The Smiths and The Cure, and at some point I got sick of just listening to them. I wanted to play it, so I learned to play guitar.”

Those taking their first steps into writing, according to Cole, can also lean on a second analogue form of AI: their band mates. You might just have a chorus or a riff to start with but then the drummer or bassist can add to it, and a song is born. AI can also play this role. “I actually think that we are in the brink of freeing up people to move beyond the same old covers and to really get into working like they do with their bands,” says Cole.

Tech.title: Xbox prices are increasing by up to €200 or £170
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

When Microsoft announced its latest round of Xbox price bumps in June, it only gave US pricing. Now we know the pricing increases for the EU and UK, and they’re dramatic. Depending on the model, Xbox prices are increasing by up to €200 or £170. The 1TB Xbox Series X with a disc drive is going up by over 30 percent from £499.99 / €599.99 to £669.99 / €799.99. The 512GB Xbox Series S is getting a price increase of over 43 percent, jumping from £299.99 / €349.99 to £429.99 / €499.99.

While other consoles have received price bumps as RAM and storage prices skyrocket due to demand from the AI industry, none have been quite as dramatic as Microsoft’s. This is the third round of price increases since May of 2025, with the highest-end model now costing $300 more than its launch price of $499.99 in 2020. The 2TB model is also being retired in the face of the storage crunch. Here’s the full list of price changes:

Tech.title: Skylight’s smart calendars are up to $90 off during its back-to-school sale
Tech.content:
The start of a new school year can feel hectic, as parents juggle their kids’ classes, extracurriculars and sports on top of work, appointments, and other responsibilities. It’s easy for things to slip through the cracks, but Skylight’s shared smart calendars can help keep everyone on track, and from August 2nd through August 9th they’re up to $90 off.

The sale includes the 10-inch Skylight Calendar for $119.99 ($50 off), the 15-inch Skylight Calendar 2 for $259.99 ($20 off), and the 27-inch Skylight Calendar Max for $479.99 ($90 off). The 10-inch model takes up the least amount of space, though the newer, larger 15-inch Calendar 2 features faster performance, a brighter display, and swappable magnetic frames. The 27-inch Calendar Max, meanwhile, offers the sharpest and largest screen and must be mounted to the wall (the other models can stand on a table or be mounted), making it the easiest option for large families to view from across the room.

Regardless of which model you choose, every Skylight Calendar includes the same set of organizational features. Each member of your household can have their own color-coded profile, and each can sync events from Google, Outlook, Apple, Cozi, or Yahoo calendars. You can also create shared lists for groceries, chores, and other to-dos that everyone can access from the calendar or the companion mobile app, and even send your grocery list to Instacart with a couple of taps. Built-in weather forecasts also can help you plan around upcoming events, and you can also share calendar access with family members and trusted contacts.

You get even more perks if you subscribe to the $79 per year Plus Plan (the first month of the service is free to try). Skylight uses AI to automatically turn emails, photos, flyers, and spreadsheets into calendar entries. It also adds meal planning, tools for assigning and rewarding completed chores, and a mode that displays your photos like a digital picture frame.

Tech.title: HP’s HyperX Omen 15 isn’t quite the budget-friendly gaming laptop its predecessor was
Tech.content:
is a reviewer covering laptops and the occasional gadget. He spent over 15 years in the photography industry before joining The Verge as a deals writer in 2021.

The HP HyperX Omen 15, which I first saw at CES, replaces the HP Victus 15, a longtime bestselling budget gaming laptop. The Victus cost just $800, or less when on sale, and was a good entry point to decent laptop gaming.

The Omen 15 has nice little upgrades over the Victus. Its RTX 5050 Laptop GPU can play 2026’s latest games, albeit on low-ish settings. But it’s also got a brighter 16:10 aspect ratio display with higher refresh rate, and a 1080p webcam to make it a little better for non-gaming stuff.

I’d call it a working-class gaming laptop, but thanks to RAMageddon, the Omen 15 starts at $1,200 — a far cry from the $800 that made its predecessor so appealing. But laptop prices are way up across the board, and if you want current-gen gaming hardware, this is about as cheap as you’re going to find it.

Our HyperX Omen 15 review unit is a $1,199 configuration sold through Walmart with an eight-core Intel Core 5 210H “Raptor Lake” chip, RTX 5050 discreet GPU, 16GB of DDR5 RAM, and 512GB SSD. There are pricier Omen 15 configs out there with RTX 5070 GPUs and OLED screens, but that’s like spending Acura money on a Honda Civic. On the lower end, HP still has a Victus 15 config with the RTX 5050 for $900, but it has 8GB of RAM — that’s not really tenable, especially for playing the latest games.

The good news is that the Omen 15 with an RTX 5050 is pretty serviceable for playing games at its 1920 x 1200 native resolution. Last-gen games like Control can get a smooth 70 to 80fps on High preset while using DLSS. Cyberpunk 2077 can run on the Ultra preset (no ray tracing) with DLSS set to Quality and get 60 to 70fps— sometimes dipping down to 40 while driving with lots of stuff onscreen. Standard frame generation boosts it to 95 to 105fps, and 70s to low 80s in a car. Multi Frame Gen, which you don’t get on last-gen GPUs, can push that ever further if you don’t mind more “fake frames.”

Newer games are a more Medium to Low affair. For example, Helldivers 2 runs comfortably at just above 60fps on its Medium preset with DLSS set to Quality — though it dips into the 40s when the bug guts hit the fan. But Battlefield 6 was lower, down in the 50fps range while running Medium preset with DLSS cranked to Performance. I also tested Halo: Campaign Evolved, which defaulted to its Very Low preset, where it looked like a potato. On Low settings, with DLSS set to Medium, it mustered between 50 to 60fps, but with frequent drops into the 40s with lots of enemies onscreen.

On the right, an ethernet jack and one USB-A. On the left, a 3.5mm audio jack, one USB-A, and the power connector. On the rear, HDMI 2.1 and one USB-C. Seriously, where’s the rest?

While playing all these games, the fans kicked up to a decent volume, but they weren’t obnoxiously loud, and the chassis stayed reasonably cool. The hottest point, a small spot under the chassis, rose to 113 degrees Fahrenheit / 45 Celsius. But the main areas that normally make contact with your hands or lap didn’t get too warm — pretty good thermals for a somewhat compact gaming laptop.

So the RTX 5050 GPU and its 8GB of VRAM can get by with the latest graphically intense games, so long as you’re not expecting a visual powerhouse. But what about living with the rest of the laptop?

Much of the Omen 15’s price has gone to its specs. That means there are some rough edges showing in the usual areas. The trackpad has a responsive mechanical click, but if you pick up the laptop by either of its front corners the chassis flexes and causes an accidental click. This is common in mostly plastic laptops, but still annoying.

The keyboard has decent enough tactility when typing. But even though I know gamers love a number pad, it makes this 15-inch laptop feel cramped. I don’t enjoy typing on it like I have other HP laptops. The speakers? A little muddy-sounding — especially for music. And the ports? It has HDMI 2.1 and gigabit ethernet, which is great, but only one USB-C to go with its two USB-A ports. And all of them are a modest 10Gbps — not particularly speedy compared to USB4 or Thunderbolt 4. Gaming laptops are supposed to have ports aplenty, but this is just ports apassable.

Previous Next











1 / 7 The screen does a decent job controlling glare.

Aside from its gaming performance, the Omen 15’s other strength is its screen. The 1920 x 1200 IPS panel isn’t particularly special, but at 400 nits it’s decently bright and it has nice contrast and colors. It’s good for games, and fine for productivity work and light content creation. I did a bit of Lightroom Classic editing on the Omen 15, and my 50-megapixel RAW files were workable at a modest clip. (It helped that I was editing a batch of under 50 images, and not, like, 2,000.) The bigger problem with trying to do creative things was the Omen’s paltry 512GB of storage. It fills up quickly when games like Battlefield 6 take up 142GB. There’s a second M.2 slot for another drive, just as there’s a second RAM slot, which is great for future upgrades — but boy will that cost you right now. You can hold out for RAM and SSD prices to come back down to Earth, but if that takes as long as it’s expected to, the Omen 15 might feel pretty outdated by then.

The Omen was also fine for my everyday work: Chrome tabs, four virtual desktops, Signal, Slack, music streaming, etc. While the 1080p webcam is a little grainy and slightly low in saturation, it looks fine on video calls. The main barrier to getting work done on the Omen 15 is that its battery never lasted me more than five and a half hours. That’s far from the worst for gaming laptops, but keep that chunky power adapter with its barrel plug nearby.

That HyperX lid logo still doesn’t look great to me, but I’m getting used to ignoring it.

The HyperX Omen 15 is a decent gaming laptop. It’s just not the value the Victus 15 used to be. But neither is anything else. Absent a really good sale, you’re going to pay over $1,000 for anything with the RTX 5050, and usually a lot more. But buying into even the bottom rung of the 50-series gets you all of Nvidia’s latest features, like Multi Frame Gen and whatever DLSS 5 eventually shapes up to be. Last-gen 40-series or AMD GPUs aren’t bad options, but Multi Frame Gen can help keep frame rates playable for longer.

It’s still worth looking for those sales, though. HP, Best Buy, and Walmart often have deals on most of HP’s product line. Even now, there’s an Omen 16 with an RTX 5060 GPU and slightly larger (but dimmer) screen for just $100 more than the Omen 15.

RAMageddon makes buying a new gaming laptop daunting. If you need to buy now and you don’t want to go open-box or secondhand, you just have to come to terms with the fact that you’re going to be paying higher prices than equivalent models from a year or two ago — even in the “entry level.” Considering the circumstances, the Omen 15 is an okay value at $1,200 for getting into laptop gaming.

Tech.title: Is paying artists enough to convince them to embrace AI?
Tech.content:
is a reporter focusing on film, TV, and pop culture. Before The Verge, he wrote about comic books, labor, race, and more at io9 and Gizmodo for almost five years.

Illustrators have spent years sounding the alarm about generative artificial intelligence startups training their models on artists’ work without permission. They’ve pointed out how the practice is tantamount to theft, and in response, many gen AI boosters have argued that it’s necessary for the technology’s evolution. This has led to contentious legal battles, but it’s also given rise to a new wave of AI startups like Pippa that market their services as being more ethical than the competition.

Like most companies selling access to text-to-video models, Pippa’s main product is short bursts of user-generated footage that can be cobbled together to tell visual stories. But what sets Pippa apart from other players in the gen AI video space is the way its business model is designed to pay artists directly. Every time a Pippa subscriber generates an image or a video clip whose style is derived from a human artist’s work, that artist is compensated by the platform.

Pippa’s cofounders, Hogan Shrum and Sean Wright, think that their focus on working with artists is what will attract customers. They also believe that their company will prove that AI firms can generate content ethically. But Pippa faces an uphill battle as it seeks to convince artists. Even as it tries to create an ethical spin on AI video generation, the company is still getting off the ground with the same sloppy models that other text-to-video services offer.

A shot from a video created with Pippa. Image: Pippa

When I recently spoke with Shrum and Wright, they told me that they see Pippa as a way to move forward from “the bloody history that the AI industry has been built on.” The duo want to set an example for their peers and show the public how AI companies don’t necessarily have to steal to make their products work.

“All of these models from the past 18 months have been trained on real people’s art without their permission — that’s how it was built,” Wright said. “I harken it back to when Napster was a thing and everybody was stealing music. But then, Apple came out with the 99-cent song, Napster got shut down, and we figured out a different way to get musical artists paid.”

Pippa’s payments to artists aren’t very large on an individual basis — especially when you compare them to how much the service charges users for monthly subscriptions (which range from $14.99 to $99.99.) The company says that artists receive $0.005 per image and $0.003 per second of video. The more generations a user makes, the larger an artist’s payments become, and Pippa also gives them access to a cut of a 5 percent royalty pool that’s funded by the platform’s overall subscription revenue. In Pippa’s press materials, the company likens its royalty payment structure to Spotify’s — a curious choice given how many artists have spoken out about being shafted by the music streamer.

Pippa’s tech still involves using art that was scraped from the internet

Pippa — which launched in May — currently has around 800 paying subscribers, and while the company has only signed licensing / model training agreements with four human artists, Shrum said they are in talks to bring four more into the fold. Artists interested in working with Pippa must first go through a multi-step vetting process to verify that the illustrations they submit are actually theirs. Once an illustrator is approved, models trained on their art become available to Pippa’s subscribers. Additionally, the service provides artists a profile page, which can be used to direct people to their work outside of the platform. But Wright noted that Pippa also gives its partner artists the option to submit their work under pseudonyms if they are concerned about being seen as “crossing the picket line.”

“We’ve had so many conversations with artists where they’re like, ‘I love this, but I don’t want to get ostracized by my community,’” Wright explained. “We’re very early in this space, so there’s some apprehension to participate in it. But we think that can change as people see the economics of how we’re paying artists and that our intent is good.”

Though Pippa hopes to fully switch to models that are trained on datasets provided by its in-house artists, that technology is still built with open models that the company says “have initial training on the broader set of content out there.” Put more bluntly, Pippa’s tech still involves some degree of using art that was scraped from the internet without creators’ express consent. The company’s intentions may be good, but it doesn’t exactly have a way to completely solve for the creative theft that’s inherent to gen AI.

A shot from a video created with Pippa. Image: Pippa

That issue isn’t unique to Pippa; it’s something that must be considered with every “ethical” AI startup whose bespoke models are trained on information that wasn’t created internally. This is why some companies — like Ben Affleck’s InterPositive — have made a point of emphasizing the fact that they develop wholly original, proprietary datasets of their own. But that requires a lot of upfront capital most startups don’t have access to, and the end result is usually very specialized AI tools that aren’t exactly designed for general consumers.

Scrolling through Pippa’s online portal where you can watch other people’s gen AI animations or prompt up your own, I didn’t see all that much that looked very different from what you would find from other text-to-video services. Right now, the site is mostly filled with kid-oriented content that’s doing a poor job of imitating Pixar’s polished aesthetics, and nothing really looks like it was inspired by an independent artist’s hand.

This makes some sense given that — while Pippa intends to incorporate more original art styles — it still uses many of the same cloud-based models that other platforms sell access to. In the near future, Pippa plans to incorporate ByteDance’s Seedance 2.5 model into its service, which may attract some subscribers because of the model’s ability to generate up to 30 seconds of video footage that can be fine-tuned without starting over from scratch. But in order for Pippa to really stand out from competitors that also offer Seedance 2.5, it will need to sign more in-house artists, which will depend on how well the company is able to pitch itself to potential partners.

Shrum and Wright believe that they will find more artists to work with, and that using Pippa will convince them to sell their communities on the idea of joining as well. In order for that to happen, though, public opinion about whether they really want to use gen AI would need to shift back in the technology’s favor.

Tech.title: Foldables are sort of boring now — and that’s great news for Apple
Tech.content:
This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on smartphones and Android, follow Dominic Preston. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes on Sunday at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here.

How it started

Believe it or not, it didn’t all start with Samsung. Royole, a now-bankrupt manufacturer of flexible displays, was the first to release a commercial folding phone, the “charmingly awful” FlexPai. Samsung’s first Galaxy Fold followed a year later, plagued by a variety of faults that saw review units break within days. That launch went so badly that it prompted Chinese rival Huawei to delay the launch of its own Mate X foldable by five months; its unusual design with the foldable screen wrapped around the outside of the phone proved unpopular regardless. Motorola was next to join with its first Razr foldable, closely followed by Samsung’s similar Z Flip; we scored each 4/10 and 6/10 respectively.

To say it was a rough first two years for foldable phones would be an understatement, but things did get better. Samsung’s subsequent generations of foldables didn’t break half as easily as the first wave, and it learned the valuable lesson that integral parts of the display stack shouldn’t be as easy to remove as a screen protector.

More manufacturers joined the market, with foldables launched by Google, OnePlus, Oppo, Vivo, Xiaomi, Honor, and more. Prices slowly came down too — while flagship book-style foldables have hovered more or less around the $2,000 mark for seven years straight, cheaper models have appeared too. Motorola’s entry-level Razr is now $799, and last year Samsung introduced a cheaper FE variant of its Z Flip 7, for $899.

The hardware evolved over that period too. Foldables got thinner, lighter, and more durable; the creases got flatter and less visible, while some displays began to include stylus support too; the cameras started to catch up to standard slab phones. Perhaps most importantly, the form factors began to shift too.

How it’s going

Until recently, foldable phones settled into two broad categories: compact flip phones, by now with square cover screens that extend across the outside of the phone’s front; and larger book-style foldables that are thin when shut and almost square when open.

Durability has improved to the point where Google’s Pixel 10 Pro Fold was able to introduce an IP68 rating; Honor’s Magic V6 has since one-upped that with IP69. That phone is also the thinnest foldable on the market, and the one with the largest battery, two feats that have been made possible by silicon-carbon battery designs, a more energy-dense technology that enables smaller batteries with larger capacities. The latest foldables are barely thicker than flagship slab phones when closed, and almost as thin as the USB-C port when open, while packing batteries that last a day or two per charge.

Oppo’s Find N6 is almost as thin and long-lived as the Honor phone, but has another trick up its sleeve: an almost invisible crease. It’s still possible to see and feel the point where the inner screen folds, but only if you really hunt for it, and even then it can often be difficult to find depending on the light.

As for cameras, this remains the one area where foldables still have work to do, but not too much. Recent foldables from Oppo and Vivo have had triple rear cameras capable of impressive quality, comparable to some slab flagships. But they still lag behind the top tier of Ultra handsets, while costing substantially more. Still, this may be one area where foldables never fully catch up — cost and design constraints likely mean that the best of the best cameras will be limited to regular phones for the foreseeable future, with foldables always a step or two behind.

Despite all these improvements, foldable phones remain an undeniably niche proposition: according to Counterpoint, they made up just 1.6 percent of the smartphone market in 2025.

What happens next

The tech behind foldable phones is now mature enough for even Apple to trust it: The first foldable iPhone is widely expected to debut next month alongside the iPhone 18 Pro models. The looming launch will be “a turning point for the foldable segment,” according to IDC analyst Francisco Jeronimo, in a report predicting Apple will claim 34 percent of the foldable market by value in its first year.

What remains to be seen is whether Apple will have the influence to grow the foldable market, drawing in customers who were skeptical until now, or simply waiting for a foldable that runs iOS. This could be the tipping point that pulls foldables from a niche to the mainstream, though assuming Apple prices the phone at a premium, there will still be pretty strict limits to its reach.

Even before its first sale, the foldable iPhone has already had an impact. Remember Huawei and Samsung’s wider folds? It’s probably no surprise that they appeared just months before Apple’s foldable, which leaks suggest will be similarly wide. More companies are likely to jump on the bandwagon, with leaks pointing to wider folds from both Oppo and Honor on the way. The next 12 months will be the test of whether this form factor is truly more popular with users, or if Android manufacturers will regret hopping on the Apple bandwagon.

It’s less clear if more manufacturers will be making trifolds, or even whether Huawei and Samsung will stick with that form factor. Huawei has made bullish claims about the sales success of its two Mate XT phones, so there’s hope it will stick with the design. Samsung, on the other hand, pulled its TriFold from the market after less than three months, though it’s unclear if that was down to low sales or simply a small manufacturing run. Rollables and other experimental form factors will likely have to wait a few more years before being commercialized.

This is a moment of major change for foldable phones. The standard models have gotten so good that they’ve become a bit boring. Outside of new form factors, the annual releases have settled into a rhythm of minor iteration, and price is now the only real reason for consumers to resist them. Foldables are undeniably good enough now, and Apple’s arrival will either open the market up more widely, or prove once and for all that most phone buyers simply don’t care about phones that fold — or at least not at the prices being charged.
